## Commentary on the Book of the Fives, etc.
## Aṅguttara Commentary
## Homage to Him, the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.
## Book of the Fives
## 1. The First Fifty
## 1. Chapter on the Powers of the Trainee
## 1. Commentary on the Brief Discourse
In the first discourse of the Book of the Fives, they are called 'Powers of the Trainee' (sekhabala) because they are the powers of the seven types of trainees (sekha). Among the powers such as the power of faith (saddhābala), it is called the power of faith because it is unshakable by the unwholesome state of lack of faith. It is called the power of moral shame (hirībala) because it is unshakable by shamelessness (ahirika). It is called the power of moral dread (ottappabala) because it is unshakable by fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappa). It is called the power of energy (vīriyabala) because it is unshakable by laziness (kosajja). It is called the power of wisdom (paññābala) because it is unshakable by ignorance (avijjā). Since these five powers are the strengths of the seven types of trainees, it is said, 'tasmā' (therefore).

## 2. Commentary on the Detailed Discourse
In the second discourse, in the words beginning with 'kāyaduccaritena', the instrumental case is used in the sense of the accusative case. The meaning is that one is ashamed of and loathes bodily misconduct and so forth, which are things to be ashamed of. In the explanation of moral dread (ottappa-niddesa), the instrumental case is used in the sense of cause (hetu). The meaning is that one is afraid and dreads because of bodily misconduct and so forth, which are the causes of dread.

'Āraddhavīriyo' means having aroused energy, thus possessing an undaunted mind. 'Pahānāya' means for the sake of abandoning. 'Upasampadāya' means for the sake of attainment. 'Thāmavā' means being endowed with the strength of energy. 'Daḷhaparakkamo' means having firm effort. 'Anikkhittadhuro kusalesu dhammesu' means having a burden that is not laid down in blameless and noble wholesome states, thus possessing undiminished energy. 'Udayatthagāminiyā' refers to wisdom that knows the arising and passing away of the five aggregates, being capable of penetrating their arising and passing away. 'Ariyāya' means noble; it refers to being endowed with pure wisdom because it is far from defilements through the power of suppression (vikkhambhana) and the power of eradication (samuccheda). 'Nibbedhikāya' means penetrative; because that insight wisdom and path wisdom penetrate defilements, they are called 'nibbedhika'; the meaning is being endowed with the wisdom that penetrates those defilements.

Between those two, insight wisdom and path wisdom, path wisdom is called 'nibbedhika' because it penetrates and breaks through the mass of greed, the mass of hatred, and the mass of delusion that were never before penetrated or broken through by the power of eradication. Insight wisdom is also called 'nibbedhika' because it penetrates and breaks through the mass of greed, the mass of hatred, and the mass of delusion by the power of temporary abandonment (tadaṅga). Alternatively, insight wisdom deserves to be called 'nibbedhika' because it leads to the attainment of path wisdom. In the phrase 'sammā dukkhakkhayagāminiyā', path wisdom is called 'sammā dukkhakkhayagāminī' because it leads to the destruction of the suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha) and the suffering of defilements (kilesa-dukkha) through the right means. Insight wisdom...
2:
One with aroused energy means one with exerted energy and an undaunted mind. 'For the sake of abandoning' means for the purpose of abandoning. 'For the sake of fulfilling' means for the purpose of attainment. 'One with strength' means one endowed with the strength of energy. 'One with firm effort' means one with steady effort. 'One who has not laid down the burden in wholesome states' means one who does not put down the burden in wholesome states, possessing undiminished energy.

'Leading to arising and passing away' refers to wisdom that leads to the arising and passing away of the five aggregates, being capable of penetrating arising and passing away. 'Endowed with wisdom' means one who is possessed of both insight wisdom and path wisdom. 'Noble' refers to wisdom that stands far from defilements through the power of suppression and eradication, being pure. 'Penetrative' means that because that wisdom penetrates (defilements), it is called 'nibbedhika'; the meaning is being endowed with that wisdom. Between those two kinds of wisdom, path wisdom is called 'nibbedhika' because it penetrates and breaks through the mass of greed, the mass of hatred, and the mass of delusion never before penetrated or broken through by the power of eradication. Insight wisdom is called 'nibbedhika' by the power of temporary abandonment. Alternatively, that insight wisdom should be called 'nibbedhika' because it leads to the attainment of path wisdom. In the phrase 'leading to the right destruction of suffering', path wisdom is called 'sammā dukkhakkhayagāminī' because it leads to the destruction of the suffering of the round and the suffering of defilements through the right means. Insight wisdom is called 'dukkhakkhayagāminī' because it leads to the destruction of the suffering of the round and the suffering of defilements by the power of temporary abandonment. Or, this insight wisdom should be understood as 'dukkhakkhayagāminī' because it leads to the attainment of path wisdom which is 'dukkhakkhayagāminī'. Thus, in this discourse, the five powers are taught as a mixture (of mundane and supramundane); the same applies to the fifth discourse.

## 6. Commentary on the Attainment Discourse
In the sixth discourse, 'attainment of the unwholesome' means the attainment of unwholesome states, the meaning being the state of being possessed of them. 'Stands having overwhelmed' means stands having enveloped and shrouded.

## 7. Commentary on the Sensual Pleasures Discourse
In the seventh discourse, 'those who sport in sensual pleasures' refers to those who sport and delight in objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) and defilement-based sensuality (kilesa-kāma). 'Sickle and carrying pole' refers to a grass-cutting sickle and a pole for carrying grass. 'A son of good family' means a son of good family who is endowed with good conduct. 'Having abandoned' means having left behind.
3:
"Alaṃ vacanāya" means it is fit for speaking. "Labbhā" means easily obtainable or possible to obtain. "Hīnā kāmā" refers to the sensual pleasures of the five low-born classes. "Majjhimā kāmā" refers to the sensual pleasures of middle-class beings. "Paṇītā kāmā" refers to the sensual pleasures of kings and their great ministers. "Kāmātveva saṅkhaṃ gacchanti" means they are called "sensual pleasures" (kāma) either by the power of the sense-objects themselves or by the power of being enjoyed. "Vuddho hoti" means he is aged. "Alaṃpañño" means one endowed with suitable wisdom. "Attagutto" means one who is guarded by oneself, or one who is capable of guarding oneself securely. "Nālaṃ pamādāya" means it is not fit for negligence. "Saddhāya akataṃ hoti" means that which should be done with faith regarding wholesome states is not done. In the remaining terms, the method should be understood in this same way. In the phrase "Monks, I am no longer concerned with that monk," it shows that when a person has performed what should be done through faith and so on, and is established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala), the Buddha is no longer concerned [about their progress]. In this sutta, the path of Stream-entry (Sotāpattimagga) is taught.

## 8. Cavana-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the eighth sutta, the Cavana Sutta, "saddhamme" means in the good Dhamma, which is the Dispensation (sāsana). "Assaddho" means one who is devoid of both types of faith: the faith of conviction (okappana-saddhā) and the faith of entering into (pakkhandana-saddhā). "Cavati nappatiṭṭhāti" means he falls away from virtues such as morality (sīla) and concentration (samādhi) in this Dispensation and is unable to stand firm. Thus, in this sutta, the inability to stand firm and the ability to stand firm in the Dispensation are taught.

## 9. Paṭhama-agārava-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the ninth sutta, the First Agārava Sutta, "nāssa gāravo" means one who has no respect (agārava). "Nāssa patisso" means one who is not obedient (appatissa), meaning one who has no superior and no humility. The remaining words in this sutta are just like the previous ones.

## 10. Dutiya-agārava-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the tenth sutta, the Second Agārava Sutta, "abhabbo" means one who is not a fit vessel (abhājana). "Vuddhiṃ" means growth in morality (sīla). "Virūḷhiṃ" means the state of being unshakable due to being firmly rooted. "Vepullaṃ" means the state of greatness. The remaining words are clear in meaning in all places.

## 2. Bala-vaggo
## 1. Ananussuta-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the second chapter, "Monks, in things unheard before by me" means, monks, in the four Truths (Sacca-dhamma) not heard before by me. "I claim to have reached the perfection of the end through direct knowledge" means that by performing the sixteenfold task through the four paths regarding the four Truths, having known them through direct knowledge, and having reached the other shore of decision because all tasks are completed, I claim to have reached the state of one who has done what was to be done (katakicca). By this, the Buddha shows his attained qualities at the seat of Great Enlightenment (Mahābodhi). "Tathāgatassa" means of the Buddha who is called "Tathāgata" for eight reasons. "Tathāgatabalāni" means the powers of knowledge that have proceeded in the same way as the previous Buddhas have gone. "Āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ" means the supreme place (or state). "Sီဟနာဒံ" means the fearless sound (lion's roar). "Brahmacakkaṃ" means the supreme wheel. "Pavatteti" means he teaches.

## 2. Kူဋ-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, "sekhabalāni" means the powers of knowledge of the trainees (sekhas). "Aggaṃ" means the foremost (the summit). Just as the peak (ridgepole) of a house encompasses the rafters, it is called "saṅgāhika" (inclusive) because it encompasses the remaining powers. It is called "saṅghātaniya" (unifying) because it causes those same powers to be united.

## 3. Saṅkhitta-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, among those powers of a trainee, it is called "satibala" (power of mindfulness) because it does not waver due to forgetfulness (muṭṭhassacca). It is called "samādhibala" (power of concentration) because it does not waver due to restlessness (uddhacca).

## 4. Vitthata-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, in the term "satinepakkena," "nepakka" means wisdom (paññā); that wisdom is taken as being helpful to mindfulness.

## 5. Daṭṭhabba-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, in order to teach the mundane and supramundane states that occur only within his own domain, the Buddha said, "Monks, where should the power of faith be seen?" and so on. For example, four sons of wealthy merchants and a king—these five friends, including the king—descended to the main street saying, "We shall play at the festival of the stars." When they arrived at the house of one of the merchant's sons, the others...
5:
Among five friends, four remain silent; only the wealthy man who is the house-owner manages the household, saying, "Give these people food and snacks; give them perfumes, garlands, ornaments, and so on." When going to the houses of the second, third, and fourth wealthy men, the other four remain silent; only the wealthy man who is the house-owner manages the household, saying, "Give these people food and snacks; give them perfumes, garlands, ornaments, and so on." Then, finally, when going to the King's house, although the King is the ruler of all places, on this occasion of the festival, he manages only his own house, saying, "Give these people food and snacks; give them perfumes, garlands, ornaments, and so on."

In the same way, although the five powers such as faith (saddhā) arise together on a single object like friends, just as the other four remain silent in the first wealthy man's house and only the house-owner manages, when reaching the factors of stream-entry (sotāpattiyanga), only the power of faith (saddhā-bala), which has the characteristic of decision (adhimokkha), is the leader and precursor; the remaining states follow that power of faith. Just as the other four remain silent in the second wealthy man's house and only the house-owner manages, when reaching the right efforts (sammappadhāna), only the power of energy (viriya-bala), which has the characteristic of exertion (paggaha), is the leader and precursor; the remaining states follow that power of energy. Just as the other four remain silent in the third wealthy man's house and only the house-owner manages, when reaching the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), only the power of mindfulness (sati-bala), which has the characteristic of establishment (upaṭṭhāna), is the leader and precursor; the remaining states follow that power of mindfulness. Just as the other four remain silent in the fourth wealthy man's house and only the house-owner manages, when reaching the jhānas and liberations (vimokkha), only the power of concentration (samādhi-bala), which has the characteristic of non-distraction (avikkhepa), is the leader and precursor; the remaining states follow that power of concentration. Finally, just as the other four remain silent when going to the King's house and only the King manages, when reaching the Noble Truths (ariyasacca), only the power of wisdom (paññā-bala), which has the characteristic of discerning (pajānana), is the leader and precursor; the remaining states follow that power of wisdom. Thus, in this sutta, the five powers are spoken of in a mixed manner.

The sixth sutta has an obvious meaning. Thus, in the eight suttas of both the previous chapter and this chapter, only the powers of a trainee (sekha-bala) are spoken of. However, the Elder Mahādatta, who resided at the Karaṇḍakola Monastery, said, "In the lower four suttas, the powers of a trainee are spoken of, and in the upper four suttas, the powers of one beyond training (asekha-bala) are spoken of."

## 7. Paṭhamahitasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, virtue and so on are spoken of only in a mixed manner. "Liberation" (vimutti) refers only to the liberation of the fruition of Arahantship (arahattaphala-vimutti). "Knowledge and vision of liberation" (vimutti-ñāṇadassana) is reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa), and that knowledge is only mundane (lokiya).

## 3. Pañcaṅgikavagga

## 1. Paṭhama-agāravasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the first sutta of the third chapter, "asabhāgavuttiko" means one who is endowed with a dissimilar (visadisa) livelihood. "Abhisamācārikaṃ dhammaṃ" refers to the virtue prescribed by way of the duties (vatta) which constitute the higher conduct. "Sekhaṃ dhammaṃ" refers to the virtue prescribed for trainees (sekha). "Sīlāni" refers to the four great virtues. "Sammādiṭṭhi" refers to insight right view (vipassanā-sammādiṭṭhi). "Sammāsamādhi" refers to both path concentration (magga-samādhi) and fruition concentration (phala-samādhi). In this sutta, virtue and so on are spoken of in a mixed manner.

## 2. Dutiya-agāravasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, "sīlakkhandha" means the aggregate of virtue. In the remaining two terms as well, the method is the same. These three aggregates are also spoken of only in a mixed manner.

## 3. Upakkilesasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, "na ca pabhassaraṃ" means not radiant. "Pabhaṅgu ca" means having the nature of perishing. "Ayo" means black iron. "Lohaṃ" in this sutta refers to metals other than the four substances mentioned. "Sajjhaṃ" means silver. "Cittassa" refers to the wholesome mind of the four planes. Let the defilements (upakkilesa) be for the minds of the three planes; how are they defilements for the supramundane mind? They are defilements by way of not allowing it to arise. Because they do not allow it to arise, for that very reason, they are called defilements for both the mundane and the supramundane. "Pabhaṅgu ca" means having the nature of perishing by reaching the state of being crushed to pieces upon the object. "Sammā samādhiyati āsavānaṃ khayāya" means it is rightly concentrated for the sake of Arahantship, which is the destruction of the taints (āsava), by way of cause and reason.
7:
By this much, he shows the Arahant who has purified the mind and is established in the fruition of Arahantship. Now, wishing to show the Arahant's penetration of supernormal knowledges (abhiññā), he said the words beginning with "Yassa yassa ca." This statement has an obvious meaning.

## 4. Dussīlasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the fourth discourse, the Dussīla Sutta, "hatūpaniso" means having a destroyed support or a destroyed cause. "Yathābhūta-ñāṇadassanaṃ" is tender insight knowledge beginning with the knowledge of defining mentality and materiality (nāmarūpa-pariccheda-ñāṇa). "Nibbidā-virāgo" refers to both weariness (nibbidā) and dispassion (virāga). Among these two, nibbidā is strong insight, and virāga is the Noble Path. "Vimutti-ñāṇadassanaṃ" refers to liberation, which is the fruition of Arahantship, and reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa).

## 5. Anuggahitasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the fifth discourse, the Anuggahita Sutta, "sammādiṭṭhi" is insight right view. In the words beginning with "cetovimutti-phalā," "cetovimutti" is concentration associated with the Path and Fruition, and "paññāvimutti" is fruition knowledge. "Sīlānuggahitā" means supported by virtue; "sutānuggahitā" means supported by learning and knowledge; "sākacchānuggahitā" means accomplished through Dhamma discussion; "samathānuggahitā" means accomplished through tranquility of mind (samatha).

To clarify this meaning, an analogy should be given of a man who tends a mango tree by planting a sweet mango seed, building an embankment around it, watering it from time to time, cleaning the roots, removing pests that have fallen on it, and destroying spider webs. The man's planting of the sweet mango seed is like insight right view. Building the embankment is like being supported by virtue. Watering is like being supported by learning (suta). Cleaning the roots is like being supported by Dhamma discussion. Removing pests is like being supported by tranquility (samatha), which is the purification of the dangers of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) that obstruct jhāna and insight. Destroying spider webs is like being supported by strong insight. Just as the mango tree thus tended grows quickly and bears fruit, the basic right view supported by virtue and so on should be understood to grow quickly by the power of the Path and yield the fruit of liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.

## 6. Vimuttāyatanasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the sixth discourse, the Vimuttāyatana Sutta, "vimuttāyatanāni" means the causes for liberation from suffering. "Yattha" means in which bases of liberation. "The Teacher teaches the Dhamma" means he teaches the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. "Atthapaṭisaṃvedino" refers to one who correctly knows the meaning of the Pali text, such as virtue, concentration, and wisdom. "Dhammapaṭisaṃvedino" refers to one who correctly knows the Pali text that expresses the meaning. "Pāmojja" is tender joy. "Pīti" is strong joy in the form of appreciation. "Kāya" is the mental body (nāmakāya). "Passambhati" means it becomes tranquil. "Sukhaṃ vedeti" means one obtains happiness. "Cittaṃ samādhiyati" means the mind becomes concentrated through the concentration of Arahantship fruition.

In truth, the monk who listens to that Pali Dhamma knows insight, Path, and Fruition at every opportunity. Joy arises in such a monk. Without allowing any retreat in the midst of that joy, he becomes one with access-meditation (upacāra-kammaṭṭhāna), develops insight, and reaches Arahantship. With reference to that meaning, it is said, "the mind becomes concentrated." In the remaining terms, the method is the same. This, however, is the distinction: "samādhinimitta" is concentration itself among the thirty-eight meditation objects. In the words beginning with "suggahitaṃ hoti," it means well-grasped, well-attended, and well-borne when learning the meditation subject from a teacher. "Suppaṭividdhaṃ paññāya" means well-realized through wisdom. "Tasmiṃ dhamme" means in that Pali Dhamma expressing the meditation subject. Thus, in this discourse, all five bases of liberation are taught as leading to Arahantship.

## 7. Samādhisutta-vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the seventh discourse, the Samādhi Sutta, "appamāṇa" is the supramundane Dhamma free from limiting factors. "Nipakā patissatā" means being endowed with wisdom that crushes defilements and with mindfulness. "Pañca ñāṇāni" are the five reviewing knowledges. "Paccattaññeva uppajjanti" means they arise only within oneself. In the words beginning with "this concentration is pleasant in the present," the concentration associated with Arahantship fruition is intended. Some also call it Path concentration.

That concentration is "presently pleasant" (paccuppanna-sukha) because it is happy at every moment of attainment. It has a "future happy result" (āyatiṃ sukhavipāka) because preceding concentration-happiness is the cause for subsequent concentration-happiness. It is "Noble" (ariya) because it is far from defilements. It is "unworldly" (nirāmisa) because of the absence of the baits of sensuality, the round of rebirth, and the world. It is "practiced by Great Men" (akāpurisasevito) because it is cultivated by the Buddha and other great beings. It is "peaceful" (santa) because of the tranquility of factors, objects, and the distress of all defilements. It is "exalted" (paṇīta) in the sense of being sublime. It is "attained through tranquility" (paṭippassaddhaladdha) because it is obtained through the stilling of defilements. "Paṭippassaddha" and "paṭippassaddhi" are identical in meaning.
9:
In essence, it is one. Alternatively, it is called 'Paṭippassaddhaladdha' because the defilements have subsided, or because it is obtained by an Arahant. It is called 'Ekodībhāvagata' because it is attained by developing the incomparable and noble concentration, or because that very state which develops the incomparable and noble concentration is desired. It is called 'Na sasaṅkhāraniggahavāritagata' because it is not attained by suppressing the opposing hindrances (nīvaraṇa) with effort and thereby blocking the defilements. At that time, the person who enters the concentration of the fruition of Arahantship, or who emerges from it, enters or emerges while being mindful, due to having reached abundance of mindfulness. Alternatively, one enters or emerges while being mindful by the power of the determined time. Therefore, for the person who reflects, 'This concentration is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant result in the future,' there arises a knowledge within oneself that is not dependent on others (self-realized); that is one knowledge. The same method applies to the remaining knowledges. Thus, these five knowledges arise within oneself.

## 8. Pañcaṅgika Sutta VaṄṄanā

In the eighth sutta, 'ariyassa' (of the noble) refers to one who stands far from the defilements that have been abandoned by suppression (vikkhamphana). 'Bhāvanaṁ desessāmi' (I will teach the development) means 'I will explain the increase and growth.' 'Imameva kāyaṁ' (this very body) refers to this physical body (karajakāya). 'Abhisandeti' (drenches) means it moistens; it moistens with the essence of rapture and pleasure (pītisukha); it produces rapture and pleasure occurring in all places. 'Parisandeti' (steeps) means it drenches from all around. 'Paripūreti' (fills) means it fills like a bellows filled with air. 'Parippharati' (suffuses) means it touches from all around. 'Sabbāvato kāyassa' (of the entire body) means that in the physical continuity of this monk's entire body, there is no place, even as small as an atom, following the skin, flesh, and blood, that is not suffused with the bliss of the first jhāna.

'Dakkho' (skilled) means a clever person capable of making, mixing, and kneading bath powder. 'Kaṁsathāle' (in a bronze vessel) means in a vessel made of any kind of bronze. An earthen vessel is not firm and would break while kneading; therefore, he did not show an earthen vessel. 'Paripphosakaṁ paripphosakaṁ' (sprinkling and sprinkling) means by repeatedly pouring water. 'Sanneyya' (should knead) means holding the bronze vessel with the left hand and repeatedly pouring a measured amount of water with the right hand, kneading it into a ball. 'Snehānugatā' (pervaded by moisture) means followed by the moisture of the water. 'Snehaparetā' (saturated with moisture) means gripped from all around by the moisture of the water.
10:
'Santarabāhirā' (internally and externally) means being suffused with the moisture of water in all places, including both the internal and external parts. 'Na ca pagghariṇī' (and not leaking) means that water droplets do not ooze out; it means it can be held with the palm or with two fingers, and it can be made into a bundle.

In the simile for the bliss of the second jhāna, 'ubbhidodaka' (with water welling up) refers to a lake with water that has burst forth; it does not mean water that wells up from below and rises to the top, but rather water that arises only from within. 'Ayamukha' (inlet) means the path of arrival. 'Deva' (deity/sky) means the rain. 'Kālena kālaṁ' (from time to time) means at various times, such as once every half-month or once every ten days. 'Dhārā' (showers) means the rain showers. 'Nānuppaveccheyya' (would not enter) means it would not enter, it would not rain. 'Cool water currents welling up' means the cool water currents burst forth while filling that lake. Indeed, water rising from below disturbs the water as it rises and breaks through. Water entering from the four directions disturbs the water with old leaves, old grass, old wood, and old sticks, etc. Rainwater also disturbs the water with the falling of showers and the formation of bubbles. However, the water that arises while being perfectly still, as if created by psychic power, has no such thing as 'it suffuses this place, but does not suffuse that place.' Therefore, there is no such thing as an unsuffused spot. In that simile, the lake is like the physical body (karajakāya), the water is like the bliss of the second jhāna, and the rest should be understood in the same way as the previous method.

In the simile for the bliss of the third jhāna, 'uppalinī' (possessing lotuses) means there are lotuses in this lake. The same method applies to the remaining two terms. Here, among the white, red, and blue lotuses, any kind is called 'uppala.' A lotus with fewer than a hundred petals is called 'puṇḍarīka,' and one with a hundred petals is called 'paduma.' Alternatively, regardless of the number of petals, a white lotus is called 'paduma' and a red one is called 'puṇḍarīka'; this is the decision here. 'Udakanuggatā' (not emerged from the water) means they have not risen out of the water. 'Antonimuggaposīnī' (thriving submerged within) means they grow and thrive while remaining submerged under the surface of the water. The rest should be understood in the same way as the previous method.

In the simile for the fourth jhāna, in the phrase 'parisuddhena cetasā pariyodātena' (with a mind that is purified and bright), it should be understood as 'parisuddha' (purified) due to the absence of defilements, and 'pariyodāta' (bright) due to its radiance. The phrase 'with a white cloth' is said for the purpose of the permeation of the temperature (utu). Indeed, the permeation of temperature does not occur with a soiled cloth; the permeation of temperature is strong only with a purified cloth washed at that moment. In this simile, the cloth is like the physical body (karajakāya), and the permeation of temperature is like the bliss of the fourth jhāna. Therefore, just as a man who has bathed well covers himself, including his head, with a clean cloth...
11:
The temperature (utu) emanating from the body of a seated person pervades the entire garment; there is no part of the garment that is not touched by it. Similarly, with the pleasure of the fourth jhāna, there is no part of the monk’s physical body (karajakāya) that is not touched by it—this is how the meaning should be understood here. Alternatively, the fourth jhāna mind is like the garment, and the matter (rūpa) produced by that mind is like the pervading temperature. Just as a pure white garment might not touch the body in a certain place, yet the temperature arising from that garment pervades and touches the entire body; similarly, the entire body of the monk is pervaded and touched by the subtle matter produced by the fourth jhāna—this is how the meaning should be understood here.

'Paccavekkhaṇanimittaṃ' refers to the reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa) itself. 'Suggahitaṃ hoti' means that just as the monk has well-grasped the jhāna, insight (vipassanā), and the path (magga), so too the reviewing sign (paccavekkhaṇanimitta) is well-grasped by successive reviewing signs. 'Añño vā aññaṃ' means one person [looking at] another; this is because one's own self is not clearly manifest to oneself. 'Ṭhito vā nisinnaṃ' is said because a seated person is clearly manifest to a standing person. In the remaining suttas, the same method should be understood. 'Udakamaṇiko' refers to a water jar with a rim. 'Samatittiko' means full to the brim. 'Kākapeyyā' means full enough for a crow perched on the rim to drink without bending its neck.

'Subhūmiyaṃ' means on level ground. In the passage 'Subhūme sukhette vihatakhāṇuke bījāni patiṭṭhāpeyya,' 'maṇḍabhūmi' (level ground) is what is meant by 'subhūmi.' 'Catumahāpathe' means at a crossroads where two main roads intersect. 'Ājaññaratho' is a carriage drawn by well-trained thoroughbred horses. 'Odhastapatodo' is a goad (whip) placed crosswise against the rail so that one standing on the carriage can easily reach it. 'Yoggācariyao' is a horse trainer (assācariya). Because that very teacher tames horses that should be tamed, he is called 'assadammasārathi' (tamer of horses to be tamed). 'Yenicchakaṃ' means by whichever path one desires. 'Yadicchakaṃ' means by whichever destination one desires. 'Sāreyya' means to drive straight forward. 'Paccāsāreyya' means to drive back (reverse).

Thus, after explaining the preparation (parikamma) for attainment through the five factors below, and showing the benefits of a proficient attainment through these three similes, he now speaks the words beginning with 'If he so desires' (so sace ākaṅkhati) to show the sequence of higher knowledges (abhiññā) of an Arahant. That statement has an obvious meaning.
12:
## 9. Caṅkamasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, 'addhānakkhama' means being able to endure or put forth effort when traveling a long distance. 'Padhānakkhama' means being able to endure the effort of exertion. 'Caṅkamādhigato samādhi' refers to any one of the eight attainments (samāpatti) of concentration gained by one who is committed to walking meditation. 'Ciraṭṭhitiko hoti' means it lasts for a long time. The reason is that a sign (nimitta) grasped while standing may be lost when one sits down; a sign grasped while sitting may be lost when one lies down. However, a sign grasped while committed to walking meditation, even though the object is in motion, is not lost whether one is standing, sitting, or lying down.

## 10. Nāgitasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, the terms 'uccāsadda-mahāsaddā' (loud and great noise) arise because the sound rises upwards (high) and because it comes from a large crowd (great). When great wealthy nobles, brahmins, and others arrive bringing grand offerings, they say, 'Give space to this person! Give space to that person!' and others reply, 'We arrived first! It is for me first! There is no space!' Thus, the sound of them talking to one another becomes high and great. 'Kevaṭṭā mañye macchavilope' means just like fishermen in a place where fish are being plundered. It is like the sound of a great crowd of people shouting 'Give to me! Give to me!' at a place where fishermen have brought baskets of fish to sell. 'Mīḷhasukha' is the pleasure found in impure defilements. 'Middhasukha' is the pleasure found in torpor or sleep. 'Lābhasakkārasilokasukha' is the pleasure that arises depending on gain, honor, and praise.

'They will follow only to the place where the Blessed One goes' means they will surely follow after Him. 'Venerable Sir, because the Blessed One's virtue and wisdom are of such a nature' is the meaning. 'May fame (entourage) not follow along with me' is the meaning. 'Piyānaṃ' means of dear ones. 'Eso tassa nissando' means this is the result of being dear. 'Asubhanimittānuyoga' means the practice of the meditation on foulness (asubha). 'Subhanimitte' refers to a pleasant object that is a cause for lust (rāga). 'Eso tassa nissando' means this is the result of practicing that meditation on foulness. Thus, in these five instances in this sutta, only insight (vipassanā) is taught.

## The Third Chapter: The Group of Five (Pañcaṅgikavagga).
13:
## 4. Sumana Vagga
## 1. Commentary on the Sumanasutta
In the first sutta of the fourth chapter, 'Sumana Rājakumārī' (Princess Sumana) is the name of the princess who received this name because she made a great offering and an aspiration. During the time of the Vipassī Sammasambuddha, the citizens of the city of Bandhumatī said, "We will invite our Teacher even if we have to fight for it." Relying on the General (Senāpati), they invited the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha and performed meritorious deeds in succession. The first day was the General's turn. On that day, the General prepared a great offering and stationed men all around, saying, "Today, do not let anyone else give even a single spoonful of alms-food to any monk in this place."

On that day, a merchant's wife said to her daughter, who was accompanied by five hundred maidens and was crying, "Dear daughter, if your father were alive today, I would have been the first to offer alms-food to the Buddha." The daughter replied, "Mother, do not worry; I will arrange it so that the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha will partake of our alms-food first."

Then, she filled a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand with pure milk-rice (pāyāsa), prepared it with ghee, honey, and sugar, covered it with another bowl, and wrapped that golden bowl all around with jasmine (sumana) garlands to make it look like a ball of flowers. When the Blessed One was entering the village, she carried it on her head herself and came out of the house surrounded by a group of nurses. Along the way, the General's attendants forbade her, saying, "Mother, do not come this way." Those with great merit have pleasant speech, and it is not easy to reject the words of those who speak repeatedly. She asked, "Uncles and elder uncles, why do you not allow me to go?" The General's attendants said, "It is because the General has forbidden anyone else from giving food or snacks." She asked, "Do you see any food or snacks in my hands?" They replied, "We only see a ball of flowers." She asked, "Does your General forbid even the offering of flowers?" They replied, "He allows it, Mother."

Then she said, "Move aside," and approached the Blessed One, saying, "Blessed One, please accept this ball of flowers." The Blessed One looked at one of the General's attendants and had him accept the ball of flowers. She paid homage to the Blessed One and made an aspiration: "Blessed One, in whatever life I am born, may I never live in longing or want. Like this jasmine flower, may I be beloved by many in every place I am born, and may my name be only Sumana." The Blessed One said, "May you be happy." She paid homage, circumambulated him to the right, and departed. The Blessed One also went to the General's house and sat on the prepared seat. The General approached with gruel (yāgu), but the Teacher covered the bowl with his hand. The General said, "Venerable Sir, the Saṅgha of monks is seated." The Teacher said, "We have already received a portion of alms-food on the way." When he removed the flowers, the alms-food was seen. The young attendant said, "Lord, that woman deceived me by saying it was a flower."
14:
"May I be beloved (by people), and may my name be only Sumana." When she made this aspiration, the Blessed One said, "May you be happy." She paid homage, circumambulated him to the right, and departed. The Blessed One also went to the General's house and sat on the prepared seat. The General approached with gruel (yāgu), but the Blessed One covered the bowl with his hand. The General said, "Venerable Sir, the Saṅgha of monks is seated." The Blessed One said, "We have a type of alms-food received on the way." He removed the flowers (on the bowl) and saw the alms-food. The young attendant said, "Lord, the woman deceived me, saying 'It is a flower.'"

The milk-rice was sufficient for all the monks, starting with the Buddha. The General gave his own offerings. The Blessed One, having finished his meal, preached a blessing and departed. The General asked, "Who was it that gave that alms-food?" They replied, "Lord, it was the merchant's daughter." He thought, "She is a wise woman; if such a woman lives in the house, it is not difficult for a man to attain the bliss of heaven." He then took that merchant's daughter and placed her in the position of chief wife.

She took wealth from both her father's house and the General's house and gave offerings to the Tathāgata throughout her life. After performing meritorious deeds and passing away, she was reborn in the sensuous-sphere deva realm (Kāmāvacara). At the very moment of her birth, a rain of jasmine flowers fell, filling the entire world to the height of the knees. The deities thought, "This goddess has come bringing her own name," and they named her "Sumana Devadhītā." For ninety-one aeons, as she wandered through the realms of devas and humans, she was never without a rain of jasmine flowers wherever she was born, and she was known only by the name "Sumana, Sumana."

Now, she took conception in the womb of the chief queen of King Kosala. On that very day, five hundred maidens also took conception in various families and were born from their mothers' wombs on the same day. At that moment, a rain of jasmine flowers fell to the height of the knees. Seeing the rain of jasmine flowers, King Kosala, with a joyful heart, said, "This maiden must be one who has made past aspirations," and saying, "My daughter has come bringing her own name," he named her Sumana. Thinking, "My daughter would not have been born alone," he had a search conducted in the city and, hearing that "five hundred maidens were born," he had them all raised by himself. Every month, he said, "Bring them and show them to my daughter." Thus, it should be understood that this woman received such a name because she made a great offering and an aspiration.
15:
When Princess Sumana was seven years old, the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika completed the Jetavana monastery and sent a messenger to the Blessed One. The Teacher, accompanied by the community of bhikkhus, traveled to Sāvatthī. Anāthapiṇḍika went to King Pasenadi of Kosala and said, "Great King, the arrival of the Teacher here is a blessing for us and a blessing for you as well. Please send Princess Sumana, along with five hundred maidens, carrying full water pots, perfumes, flowers, and so on, to welcome the Ten-Powered One." The King replied, "Very well, Great Merchant," and did as requested. The princess, following her father's instructions, went to the Teacher, paid homage, made offerings of perfumes and flowers, and stood to one side. The Teacher preached the Dhamma to her. She, along with the five hundred maidens, was established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). Another five hundred maidens, five hundred women, and five hundred lay followers also attained the fruit of stream-entry at that moment. Thus, on that day, even while on the journey, two thousand stream-enterers (sotāpanna) arose.

Regarding the phrase "approached where the Blessed One was," why did she approach? Because she wished to ask a question. It is said that in the time of Kassapa Buddha, there were two monks who were friends. One of them fulfilled the duties of social concern (sāraṇīyadhamma), while the other fulfilled the duties of the refectory (bhattaggawatta). The one who fulfilled the sāraṇīyadhamma said to the other, "Friend, there is no benefit for one who does not give; it is proper to give what one has obtained to others and then consume it." The other, however, said, "Friend, you do not understand; it is not proper to waste the offerings. It is proper to fulfill the refectory duties by taking only enough for one's own sustenance." Neither of them could convince the other to adopt his view. Both fulfilled their respective practices, and upon passing away, they were reborn in the sense-sphere heavenly realm. In that heavenly realm, the deity who had practiced the sāraṇīyadhamma surpassed the other deity in five aspects.

Thus, wandering through the realms of devas and humans, they spent the interval between two Buddhas and were now reborn in Sāvatthī. The one who had practiced the sāraṇīyadhamma was conceived in the womb of King Kosala's chief queen, while the other was conceived in the womb of that queen's servant. Both were born on the same day. On the day of the naming ceremony, after they were bathed and laid in the auspicious chamber, both mothers were outside arranging offerings. Of the two infants, the prince who had practiced the sāraṇīyadhamma opened his eyes, saw the great white parasol, the well-prepared auspicious bed, and the decorated palace, and realized, "I have been born into a royal family." He...
16:
Reflecting, "What wholesome deed did I perform to be born here?" he realized, "It is due to the result of the sāraṇīyadhamma." Then, wondering, "Where has my friend been born?" he looked and saw him lying in a lowly place. He thought, "This person did not accept my words when I said I would fulfill the sāraṇīyadhamma; now it is proper to rebuke him in this place." He said, "Friend, you did not follow my words." When asked, "What has happened?" he replied, "Look at my prosperity; I lie on an auspicious bed under a white parasol, while you lie on a low couch with only a coarse covering." The other replied, "Why do you take pride based on such things? Is not all this merely the earth element (pathavī-dhātu), made of bamboo strips and wrapped in old rags?"

Princess Sumana heard their conversation and thought, "There is no one else near my brothers." While she was standing by the door as she approached them, she heard the word "element" (dhātu) and thought, "This word 'element' does not exist outside the Dispensation. My brothers must be devas who were formerly monks." She further thought, "If I tell my parents that they are speaking like this, they will say, 'These are non-humans (ogres),' and have them removed. Without telling anyone else, I will ask my father-like Gautama, the Ten-Powered One, who is like a goldsmith capable of cutting away all doubts." After eating her morning meal, she approached the King and said, "I will go to attend upon the Blessed One." The King had five hundred chariots prepared. Indeed, on the surface of Jambudīpa, only these three princesses received five hundred chariots from their fathers: Princess Cundī, the daughter of King Bimbisāra; Visākhā, the daughter of the merchant Dhanañjaya; and this Princess Sumana. Carrying perfumes and flowers, she stood on her chariot and, surrounded by five hundred chariots, approached the Blessed One, thinking, "I will ask this question."

"Idhassu" means they would be in this Dispensation. "Eko dāyaka" (one who is a giver) refers to one who, from the gains he has obtained himself, gives to others and then consumes—the one who fulfills the sāraṇīyadhamma. "Eko adāyaka" (one who is not a giver) refers to one who consumes what he has obtained himself without giving to others—the one who fulfills the refectory duties (bhattaggawatta). "Devabhūtānaṃ pana nesaṃ" means of those who have become devas. "Adhigaṇhāti" means to surpass, to overcome, to excel, or to predominate. "Ādhipateyyena" means by way of being a leader or superior. "By these five aspects" means surpassing by these five reasons, just as Sakka, the king of devas, surpasses the other devas.
17:
In the passages beginning with *mānusakena* (human), one becomes a superior leader through these five reasons: in terms of longevity, like the Elder Mahākassapa, the Elder Bākula, and the Elder Ānanda; in terms of appearance, like the Elder Mahāgatimba Abhaya and the Bhaṇḍāgāra Minister; in terms of happiness, like the clansman Raṭṭhapāla, the merchant's son Soṇa, and the youth Yasa; and in terms of fame and authority, like King Siridhammāsoka.

*Yācitova bahulaṃ* (mostly when invited) means that like the Elders Bākula, Sīvali, and Ānanda, one becomes a superior leader by using many requisites such as robes only when invited. *Yadidaṃ vimuttiyā vimuttiṃ* (this liberation compared to that liberation) means: 'If there were any distinction to be made regarding the liberation of one person compared to the liberation of another, I would not say so.' This is because there is no distinction in the supramundane path (*lokuttaramagga*) realized, whether it be by a seven-year-old child, a hundred-year-old elder, a monk, a nun, a layman, a laywoman, a deva, Māra, or Brahmā. *Alameva* means 'it is indeed appropriate'. *Yatra hi nāma* means 'whatever wholesome deeds'.

*Gacchaṃ ākāsadhātuyā* means traveling through the sky. *Saddho* means one who has faith in the virtues of the Triple Gem. *Thanayaṃ* means the rumbling of thunder. *Vijjumālī* means being endowed with streaks of lightning moving in the clouds like garlands of flowers. *Satakkakū* means having countless peaks; it refers to being endowed with hundreds of cloud-peaks rising here and there. *Dassanasampanno* means a Stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*). *Bhogaparibyūḷho* means being surrounded by wealth given through the power of generosity, as if overflowing with a current of water, and thus reaching the celestial realm. *Pecca* means in the world beyond. *Sagge pamodati* means rejoicing in whichever heaven one is reborn.

## 2. Cundīsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, *pañcahi rathasatehi* (with five hundred chariots) means that after having breakfast, she sent word to her father, King Suddhodana, to prepare five hundred chariots, and she was surrounded by those five hundred chariots. *Upasaṅkami* (approached) means she approached, bringing perfumes, flowers, and scented powders, intending to discuss and ask questions about the issues that had arisen with her brother. *Yadeva so hoti* means 'at whatever time that person is' or 'whoever that person is'. *Ariyakantāni sīlāni* refers to the virtues associated with the Path and Fruition.
18:
Virtues associated with the Path and Fruition (are called *ariyakantasīla*). These virtues are dear to the Noble Ones and are not abandoned even in another life. The remaining meaning should be understood in the same way as stated in the Aggappasāda Sutta of the Catukka Nipāta.

## 3. Uggahasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third (Uggaha) Sutta, *Bhaddiye* means in the city of Bhaddiya. *Jātiyāvana* refers to a natural, unplanted forest grove connected to the Himālaya mountains; the Buddha was staying in that forest depending on that city. *Attacatuttho* means himself as the fourth (i.e., with three others). Why did the merchant's son Uggaha invite the Buddha along with only three other monks? Because there was a great auspicious ceremony at his house, and many people would gather. He thought it would be difficult to serve and support a large Saṅgha of monks while also attending to the crowd, so he invited only four, including the Buddha. Alternatively, he thought: 'Young maidens might be hesitant in mind to receive instructions if the Teacher exhorts them in the midst of a large Saṅgha of monks.' For this reason also, he invited only four, including the Buddha. 'Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One exhort these maidens.' Here, the genitive case *tāsaṃ* is used in the sense of the accusative case. *Yaṃ tāsaṃ* refers to whatever exhortation and instruction these maidens should receive. Having spoken thus, the merchant thought, 'These maidens might feel shy if they receive instruction in my presence,' so he paid homage to the Buddha and departed.

*Bhattu* means of the husband. *Anukampaṃ upādāya* means based on compassion. *Pubbuṭṭhāyiniyo* means those who habitually rise before everyone else. *Pacchānipātiniyo* means those who habitually go to sleep after everyone else. It is not proper for women to eat before others and go to bed. It is proper to sleep only after feeding all the household members, arranging the household utensils, knowing whether the cattle and so on have returned or not, planning the work to be done the next day, holding the keys and signet rings in hand, eating if there is food, or having more cooked if there is none, and satisfying everyone. Even when lying down, one should not sleep until sunrise. Rather, one should rise before everyone else, call the servants and workers, and manage the work saying, 'Do this and that,' have the cows milked, and perform all household duties under one's own supervision. With reference to this meaning, it is said: 'rising early and sleeping late'.
19:
It is appropriate. It is not appropriate for women to eat before everyone else and then go to bed to sleep. Rather, it is appropriate to sleep only after feeding all members of the household, after storing away the household utensils, after ascertaining whether the cattle and other animals have returned, after planning the tasks for the next day, after putting away the keys and signet rings, and after ensuring everyone is satisfied by eating existing food or cooking fresh food if none remains. Regarding sleep, it is appropriate not to sleep until sunrise, but to rise before everyone else and manage the work by calling the servants and laborers, overseeing all domestic matters such as milking the cows in one's own presence. With reference to this meaning, it was said: "One who habitually rises before the household members, and habitually sleeps after the household members."

"One who is obedient, thinking 'What task shall I do?'" refers to one who habitually manages by looking at the face [of the husband/superiors] and asking, "What task shall I do? How shall I do it?"

"One who habitually acts pleasingly" refers to one who habitually performs only that which is pleasing.

"One who habitually speaks endearing words" refers to one who habitually speaks only endearing words to the husband.

"We shall honor" means we shall honor by offering the four requisites.

"An arrived guest" refers to a person who has come to one's presence. "We shall honor with seats and water for washing the feet" means we shall honor with a place to sit and with water for washing the feet. In this context, respect should be paid daily to one's parents. As for the samanas and brahmins who arrive, one should provide them with a seat, wash their feet, and pay them respect.

"Uṇṇā" means wool. "We shall be skilled in that work" means we shall be expert in cleaning, washing, dyeing, and carding wool, as well as in spinning, grinding, fluffing, and weaving cotton. "Endowed with wisdom in the management of that work" means being endowed with the investigative wisdom that arises as, "At this time, it is appropriate to do this specific task," which serves as the means for managing that wool and cotton. "Capable of doing and capable of organizing" means being suitable and able to perform the task oneself as well as to direct others to do it.

"We shall know the performed task as performed, and the unperformed task as unperformed" means we shall know thus: "It is appropriate to give this or do this for those who return after working all day, for those who return after working half a day, and for those who sit at home without work."

"We shall also know the strength and weakness of the sick" means that if, during their illness, one does not provide them with medicine, food, and so on to make the disease comfortable, they might think, "These householders made us do whatever they wanted when we were healthy, but when we are sick, they do not even know of our existence." Being thus neglected, they may not perform tasks in the future, or they may perform them poorly. Therefore, it is shown that you should practice thus: "Knowing their strength and weakness, we shall know what should be given and what should be done."

"The food and snacks of those household members" refers to the snacks and food of the group of people living within that house. "By portion" means according to the portion to be received, in accordance with the respective shares each is to obtain. "We shall distribute and give" means we shall give. "We shall fulfill" means we shall act to make it complete.
20:
"Adhuttī" refers to those who are not frivolous by way of being a flirt with men or being a drunkard. "Athenī" refers to one who does not steal (a non-thief). "Asoṇḍī" refers to one who is not addicted to drink by way of being a drunkard and so forth.

Having thus concluded the Sutta, the Buddha now spoke the verses starting with "Yo naṃ bharati sabbadā" to highlight the essence. In that passage, "bharati" means nurturing or looking after. "Sabbakāmaharā" has the meaning of granting all sensual desires. "Sotthī" means a good woman. "Evaṃ vattati" means conducting oneself by fulfilling this much of the duties. "Manāpā nāma te devā" refers to the Nimmānaratī deities. Because those deities delight in creating whatever forms they desire, they are called both "Nimmānaratī" and "Manāpā."

## 4. Sīhasenāpati Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, "sandiṭṭhika" means that which is to be seen by oneself. "Dāyaka" means one who is brave in giving. The meaning is that such a person does not stop at mere faith but is also able to relinquish and donate. "Dānapati" (Lord of Giving) means one gives as the master of the gift, not as a slave or a friend. One who eats sweet food himself but gives unsweetened (poor quality) food to others gives as a slave to the gift known as dāna. One who gives exactly what he eats himself gives as a friend to the gift. However, one who sustains himself with whatever is available but gives sweet and excellent food to others gives as a master, a senior, or a lord. With reference to such a person, it is said: "Dānapati."

"Amaṅkubhūto" means one whose face is not downcast, one who possesses majesty. "Visārado" means having attained wisdom and joy. "Sahabyataṃ gatā" means having reached a state of togetherness or unity. "Katāvakāsā" means those who have gained the opportunity because they have performed the kamma that grants opportunity in that celestial realm. Since that kamma is only wholesome, it is said: "katakusalā" (having performed merit). "Modare" means they especially rejoice. "Asitassa" refers to the Buddha who does not rely on (is free from) craving. "Tādino" refers to the Buddha who has attained the quality of steadfastness (tādi-lakkhaṇa).

## 5. Dānānisaṃsa Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, "gihidhamma anapagato hoti" means being endowed with the unbroken Five Precepts. "Sataṃ dhammaṃ anukkamanti" means following the Dhamma of the virtuous and great men.
21:
...follows in order. "Santo naṃ bhajanti" means that the virtuous ones—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha—associate with that donor.

## 6. Kāladānasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, "kāladānāni" refers to timely gifts, appropriate gifts, and suitable gifts. "Navasassāni" refers to the first crops. "Navaphalāni" refers to the first fruits that arise from an orchard. "Paṭhamaṃ sīlavantesu patiṭṭhāpeti" means first giving to those endowed with virtue and only afterwards consuming it oneself. "Vadaññū" refers to one who understands the words of the recipients. "Kālena dinnaṃ" refers to a gift given at a proper and suitable time. "Anumodanti" means they rejoice while standing to one side. "Veyyāvaccaṃ" means performing acts of service with the body. "Appaṭivānacitto" means having an undaunted mind. "Yattha dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ" means one should give in a place where the gift given will yield great fruit.

## 7. Bhojanasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta, "āyuṃ deti" means one gives the gift of life. "Vaṇṇaṃ" means physical beauty; "sukhaṃ" means both physical and mental happiness; "balaṃ" means physical strength; "paṭibhānaṃ" means the gift of wisdom that arises appropriately and freely.

## 8. Saddhasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, "anukampanti" means they favor or support. "Khandhimāva mahādumo" means like a great tree endowed with a trunk. "Manorame āyatane" means in a delightful meeting place. "Chāyaṃ chāyatthikā yanti" means it is like those desiring shade approaching the shade. "Nivātavuttiṃ" means having a humble manner. "Atthaddhaṃ" means being free from harshness caused by anger and pride. "Sorataṃ" means being endowed with gentle physical conduct and pure virtue. "Sakhilaṃ" means having speech that causes great joy.

## 9. Puttasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, "bhato vā no bharissati" means the son whom we have supported and nurtured by breastfeeding and developing his limbs, etc., will in turn support us when we are old and frail by washing our hands and feet, bathing us, and providing us with gruel and rice. "Kiccaṃ vā no karissati" means setting aside his own work, he will go to attend to matters arising for us at the royal court, etc.
22:
...will perform (matters arising for us at the royal court, etc.). "Kulavaṃso ciraṃ thassati" means if there is a son who protects our property such as fields, gold, silver, etc., without letting it perish, the family lineage will endure for a long time; or he will continue the distribution of food-tickets, etc., established by us without interruption; in this way too, our family lineage will endure for a long time. "Dāyajjaṃ paṭipajjissati" means by conducting himself in a manner suitable for the lineage, making himself worthy of inheritance, he will receive our property as an inheritance. "Dakkhiṇaṃ anuppadassati" means having performed the sharing of merit, he will give gifts starting from the third day onwards.

"Santo sappurisā" means in this context, they are known as virtuous ones whose defilements are calmed through proper conduct toward their parents. "Pubbe katamanussaraṃ" means recollecting the benefits and virtues previously performed by the parents. "Ovādakārī" means one who follows the advice given by the parents. "Bhataposī" means one who nurtures those parents who nurtured him. "Pasaṃsiyo" means one who is to be praised by the multitude even in the present life.

## 10. Mahāsālaputtasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, "mahāsālā" refers to great trees. "Sākhāpattapalāsena vaḍ膽hanti" means they grow by means of small branches and foliage known as leaves. "Araññasmiṃ" means in a place where there is no village. "Brahāvane" means in a great forest or jungle. The remaining words have clear meanings in all places.

In the third sutta, "āyusaṃvattanikā paṭipadā" refers to the practice of merit such as giving (dāna) and virtue (sīla). The same method applies to the remaining terms. "Atthābhisamayā" means due to the meeting with the benefit, or it means due to the attainment of the benefit.

## 4. Manāpadāyīsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, "Ugga" is the name of a merchant who was so named because he was noble (uggata) in qualities. "Sālapupphaka khādanīya" is a snack resembling a sāl flower, made of rice flour mixed with the four sweets (catumadhura). Indeed, that snack resembling a sāl flower is made with distinct filaments, cooked in ghee mixed with spices such as cumin, then the ghee is drained, and it is placed in a pot until full, infused with fragrances, closed, sealed, and kept. The merchant Ugga, wishing to offer it to the Blessed One during the interval between meals after the Blessed One had finished drinking gruel, spoke thus. The phrase "The Blessed One accepted" is merely a manner of teaching; in reality, that lay devotee offered it to the Blessed One and to the five hundred monks. Just like that snack, he also offered pork and so on.

Among those offerings, "sampannakolaka" means having excellent jujubes. "Sūkaramaṃsa" is the meat of a one-year-old pig cooked with sweet-tasting jujubes and spices such as cumin. "Nibbattatelaka" means with the oil removed. "Nāliyasāka" is water spinach kneaded with rice flour, cooked in ghee mixed with spices such as cumin, then mixed with the four sweets, infused with fragrance, and kept. In the passage "This is not suitable for the Blessed One," it means that starting from unsuitable things like a lion-shaped throne, even suitable things were [initially] considered unsuitable. However, the merchant had all those unsuitable items brought and piled up, sent whatever was unsuitable to the market, and offered only suitable goods for use and consumption.

The sandalwood board was not too large, being three cubits long including the bark and one and a half cubits wide including the bark. Because it was a noble item made of heartwood, it was very expensive. The Blessed One accepted that sandalwood board, had it cut into pieces, and gave it to the monks for the purpose of grinding eye-ointment.

"Ujjubhūtesu" means among those who are upright in body, speech, and mind. "Chandasā" means with affection. In the words beginning with "cattaṃ," "cattaṃ" means given up by the power of relinquishment. "Muttaṃ" means released because of being freely given. "Anuggahītaṃ" means not grasped by the mind because of being a mind without attachment. "Khettūpame" means among those who are like a field because of the sense of growth.

"Aññataraṃ manomayaṃ" refers to a certain group of devas born of a single jhanic mind in the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa). "Yathādhippāyo" means according to one's own wish. What is asked by this? It is said that while he was in the human world, he had the intention for the sake of Arahantship; "I will ask about that intention," thus he asks. The deva, having reached Arahantship, said, "Indeed, Bhante, it is according to my wish." "Yattha yatthūpapajjati" means wherever he is born, whether in the three types of family success or in the six sensual heavens, in those various places he becomes long-lived and famous. ## 8. Alabbhanīyaṭṭhānasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, "alabbhanīyāni" means things that cannot be obtained, things one is unable to get. "Ṭhānāni" means causes. "Abbuhi" means he has pulled out.

"Yato" means at which time. "Āpadāsu" means in calamities. "Na vedhati" means he does not tremble and does not sorrow. "Atthaviniccayaññū" means one who is skilled in determining the cause and benefit. "Purāṇaṃ" means just as it was before, because of the absence of change. "Jappena" means by praising qualities. "Mantena" means by reciting powerful mantras. "Subhāsitena" means by speaking well. "Anuppadānena" means by giving wealth of a hundred or a thousand. "Paveṇiyā vā" means by way of lineage, or by explaining the lineage thus: "This practice has been observed by our lineage; this has not been observed." In whatever way and in whatever place one might obtain the benefit of non-aging etc. for things subject to aging etc., in that way and in that place one should strive. "Kammaṃ daḷhaṃ" means "I have firmly performed and accumulated karma that leads to the round of rebirth; what can I do now?"—reflecting thus, he should endure.

## 1. Āvaraṇasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the Dutiyapaṇṇāsaka, they are called 'obstructions' (āvaraṇa) because of their power to obstruct. They are called 'hindrances' (nīvaraṇa) because of their power to prevent without exception. They are called 'overpowering the mind' (cetaso ajjhhāruhā) because they overwhelm and ascend upon the mind. They are called 'weakening wisdom' (paññāya dubbalīkaraṇā) in the sense that they prevent the arising of insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) and path wisdom (magga-paññā), thereby making them weak. Alternatively, they are called 'weakening wisdom' because they make the wisdom that arises in association with these hindrances weak. 'Abalāya' means being devoid of strength because of being covered over by the five hindrances. 'Uttari manussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesaṃ' refers to a distinction in knowledge and vision capable of making one a noble one (ariya), which surpasses the human states known as the ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakamma-patha). 'Hāraharinī' means capable of carrying away things that should be carried away, such as grass and trees on the riverbank. 'Naṅgalamukhāni' refers to the mouths of the channels. These are called 'naṅgalamukhāni' because they resemble the head of a plow and because they are dug with plows.

In this simile, 'evameva kho', insight wisdom (vipassanā-ñāṇa) should be understood as the current. The time when the restraint of the six sense doors is released should be understood as the time when the mouths of the channels on both sides are opened. The time when one is covered by the five hindrances should be understood as the time when the water is dispersed and scattered in all directions because the river has been blocked in the middle by driving in stakes and using straw, grass, and lumps of earth. It should be understood that just as the water, having lost its momentum due to being blocked, is unable to reach the ocean by pulling along grass and leaves, so too is one unable to reach the ocean of Nibbāna by destroying all unwholesome states with insight wisdom. In the case of the 'bright side' (sukkapakkha - the wholesome side), the application should be understood by the opposite of the meaning already stated. In this sutta, the round of suffering (vaṭṭa) and the ending of the round (vivaṭṭa) are taught. The second sutta has an obvious meaning.

## 3. Padhāniyaṅgasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, 'padhāniyaṅgāni' is used; 'padhāna' is said because of the sense of striving. One who possesses that striving is called 'padhāniya', and the factors of such a striving monk are called 'padhāniyaṅga'. 'Saddho' means being endowed with faith (saddhā). That faith is fourfold: faith through tradition (āgama-saddhā), faith through attainment (adhigama-saddhā), confirmed faith (okappana-saddhā), and faith through devotion (pasāda-saddhā). Among these, the faith of the Omniscient Bodhisattas is called 'āgama-saddhā' because it has come down from the time of their initial aspiration. The faith of the noble disciples (ariya-sāvaka) is called 'adhigama-saddhā' because it is obtained through the penetration of the Four Noble Truths. The unshakeable belief and entry into the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha is called 'okappana-saddhā'. The arising of clarity and devotion is called 'pasāda-saddhā'. In this sutta, 'okappana-saddhā' is intended. 'Bodhi' refers to the four path knowledges (magga-ñāṇa). One believes that the Blessed One has well-penetrated that path knowledge. Although this is the peak of the teaching, by this factor, faith in all Three Jewels is intended.

Bhavābhavo means the duration of the cycle (vaṭṭa), the destination (gati), and repeated existence. Purakkhatā means those that go before, those that have gone ahead. Ye ca kāme pariññāya means those wise ones who, having fully understood the two kinds of sense desires through the three types of full understanding (pariññā), [wander about]. Akutobhaya means for the Arahants whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), there is no fear from any cause; therefore, those Arahants wander about being fearless from any cause. In the phrase pāraṅgatā, the "beyond" (pāra) refers to Nibbāna; it means they have reached that Nibbāna and remain having realized it. Āsavakkhayaṃ means the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). In this sutta, only the cycle (vaṭṭa) is discussed, but in the verses, both the cycle and the cessation of the cycle (vivaṭṭa) are discussed.

## 6. Commentary on the Upajjhāya Sutta

In the sixth sutta, madhurakajāto means a state of extreme heaviness has arisen. Disā me na pakkhāyanti means "the four directions and the intermediate directions are not clear to me." Dhammā ca maṃ nappaṭibhanti means "the teachings of tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) also do not appear to me." Anabhirato ca brahmacariyaṃ carāmi means being dissatisfied (ukkaṇṭhita) in the Dispensation, one lives the holy life. Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami means having heard that monk's words, [the preceptor] approached the Blessed One to report the matter, thinking, "This monk is a person to be guided by the Buddha." Avippasakkassa kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ means for one who does not contemplate, does not seek, and does not search for wholesome states. Bodhipakkhiyānaṃ dhammānaṃ refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna).

## 7. Commentary on the Abhiṇhapaccavekkhitabbaṭṭhāna Sutta

In the seventh sutta, jarādhammomhi means "I am of the nature to age." Jarāṃ anatīto means "I have not gone beyond aging; I wander only within aging." The same method applies to the remaining terms. In kammassako etc., "kamma is my own property, my own possession," thus "I am the owner of my kamma." Kammadāyādo means kamma is my inheritance, my owned property. Because kamma is my cause (yoni), it is called kammayoni. Because kamma is my kinsman (bandhu), it is called kammabandhu, meaning one who has kamma as a relative. Because kamma is my refuge and support, it is called kammapaṭisaraṇo. Tassa dāyādo bhavissāmi means "I will be the heir of that kamma, the recipient of the results given by that kamma." Yobbanamado is the intoxication arising based on youth. The same method applies to the remaining terms. Maggo sañjāyati means the supramundane path arises. Saṃyojanāni sabbaso pahīyanti means the ten fetters are entirely abandoned. Anusayā byantīhonti means the seven underlying tendencies come to an end through removal or through being delimited.

...are in the vicinity. Thus, in this context, insight (vipassanā) is taught regarding the five subjects below, and the supramundane path is taught regarding these five.

Now, bringing it to a climax with verses, he said "byādhidhammā" and so on. In those verses, ñatvā dhammaṃ nirūpadhiṃ means having known the path of Arahantship which is free from acquisitions (upadhi). Sabbe made abhibhosmi means "I stand having overcome and transcended all these three types of intoxication." Nekkhammaṃ daṭṭhu khemato means having seen the state of a monk as secure. Tassa me ahu ussāho, nibbānaṃ abhipassato means "For me, who was looking toward Nibbāna, energy arose." Anivatti bhavissāmi means "I shall be one who does not turn back from the state of a monk, from living the holy life, and from the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa)." Brahmacariyaparāyaṇo means one whose final resort is the holy life of the path. By this Pali, the supramundane Noble Eightfold Path is taught.

## 8. Commentary on the Licchavikumāraka Sutta

In the eighth sutta, sajjāni dhanūni means bows that have been prepared and strung. Addasu means they saw. Bhavissanti vajji means the Vajjian princes will prosper. In the terms raṭṭhikassa etc., one is called raṭṭhika because he enjoys the country. One is called pettanika because he enjoys the wealth given by his father. One is called senāpatika because he is the lord and leader of the army. Gāmagāmaṇikassa means of the village headman, the one who carries out the affairs of the village residents. Pūgagāmaṇikassa means of the leader of a guild. Kulesu means in various families. Paccekādhipaccaṃ kārenti means they each exercise leadership. Khettakammantassāmanta-sabyohāre refers to the owners of adjacent fields near one's own farm work, and the ministers of justice who measure the land with measuring ropes. Balipaṭiggāhikā devatā refers to the guardian deities descended through the family lineage. Sakkaroti means he honors those deities with the first portion of gruel, the first portion of rice, and so on.

Kiccakaro means one who performs the duties that have arisen. Ye cassa anujīvino refers to those who live depending on that person. Ubhinnañceva atthāya means he practices for the benefit of both sides. Pubbapetānaṃ means of those who have gone to the other world (the deceased). Diṭṭhe dhamme ca jီvataṃ means of those who are living in the present life.
