## (8) 3. Yodhājīvavagga

## 1. Paṭhamacetovimuttiphalasutta-vaṇṇanā
1. In the first sutta of the third chapter, the discourse beginning with 'yato kho, bhikkhave' is started for the purpose of praising the virtues of a monk who has attained the fruit of Arahantship by developing insight according to the method mentioned below. In that passage, 'yato kho' means 'when'. 'Ukkhittapaligho' means one who stands having lifted and removed the cross-bar of ignorance. 'Saṃkiṇṇaparikho' means one who stands having destroyed the moat of Saṃsāra. 'Abbuḷhesiko' means one who stands having pulled out the pillar of craving. 'Niraggaḷo' means one who stands having opened the door-leaf of the hindrances. 'Pannaddhajo pannabhāro' means one who stands having lowered the banner of conceit and the burden of the aggregates, formations, and defilements. 'Visaṃyutto' means one who is detached from the round of rebirth. The rest should be understood according to the Pali method. By this sequence of teaching, the Blessed One shows the time of an Arahant who, having exhausted defilements through the path, has reached the noble bed of cessation and dwells having attained the fruition attainment with Nibbāna as the object.

For example, just as there are two cities, one a city of thieves and one a city of safety. Then, a great warrior might think: 'As long as this city of thieves exists, the city of safety cannot be free from danger. Therefore, I will make this city of thieves no longer a city.' Having thought thus, he puts on his armor, takes a sharp weapon, approaches the city of thieves, cuts the banners erected at the city gate, destroys the doorposts and door-leaves, lifts the cross-bar, demolishes the wall, destroys the moat, lowers the banners erected for the city's beauty, sets the city on fire, and enters the city of safety (so too is the Arahant).
33:
'Dhammapaññatti' means for the purpose of making the Dhamma known (designating it). 'He learns the Dhamma' means he learns, recites, and teaches the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths by way of the ninefold division (navanga). 'He does not neglect seclusion' means he does not abandon being alone. 'He devotes himself to internal tranquility of mind (cetosamatha)' means he dwells in and develops concentration of mind within himself, being constantly diligent in the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) of tranquility (samatha).

'Hitesinā' means by one who seeks welfare (the Buddha). 'Anukampakena' means by one who is compassionate. 'Out of compassion' means having taken compassion into the heart (as a basis). 'I have done for you what should be done' means 'I have performed that duty for you by teaching the Dhamma to these five types of persons.' Indeed, the duty of a compassionate teacher (the Buddha) is merely the teaching of the undistorted Dhamma. Practice (paṭipatti), other than this teaching of Dhamma, is the duty of the disciples. Therefore, he said: 'Bhikkhus, these are the roots of trees... this is our instruction.' In that text, by the words 'roots of trees,' he shows dwelling at the foot of a tree. By the words 'empty huts,' he shows places secluded from people. By both of these, he points out dwellings suitable for exertion and hands over the inheritance (of the Dhamma).

'Enter into jhāna' means 'Contemplate the thirty-eight objects by way of object-scrutiny (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna), and contemplate the aggregates, bases, etc., as impermanent and so forth by way of characteristic-scrutiny (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna).' It means 'Develop tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā).' 'Do not be negligent' means do not be careless. 'Do not be those who regret later' means, in detail: those who, in the past when they were young, healthy, possessed of suitable food and conditions, and in the presence of the Teacher, were devoid of wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), remained still like bedbugs day and night, and being devoted to the pleasure of sleep and the pleasure of drowsiness, remained negligent. Later, in old age, in sickness, at the time of death, at the time of ruin, and at the time of the Teacher's Parinibbāna, they remember that past life of negligence. Seeing the heaviness of death along with rebirth, they become regretful (troubled in heart). Wishing to show the meaning 'Do not be such persons,' he said: 'Do not be those who regret later.' 'This is our instruction to you' means 'This instruction from our presence, "Enter into jhāna, do not be negligent," is the advice and exhortation for you.'

## ၄။ ဒုတိယဓမ္မဝိဟာရီသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ

In the fourth sutta, 'beyond that, he does not understand the meaning with his wisdom' means he does not understand the meaning and benefit with the path-wisdom (maggapaññā) together with insight (vipassanā) which is beyond that scriptural learning (pariyatti).
34:
It means not knowing the benefit, not seeing the Four Noble Truths, and not penetrating them. In the remaining cases, the method is the same. Thus, in both these suttas, six types of persons—the learned monk, the monk practicing insight (vipassanā), the stream-enterer (sotāpanna), the once-returner (sakadāgāmī), the non-returner (anāgāmī), and the Arahant—should be known as 'dwellers in the Dhamma' (dhamma-viharī).

## 5. Paṭhamayodhājīvasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, 'yodhājīvā' refers to warriors who live by means of fighting. 'Rajaggaṃ' refers to the cloud of dust (mass of dust) rising from the ground that has been broken by the trampling of elephants, horses, and so on. 'Na santhambhati' means being unable to stand firm. 'Sahati rajaggaṃ' means being able to endure even upon seeing the cloud of dust. 'Dhajaggaṃ' refers to the tips of the banners hoisted on the backs of elephants and horses, or on chariots. 'Ussāraṇaṃ' refers to the great and loud noise produced by elephants, horses, chariots, and the army. 'Sampahāre' refers to the slight strikes and blows that occur. 'Haññati' means falling into distress and suffering. 'Byāpajjati' means falling into corruption and abandoning one's natural state. 'Sahati sampahāraṃ' means being able to endure even after receiving two or three blows. 'Tam-eva saṅgāmasīsaṃ' refers to that very victory camp or battlefield. 'Ajjhāvasati' means dwelling and occupying for about seven days. For what reason? It is for the purpose of tending to the wounds of those who were struck, for the purpose of granting rank and position after recognizing the special deeds of those who performed their duties, and for the purpose of enjoying the happiness of sovereignty.

Now, although the Blessed One has no need for warriors, this simile is brought forth to show five types of persons in this Dispensation (sāsana) who are like those warriors. Therefore, wishing to show those persons, He said the words beginning with 'evam-eva kho'. In those words, 'saṃsīdati' means sinking or entering into wrong thoughts (micchā-vitakka). 'Brahmacariyaṃ santhāretuṃ na sakkoti' means being unable to protect the holy life without interruption. 'Sikkhādubbalyaṃ āvikatvā' means declaring one's weakness in the training and [disrobing]. 'Kimassa rajaggasmiṃ' means the desire to ask, 'What is the cloud of dust for this person?' 'Abhirūpā' refers to a beautiful woman. 'Dassanīyā' refers to a woman worthy of looking at. 'Pāsādikā' refers to a woman who brings joy to the heart just by being seen. 'Paramāya' means supreme (most excellent). 'Vaṇṇapokkharatāya' means being endowed with beauty of complexion and the form of the limbs. 'Ūhasati' means smiling or laughing with a base nature. 'Ullapati' means talking or conversing.
35:
'Ujjhagghati' means laughing loudly while clapping one's hands. 'Uppaṇḍeti' means speaking mockingly or in jest. 'Abhinisīdati' means sitting nearby or on the same seat in an overpowering manner. In the second phrase, the method is the same. 'Ajjhottharati' means overwhelming. 'Viniveṭhetvā vinimocetvā' means removing and freeing that woman's hand from where it was held. The remaining words in this sutta have clear meanings. In this sutta, the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) are taught.

## 6. Dutiyayodhājīvasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, 'asicammaṃ gahetvā' means taking a sword and a shield. 'Dhanukalāpaṃ sannayhitvā' means preparing a bow and a quiver of arrows. 'Viyūḷhaṃ' means being arrayed according to the battle formation. 'Saṅgāmaṃ otarati' means descending into the great battlefield. 'Ussahati vāyamati' means exerting and making an effort. 'Haññanti' means killing. 'Pariyāpādenti' means ending life. 'Upalikkhanti' means striking or wounding. 'Apanenti' means taking away one's own soldiers. 'Apanetvā ñātakānaṃ nenti' means after taking one's own soldiers away, then sending them to their relatives. 'Nīyamāno' means when being carried to one's own home or to the remaining relatives. 'Upaṭṭhahanti paricaranti' means caring for and protecting them while performing tasks such as cleaning the blows (wounds) and dressing the sores.

'Arakkhitena-eva kāyena' means with an unguarded body-door. 'Arakkhitāya vācāya' means with an unguarded speech-door. 'Arakkhitena cittena' means with an unguarded mind-door. 'Anupaṭṭhitāya satiyā' means without well-established mindfulness. 'Asaṃvutehi indriyehi' means by leaving the faculties, with the mind as the sixth, unclosed and unprotected. 'Rāgo cittaṃ anuddhaṃseti' means that as soon as lust arises, it destroys the mind of calm (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) and casts it far away. 'Rāgapariyuṭṭhitomhi āvuso rāgapareto' means, 'Friend, I am stained by lust and I am following the lead of lust.'

In the phrases beginning with 'aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā': 'aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā' (the simile of a skeleton) is because there is very little gratification. 'Maṃsapesūpamā' (the simile of a piece of meat) is because it is common to many. 'Tiṇukkūpamā' (the simile of a grass torch) is because of the nature of burning. 'Aṅgārakāsūpamā' (the simile of a pit of glowing coals) is because of the nature of great heat. 'Supinakūpamā' (the simile of a dream) is because it appears only for a moment. 'Yācitakūpamā' (the simile of borrowed goods) is because it is only temporary. 'Rukkhaphalūpamā' (the simile of fruit on a tree) is because it causes the destruction of all limbs and parts. 'Asisūnūpamā' (the simile of a butcher's knife and block) is because it is a place of repeated cutting. 'Sattisūlūpamā' (the simile of a sword-stake) is because of the nature of piercing. 'Sappasirūpamā' (the simile of a snake's head) means they are similes like a snake's head because they are accompanied by danger.
36:
It is because of the meaning of being suspicious of danger. 'I will strive' means I will make an effort. 'I will bear' means I will bear the state of a monk (samaṇa). 'I will delight' means I will produce delight and will not be dissatisfied. The remaining words in this sutta have clear meanings. In this sutta, the cycle (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the cycle (vivaṭṭa) are taught.

## 7. Commentary on the First Paṭhama-anāgatabhaya Sutta

In the seventh sutta, 'one who lives in the forest' means a forest dweller (āraññaka). 'One who has not yet attained' means not yet reaching the distinction of the Dhamma consisting of jhāna, insight (vipassanā), the path (magga), and the fruit (phala). In the remaining terms, the method should be understood in the same way. 'That would be a danger to me' means that those creatures such as snakes and scorpions would be a danger to my life and a danger to the holy life (brahmacariya). If one dies as a worldling (puthujjana), it would be a danger to heaven and a danger to the path. 'Handa' is a particle in the sense of relinquishment. 'I will initiate effort' means I will make twofold effort. 'Like weapons' refers to winds that cut the joints like a weapon. 'Wild animals' (vāla) means fierce creatures. 'Young men' (māṇava) means thieves. Regarding 'those who have committed a crime or those who have not yet committed a crime,' those who come out after committing a robbery are called 'those who have committed a crime,' and those who are going to commit a robbery are called 'those who have not yet committed a crime.' Among them, those who have committed a crime, because the robbery is completed, take the throat-blood of beings and make offerings to the deities. Those who have not yet committed a crime also make offerings to the deities first, thinking, 'May our robbery be successful.' Intending this, it is said, 'They might deprive me of life.' 'Fierce non-humans' means cruel and wicked non-humans such as ogres (yakkha), etc.

## 8. Commentary on the Second Dutiya-anāgatabhaya Sutta

In the eighth sutta, 'before that Dhamma reaches me' means that before that nature (of old age) reaches me, I will initiate effort beforehand. 'Those who have become like milk and water' means those who have become one, reaching a state of unity like milk and water. 'With eyes of love' means with eyes associated with loving-kindness (mettā).

## 9. Commentary on the Third Tatiya-anāgatabhaya Sutta

In the ninth sutta, 'corruption of the Vinaya because of corruption of the Dhamma' means the fivefold Vinaya is corrupted because of the corruption of the Dhamma of tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). How is it that when the Dhamma is corrupted, the Vinaya is corrupted? When the essence cannot be grasped in the Dhamma of tranquility and insight, the fivefold Vinaya can no longer arise. Thus, when the Dhamma is corrupted, the Vinaya is corrupted. Alternatively, for one who lacks virtue (sīla), there can be no such thing as the Vinaya of restraint (saṃvara-vinaya). When that restraint-Vinaya is absent, tranquility and insight cannot grasp the essence. Thus, the corruption of the Dhamma because of the corruption of the Vinaya should also be understood. 'Abhidhamma-kathā' means noble talk on the Dhamma such as virtue (sīla), etc. 'Vedalla-kathā' means talk connected with wisdom (ñāṇa) or mixed with wisdom. 'Entering dark states' means entering dark states by seeking opportunities or seeking to blame. Alternatively, monks who blame others with a malicious mind, or monks who speak of those dark unwholesome states that have come to them for the sake of gain and honor, are also entering dark states. 'Deep' means depth by way of the Pali text. 'Deep in meaning' means depth by way of the meaning. 'Supramundane' (lokuttara) means being able to show the supramundane Dhamma. 'Connected with voidness' means connected with the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), and dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). 'Will not set the mind elsewhere' means they will not set the mind elsewhere for the sake of knowledge. For the sake of learning, for the sake of studying the surroundings...
37:
Thus, when the Dhamma of tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) is corrupted, the Vinaya is corrupted. Alternatively, for one who lacks virtue (sīla), there is no such thing as the Vinaya of restraint (saṃvara-vinaya); when that restraint-Vinaya is absent, tranquility and insight cannot grasp the essence (cannot be successfully achieved). Thus, the corruption of the Dhamma because of the corruption of the Vinaya should also be understood.

'Abhidhamma-kathā' means noble talk on the Dhamma such as virtue (sīla), etc. 'Vedalla-kathā' means talk connected with wisdom (ñāṇa) or mixed with wisdom. 'Entering dark states' (kaṇha-dhammaṃ okkamamānā) means entering dark states by way of seeking opportunities or seeking to blame. Alternatively, monks who blame a person with a malicious mind, or those who bring those dark unwholesome states to themselves, or monks who speak for the sake of gain and honor, are also entering dark states.

'Deep' (gambhīrā) means depth by way of the Pali text. 'Deep in meaning' (gambhīratthā) means depth by way of the meaning. 'Supramundane' (lokuttara) means being able to show the supramundane Dhamma. 'Connected with voidness' (suññatā-paṭisaṃyuttā) means connected with the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), and dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). 'Will not set the mind elsewhere' (na aññacittaṃ upaṭṭhapessanti) means not setting the mind elsewhere for the sake of knowledge. 'To be learned and mastered' (uggahetabbaṃ pariyāpuṇitabbaṃ) means what should be learned and what should be used. 'Composed by poets' (kavitā) means words made by the wise by way of composing verses (gāthā), etc. 'Poetic' (kāveyya) is just a synonym for that 'kavitā.' 'External' (bāhirakā) means those who stand outside the Dispensation (sāsana). 'Spoken by disciples' (sāvakabhāsitā) means words spoken by the disciples of sectarians (titthiya) who are outside the Dispensation. The remaining words here have clear meanings because they follow the method already mentioned and are easy to understand.

## 10. Commentary on the Fourth Catuttha-anāgatabhaya Sutta

In the tenth sutta, 'desiring good' (kalyāṇakāma) means desiring what is beautiful. 'Excellent tastes' (rasaggāni) means having supreme flavors. 'Will live in association' (saṃsaṭṭhā viharissanti) means they will live mixed with the fivefold association. 'Consumption of stored items' (sannidhikāra-paribhoga) means using requisites that have been stored. In the phrase 'gross sign' (oḷārikaṃ nimittaṃ), if one digs the earth or commands another to dig, it is called making a gross sign in the earth. If one cuts grass, wood, branches, or leaves, or commands another to cut them, it is called making a gross sign in green plants. There is no need to say that a monk who causes others to take vegetables, etc., for the sake of livelihood, or who picks fruits or causes others to pick them, is making a gross sign. In these four suttas, the Teacher taught the growth and decline of the Dispensation.

## (9) 4. Theravagga

## 1. Rajanīyasutta Vaṇṇanā
In the Rajanīyasutta, the first sutta of the fourth chapter, the term 'rajanīyesu' means in the objects that are the causes of lust (rāga). The same method applies to the remaining terms.

## 2. Vītarāgasutta Vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, 'makkhī' refers to one who denigrates the virtues of others. 'Paḷāsī' refers to one who is endowed with rivalry, characterized by the act of competing for superiority.

## 3. Kuhakasutta Vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, 'kuhako' refers to one who is endowed with the three grounds of scheming to cause wonder. 'Lapako' refers to one who is endowed with prattling or intimidating speech for the sake of gain. 'Nemittiko' refers to one who performs gestures or gives hints to induce the offering of requisites. 'Nippesika' refers to one who is endowed with speech that belittles or crushes others. 'Lābhena ca lābhaṃ nijigīsitā' refers to one who seeks gain from others using the gain they have already acquired. The 'bright side' (sukkapakkha) should be understood by the opposite of what has been stated. The fourth sutta has a clear meaning.

## 5. Akkhamasutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, the Akkhamasutta, the phrase 'akkhamo hoti rūpānaṃ' means one is unable to endure (or resist) visual objects; one is overcome by lust and other defilements that arise based on those objects. This same method applies to all terms.

## 6. Paṭisambhidāpattasutta Vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, 'attha-paṭisambhidāpattā' refers to one who has reached the analytical insight into the five types of meanings. 'Dhamma-paṭisambhidāpattā' refers to one who has reached the analytical insight into the four types of truths. 'Nirutti-paṭisambhidāpattā' refers to one who has reached the analytical insight into the linguistic expressions (Māgadha language) of the Dhamma. 'Paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidāpattā' refers to one who has reached the analytical insight into those three previous insights. Such a person only knows those three insights but does not perform their functions. 'Uccāvacāni' refers to matters both great and small. 'Kiṃkaraṇီyāni' refers to duties and tasks to be performed, such as asking, "What work should be done in this way?"
39:
## 7. Sīlavantasutta Vaṇṇanā
The seventh sutta, the Sīlavantasutta, has a very clear meaning. However, in this sutta, 'virtue' (sīla) refers only to the virtue of an Arahant (khīṇāsava-sīla). 'Great learning' (bāhusacca) also refers only to the great learning of an Arahant. 'Speech' (vācā) refers only to the good speech of an Arahant. 'Meditative absorptions' (jhānas) should be understood as referring only to the functional absorptions (kiriya-jhāna).

## 8. Therasutta Vaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, the Therasutta, 'thera' refers to one who has reached the state of stability and firmness. 'Rattaññū' refers to one who knows many nights that have passed since the day of ordination, meaning a senior monk. 'Ñāta' refers to one who is well-known and famous. 'Yasassī' refers to one who is endowed with a following and fame. 'Micchādiṭṭhika' refers to one who holds perverted views. 'Leading away from the true Dhamma' (saddhammā vuṭṭhāpeတွā) means causing one to depart from the ten wholesome courses of action. 'Establishing in the false Dhamma' means establishing one in the unwholesome courses of action.

## 9. Pathamasekhasutta Vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, the Pathamasekhasutta, 'sekha' refers to a trainee, one who still has work to do. 'For decline' (parihānāya) means for the sake of declining from higher virtues. 'Kammārāmatā' is the state of delighting in new works (projects). 'Bhassārāmatā' is the state of delighting in talk and conversation. 'Niddārāmatā' is the state of delighting in sleep. 'Saṅgaṇikārāmatā' is the state of delighting in congregating and staying with a group or following. 'Does not review the liberated mind' (yathāvimuttaṃ cittaṃ na paccavekkhati) means not reflecting on how one's mind was liberated, which defilements have been abandoned, and what virtues have been attained, and thus not making an effort to attain higher virtues. Thus, in this sutta, the causes of decline from and the causes of growth in higher virtues for the seven types of trainees are explained. Those things which are causes of decline for a trainee are, for a worldling (puthujjana), causes of decline from the very beginning.

## 10. Dutiyasekhasutta Vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, the Dutiyasekhasutta, 'viyatta' refers to one who is wise and skillful. 'In duties' (kiṃkaraṇīyesu) refers to tasks to be performed after inquiring, "What work should be done in this way?" 'Ceto-samatha' refers to the meditation subject of concentration (samadhi-kammaṭṭhāna). 'Ananulomikena' means by a way that is unsuitable for the Dispensation. 'Atikālena' means at a time that is too early. In the term 'atidivā', 'divā' refers to midday, and 'atidivā' means past that midday (too late). 'Ābhisallekhikā' refers to talk that leads to the extreme effacement of defilements. 'Cetovivaraṇasappāyā' refers to talk that is suitable for tranquillity and insight, which are called the opening of the mind. 'Appicchakathā' is the kind of talk that says, "Be one of few wishes."
40:
Talk that says, "Be those who have few wishes," is called talk on having few wishes (appicchakathā). Talk that says, "Be those who are contented with the four requisites," is called talk on contentment (santuṭṭhikathā). Talk that says, "Be those who are secluded through the three kinds of seclusion (seclusion of body, seclusion of mind, and seclusion from the substrata of existence)," is called talk on seclusion (pavivekakathā). Talk that says, "Be those who are not associated with the five kinds of association," is called talk on non-association (asaṃsaggakathā). Talk that says, "Exert the two kinds of energy," is called talk on the arousal of energy (vīriyārambhakathā). In the sections such as talk on virtue, talk that is based on virtue is called talk on virtue (sīlakathā). Talk based on concentration, talk based on wisdom, talk based on the five kinds of liberation (the fruit of Arahantship), and talk based on the knowledge and vision of liberation, which consists of the nineteen kinds of reviewing, is called talk on the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassanakathā). In the phrases such as "na nikāmalābhī," the meaning is: not obtaining as much as desired, not obtaining without difficulty, and not obtaining abundantly. The remaining words have clear meanings.

## 1-2. Commentary on the Two Sampadā Suttas

91-92. In the first sutta of the fifth vagga, the five accomplishments (sampadā) are taught in a mixed manner. In the second sutta, the first four accomplishments are taught in a mixed manner, while the fifth is taught as purely mundane.

## 3. Commentary on the Byākaraṇa Sutta

In the third sutta, "aññābyākaraṇāni" refers to the declarations of the fruit of Arahantship. "Mandattā" means due to dullness or lack of knowledge. "Momūhattā" means due to extreme delusion. "Aññaṃ byākaroti" means saying, "I have reached the fruit of Arahantship." "Icchāpakato" means being overcome by evil desire. "Adhimānena" means due to the conceit of thinking one has attained what one has not. "Sammadeva" means only by way of cause, method, or reason.

## 4-5. Commentary on the Phāsuvihāra Sutta etc.

94-95. In the fourth sutta, "phāsuvihārā" means pleasant dwellings. In the fifth sutta, "akuppaṃ" refers to the fruit of Arahantship.
41:
## 6. Commentary on the Sutadhara Sutta

In the sixth sutta, "appaṭṭha" means having little exertion. "Appakicca" means having few duties to perform. "Subhara" means one who is easily supported, well-nourished. "Susaññosa" means being well-contented with the three kinds of contentment. "Jīvitaparikkhāresu" means in the supports of life. "Appāhāra" means having little food. "Anodarikatta" means not pursuing the state of being gluttonous, but exerting oneself in the state of non-gluttony. "Appamiddho" means not sleeping much. The seventh and eighth suttas have clear meanings.

## 9. Commentary on the Sīha Sutta

In the ninth sutta, "gives only respectfully, not disrespectfully" means giving without looking down [on the recipient] and without failing [in the manner of giving], not giving while looking down and failing. "May my path of exertion not perish" means may the path of cause for exertion performed by me not perish for me; the meaning is: let there be no people who would say, "A lion, rising and striking a cat, struck it failing [his mark]." In the word "annabhāranesādānaṃ," "anna" refers to barley-rice; because they have the burden of that barley-rice, they are called "annabhāra." This is a name for beggars (yācaka). "Nesāda" refers to fowlers (bird-killers). Thus, even to those beggars and fowlers who are at the very lowest end of all people, he teaches the Dhamma only respectfully.

## 10. Commentary on the Kakudhatthera Sutta

In the tenth sutta, "attabhāvapāṭilābha" means the acquisition of a physical body. In the phrase "two or three Magadhan village-fields," there are small, medium, and large Magadhan village-fields (gāmakhetta). A small village-field is forty usabhas from this [center] and forty usabhas from that, making one gāvuta. A medium one is one gāvuta from here and one gāvuta from there, making half a yojana (two gāvutas). A large one is one and a half gāvutas from here and one and a half gāvutas from there, making three gāvutas. Among those village-fields, the physical body of that [deva Kakudha] was the size of three small village-fields, or the size of two village-fields (one small and one medium). Indeed, his body was three gāvutas [in height]. "Pariharissāmi" means I will attend to, I will protect. "Rakkhassetaṃ" should be resolved as "rakkhassu etaṃ" (protect this [word]). "Moghapurisa" means a hollow man. "Nāssassa" means...
42:
It would not be pleasing to that teacher. "Samudācareyyāma" means we should speak. "Sammannati" means he shows respect. "Yaṃ tumo karissati tumova tena paññāyissati" means whatever deed this teacher will do, this teacher alone will be known by that deed of his. All the remaining words have clear meanings.

## (11) 1. Phāsuvihāra Vagga

## 1. Sārajja Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the third vagga, "vesārajjakaraṇā" refers to the qualities that bring about the state of fearlessness. "Sārajjaṃ hoti" means that dissatisfaction (domanassa) occurs.

## 2. Ussaṅkita Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, "ussaṅkitaparisaṅkito" means being suspected and being suspected from all sides. "Api akuppadhammopi" means that even if one is an Arahant who possesses the unshakeable Dhamma (Arahattaphala), they are suspected by others from all sides along with evil monks. In the terms starting with "vesiyāgocaro", women who live by their beauty are called "vesiyā" (prostitutes). Since those prostitutes are the resort (gocara) of that monk, it is called "vesiyāgocaro". It means frequently going to their houses. The same method applies to the remaining terms. Among those terms, "vidhavā" refers to widows. "Thullakumārikā" refers to elderly maidens who have passed their prime.

## 3. Mahācora Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, "ito bhogena paṭisanthariṣṣāmi" means "I will take wealth from my possessions and make a connection with the one who speaks of my faults, and I will close the gap between that person and me." "Gahaṇāni" refers to the acts of taking the property of others. "Guyhamantā" refers to words of secret consultation. "Antaggāhikāyā" refers to one who holds a view fixed on either eternalism (sassata) or annihilationism (uccheda). All remaining phrases have clear meanings. In the fourth sutta, all meanings follow the method already mentioned below.

## 5. Phāsuvihāra Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, "mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ" refers to bodily action performed with a mind associated with loving-kindness (mettā). "Āvi ceva raho ca" means both in presence and in private. The same method applies to the remaining terms. The words starting with "yāni tāni sīlāni" are spoken by way of the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla).
44:
"Samādhisamvattanikāni" refers to virtues that bring about path-concentration (maggasamādhi) and fruition-concentration (phalasamādhi). "Sīlasāmaññagato" means having reached the state of having equal virtue, meaning being one with identical virtue. "Takkarassa" means for the one who does that act. Thus, in this sutta, virtue is taught mixed with insight (vipassanā). "Diṭṭhi" refers to insight right view (vipassanā-sammādiṭṭhi).

## 6. Ānanda Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, "no ca paraṃ adhisīle sampavattā hoti" means one does not blame or accuse others regarding their virtue. "Attānupekkhī" means one who frequently observes oneself by knowing what has been done and what has not been done by oneself. "No parānupekkhī" means one who does not concern oneself with what has been done or not done by others. "Apaññāto" means an obscure person with little merit. "Apaññātakena" means because of being obscure, due to obscurity and having little merit. "No paritassati" means one does not reach craving (or anxiety). Thus, in this sutta, only the Arahant is spoken of.

## 7-8. Sīla Sutta Vaṇṇanā, etc.
107-108. In the seventh sutta, virtue, concentration, and wisdom are taught mixed together. "Vimutti" refers to the fruition of Arahantship (arahattaphala). "Vimuttiñāṇadassana" refers to the knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇāñāṇa) and is only mundane knowledge (lokiya). In the eighth sutta, it is the same method. However, here, because the knowledge of reviewing arises for the Asekha (Arahant), it is called "Asekha".

## 9-10. Cātuddisa Sutta Vaṇṇanā, etc.
109-110. In the ninth sutta, "cātuddiso" refers to one who travels without obstruction in the four directions. In this sutta also, only the Arahant is spoken of. In the tenth sutta, "alaṃ" means suitable. Here also, only the Arahant is spoken of.

## (12) 2. Andhakavinda Vagga

## 1. Kulūpaka Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the second vagga, "asanthavavissāsī" refers to one who becomes intimate only with those who are not intimate (or do not wish to be intimate) with oneself.
45:
"Anissaravikappī" refers to one who, despite not being in control, manages and directs like a person in control, saying, "Give this, take this." "Vissaṭṭhupasevī" refers to one who associates with divided families for the purpose of reconciling them. "Upakaṇṇakajappī" refers to one who consults and speaks in whispers near the ear. The bright side (sukkapakkha) should be understood by the opposite of the meaning already mentioned.

## 2. Pacchāsamaṇa Sutta Vaṇṇanā

"Na nivāreti" means not knowing that this speech is a word of committing an offense (āpatti). Or even if knowing, not forbidding it by saying, "Venerable sir, it is not proper to speak such words." ## 2. Commentary on the Second Cakkānuvattana Sutta
In the second sutta, regarding "the wheel set in motion by the father," when a Wheel-turning Monarch ordains or passes away, the Wheel Treasure remains for only seven days and then disappears; why then is it said that he "sets that wheel in motion again"? It is because, while standing in the lineage of his father, fulfilling the duties of a Wheel-turning Monarch and exercising sovereignty, he is said to set in motion again only the wheel that was set in motion by his father.

In the phrase 'up to the seventh generation of grandfathers' (yāva sattamā pitāmahayugā), the father's father is called 'grandfather' (pitāmaha), and the generation of the grandfather is called 'pitāmahayuga'. Thus, it shows that one has a pure womb up to the seventh generation, or that one is not rejected or censured in terms of birth. 'Akkhitto' means not rejected (anavakkhitto), as in saying, "Remove this person, what use is he?" 'Anupakkuṭṭho' means not censured, or never having previously encountered abuse or blame. In the words beginning with 'aḍḍho', it refers to anyone who is wealthy with their own possessions. ## 1. Avajānāti Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the fifth vagga, "saṃvāsena" means by living together. "Ādeyyamukho" means having a face that is accepted through trust, or having a face that is taken. ## 2. Ārabhati Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, "there is transgression and there is remorse" means one both transgresses by way of violating an offense and becomes remorseful because of that. "Does not know" means not knowing because of not having attained. "Transgresses but there is no remorse" means although one falls into an offense, there is no remorse because one has risen from the offense. ## 3. Sārandada Sutta Vaṇṇanā

## 4. Tikaṇḍakī Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, "appaṭikūle" means in an object that is not repulsive. "Paṭikūlasaññī" means having the perception that "it is repulsive." This method should be understood in the same way for all terms. How does this monk dwell in this manner? In a desirable object, he either pervades it with the perception of foulness (asubha) or reflects on it as impermanent (anicca). Thus, he first dwells perceiving the non-repulsive as repulsive. In an undesirable object, he either pervades it with loving-kindness (mettā) or reflects on it as elements (dhātu/ultimate reality). Thus, he dwells perceiving the repulsive as non-repulsive.

Regarding both types of objects (repulsive and non-repulsive), the third and fourth cycles are taught by way of the previous and subsequent methods. The fifth cycle is taught by way of the six-factored equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā). This six-factored equanimity is similar to the equanimity of an Arahant, but it is not the actual equanimity of an Arahant. In that context, "upekkhako vihareyya" means he should dwell established in a state of neutrality. "Kvacani" means in any object. "Katthaci" means in any place. "Kiñcana" means even a little bit.

Thus, in this sutta, insight (vipassanā) alone is taught in five places. A monk who has begun insight (āraddha-vipassaka) is able to do this; a monk who is wise, possessing superior wisdom, and learned (bahussuta) is also able to do this. Stream-enterers (sotāpanna), Once-returners (sakadāgāmi), and Non-returners (anāgāmi) are certainly able to do this; as for the Arahant (khīṇāsava), it goes without saying. The fifth sutta has a clear meaning.

## (17) 2. Āghātavagga

## 1. Commentary on the Paṭhama-āghātapaṭivinaya Sutta

In the first sutta of the second vagga, they are called "āghātapaṭivinaya" (the dispelling of resentment) because they dispel and appease resentment. "Yattha bhikkhuno uppanno āghāto sabbaso paṭivinetabbo" means that in whatever object resentment has arisen for a monk, all that resentment should be dispelled by these five means. "Mettā tasmiṃ puggale bhāvetabbā" means that loving-kindness (mettā) should be developed through the power of the threefold and fourfold jhānas. The same method applies to compassion (karuṇā). Equanimity (upekkhā), however, should be developed through the power of the fourfold and fivefold jhānas. Because the mind is not at peace for one who looks at that person, and appreciative joy (muditā) cannot be established in that person, therefore muditā is not mentioned. "Asati-amanasikāro" means that one should reach the state of non-mindfulness and non-attention toward that person with whom resentment is held. One should reach the state of non-mindfulness and non-attention toward that person in such a way that the person does not appear, as if obstructed by a wall or similar object. The remaining words are clear according to the method already mentioned below.

## 2. Commentary on the Dutiya-āghātapaṭivinaya Sutta

In the second sutta, it is called "āghātapaṭivinaya" because resentment is dispelled toward those persons with whom resentment is held, and also because resentment is dispelled by those good practices. Indeed, this word "paṭivinaya" is a designation for both the persons who are the objects of resentment to be destroyed and the good practices which are the causes for destroying resentment; both are appropriate here. The five persons are the objects (vatthu) for destroying resentment, and the five practices illustrated by the five similes are the causes for destroying resentment. "Labhati ca kālena kālaṃ cetaso vivaraṃ cetaso pasādaṃ" means that from time to time, one obtains the opening (vivara) known as the opportunity for the arising of the mind of tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), and the clarity (pasāda) known as the state of being endowed with faith.

"Rathiyāya" means on the main road. "Nantakaṃ" refers to a piece of worn-out cloth. "Niggahētvā" means by treading upon. "Yo tattha sāro" means whatever strong part is there in that worn-out cloth. "Taṃ paripātētvā" means by plucking out that strong part. In this phrase "evameva kho," the person who dwells in loving-kindness should be understood like the monk who wears rag-robes (paṃsukūlika); the enemy person should be understood like the worn-out cloth on the road; the impure bodily conduct should be understood like the weak part; and the pure verbal conduct should be understood like the strong part. Just as in the time when one discards the weak part, takes the strong part, sews it, dyes it, and wears it while wandering about, one should (likewise) not attend to the impure bodily conduct but attend to the pure verbal conduct.
57:
Just as the time when (the rag-robe monk) wanders about wearing (the robe made from the rag), it should be understood as the time of living happily by appeasing the (angry) mind toward the enemy, not attending to the state of having impure bodily conduct but attending to the state of having pure verbal conduct.

'Sevālapannaka-pariyonaddhā' refers to a pond covered with moss and water-weeds. 'Ghamma-pareto' is a person overcome by the heat. 'Kilanto' is a person tired from a journey. 'Tasito' is a person overcome by craving (thirst). 'Pipāsito' is a person desiring to drink water. 'Apavyūhitvā' means having pushed aside. 'Pivitvā' means having drunk the clear water. In this simile 'evameva kho,' the person who dwells in loving-kindness should be understood like the man overcome by heat. Impure verbal conduct should be understood like the moss and water-weeds. Pure bodily conduct should be understood like the clear water. Just as going after pushing aside the moss and water-weeds and drinking the clear water, it should be understood as the time of living happily by appeasing the (angry) mind toward the enemy, not attending to the impure verbal conduct but attending to the pure bodily conduct.

'Khobhessāmi' means I will stir up. 'Loḷessāmi' means I will make it turbid and messy. 'Apeyyampi taṃ karissāmi' means I will make that water undrinkable. 'Catukkuṇḍiko' means being a person on all fours by resting on the ground with both knees and both hands. 'Gopītakaṃ pivitvā' means drinking by drawing in with the mouth like a cow. In this simile 'evameva kho,' the person who dwells in loving-kindness should be understood like the man overcome by heat. The enemy person should be understood like the puddle in a cow's footprint. The small amount of merit within that person should be understood like the small amount of water in the cow's footprint. Just as drinking like a cow on all fours and then departing, one should know the appeasing of the (angry) mind by attending to that (small merit), not attending to that person's impure bodily and verbal conduct, but attending to whatever joy and gladness, known as the opening and clarity of mind, that he obtains from time to time based on hearing the Dhamma.

'Ābādhiko' is one who is pained by an incompatible disease that breaks the postures. 'Puratopissa' means it would also be in front of him. 'Anaya-vyasanaṃ' refers to non-prosperity and ruin. In this simile 'evameva kho,' the person endowed with all dark states should be known like that helpless sick person. Saṃsāra, whose beginning is unknown, should be known like the long journey. The distance of Nibbāna should be known like the distance of the villages in front and behind. The failure to obtain the fruit of the Noble Path (Ariya-phala) should be known like the failure to obtain suitable food. The failure to obtain tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā) should be known like the failure to obtain suitable medicine. The failure to obtain teachers who will give advice and instruction should be known like the failure to obtain a suitable attendant. The failure to obtain the Buddha or a disciple (sāvaka) who will lead one to Nibbāna should be known like the failure to obtain a guide who will lead one to a village. Just as a certain man sees (that sick person) and feels pity and compassion, the person who dwells in loving-kindness toward that enemy person should know the appeasing of the (angry) mind by generating compassion.

'Sādudaka' means having clear (sweet) water. 'Sītudaka' means having cool water. 'Setaka' means having a white appearance where the waves break. 'Suppatittha' means (having a good landing place)...
58:
One should understand the absence of Samatha and Vipassanā as being like not obtaining suitable medicine. One should understand the absence of teachers who can treat defilements (kilesa) through advice and instruction as being like not obtaining suitable attendants. One should understand the failure to meet the Blessed One or a disciple of the Buddha who can lead one to Nibbāna as being like not obtaining a guide to a village. Just as compassion (karuṇā) arises upon seeing a certain man, one who dwells in loving-kindness (mettā) should be understood to cool the mind by generating compassion for that person.

'Acchodakā' means having clear water. 'Sātodakā' means having sweet water. 'Sītodakā' means having cool water. 'Setakā' means being white in color at the places where waves break. 'Supatitthā' means having even landing places.

In the phrase 'Evameva kho', the one who dwells in loving-kindness should be seen like the man oppressed by the heat of the sun. The person whose sense-doors are entirely purified should be seen like that pond. Just as bathing, drinking, coming out of the pond, lying in the shade of a tree, and going as one pleases, one should understand the cooling of the mind by taking whatever object one desires at those doors. The third and fourth suttas follow the same method as previously mentioned.

## 5. Pañhapucchāsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, 'paribhavanti' means asking for the purpose of disparaging, thinking, "I will disparage him in this way." 'Aññātukāmo' means wishing to know.

## 6. Nirodhasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, 'atthetaṃ ṭhānaṃ' means there is this reason. 'No ce diṭṭheva dhamme aññaṃ ārādheyya' means if one does not reach the fruit of Arahatship in this very life. 'Kabaḷīkārāhārabhakkhānaṃ devānaṃ' refers to the devas of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara). 'Aññataraṃ manomayaṃ kāyaṃ' refers to a certain group of Suddhāvāsa Brahmās produced by the jhāna mind. 'Udāyī' refers to Lāḷudāyī. Hearing the word "mind-made" (manomaya), he objected, saying, "It should not be in the formless realm." While monks were rebuking such words in the presence of the Venerable Sāriputta, saying, "What does Sāriputta know?", the Elder, in order to prevent the emergence of the views of fools, did not tolerate that speech and approached the Blessed One.

'Atthi nāma' is a particle used in the sense of intolerance. Therefore, the future tense 'ajjhupekkhiṣṣatha' is used here. The meaning here is: "Ananda, you [plural]..."
61:
Alternatively, for one who sees that object in such a manner, the destruction of taints (āsavānaṃ khaya) occurs immediately; thus, the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala) arises. In the passage "Yathā suṇato," the same method applies. Or else, having seen a visible object with the eye-sensitivity and immediately establishing insight (vipassanā), one reaches Arahantship; that Arahantship of his is said to occur immediately after eye-consciousness (cakkhuviññāṇa). With reference to this, it was said: "This is the foremost of visions." In the second phrase, the same method applies.

"Yathā sukhitassa" means for one who is happy with the bliss of the path (maggasukha), the destruction of taints occurs immediately; thus, Arahantship arises immediately. "This is the foremost of happiness" means this bliss of the path is superior to all forms of happiness. In "Yathā saññissa," only the perception associated with the path (maggasaññā) is intended. "Yathā bhūtassa" means for one who stands in such an existence or such an individuality (attabhāva), Arahantship arises immediately. "This is the foremost of existences" means this final individuality is the foremost among existences. Alternatively, "Yathā bhūtassa" means for one who is present at the moment of the path with such aggregates (khandha), the destruction of taints occurs immediately; thus, the fruit arises immediately after the path. "This is the foremost of existences" means the group of five aggregates at this moment of the path is the foremost among existences.

## 1-3. Commentary on the Sārajjasutta, etc.

171-173. In the first, second, and third suttas of the third chapter, the practice of householders (agāriyappaṭipatti) is taught. Whether they be Stream-enterers or Once-returners, it is indeed appropriate.

## 4. Verasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, "Bhayāni" refers to fears known as mental terrors. "Verāni" refers to both the enmities of unwholesome states and the enmities of persons. "Cetasikaṃ" means a state dependent on the mind. "Dukkhaṃ" means suffering that has the physical sensitivity (kāyapasāda) as its basis. "Domanassaṃ" means the feeling of displeasure (domanassa-vedanā). In this sutta, abandoning by way of abstinence (viratipahāna) is taught.
62:
## 5. Caṇḍālasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, 'upāsakapatikuṭṭha' refers to the lowest or most contemptible lay follower. 'Kotūhalamangalika' refers to one who is endowed with omens of what is seen, heard, and sensed (diṭṭha, suta, muta), which are called superstitious excitements, occurring in the form: "Because of this, such a blessing will occur." 'Mangalaṃ pacceti no kammaṃ' means trusting and believing only in omens, and not trusting or believing in kamma. 'Ito ca bahiddhā' means outside of this Dispensation (Sāsana). 'Pubbakāraṃ karoti' means performing meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna) and so forth, first of all.

## 6. Pītisutta-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, 'kinti mayaṃ' means "By what means do we?" 'Pavivekaṃ pītiṃ' refers to the joy (pīti) that arises depending on the first and second jhānas. 'Kāmūpasaṃhitaṃ' means arising depending on the two types of sensuality: objective sensuality (vatthukāma) and subjective sensuality (kilesakāma). 'Akusalūpasaṃhitaṃ' means arising depending on the unwholesome, such as when shooting an arrow with the thought, "I will shoot a deer, a pig, etc.," and when that arrow misses, thinking, "I have missed." However, in such places where deer, pigs, etc., are shot, the pleasure and joy (sukha somanassa) that arises in one who does not miss, thinking, "I have shot well, I have struck well," is called 'akusalūpasaṃhita sukhasomanassa' (unwholesome-related pleasure and joy). On the other hand, the pain and grief (dukkha domanassa) that arises due to the incompleteness of meritorious foundations such as giving (dāna) should be understood as 'kusalūpasaṃhita dukkhadomanassa' (wholesome-related pain and grief).

## 7. Vaṇijjāsutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, 'vaṇijjā' refers to the acts of trading. 'Upāsakena' refers to a lay follower who has gone to the Three Refuges. 'Satthavaṇijjā' is the making of weapons and selling them. 'Sattavaṇijjā' is the selling of human beings. 'Maṃsavaṇijjā' is the raising of animals such as pigs and deer and selling them. 'Majjavaṇijjā' is the making of any kind of intoxicant and selling it. 'Visavaṇijjā' is the making of poison and selling it. Thus, all these types of trade should not be done by oneself, nor should one encourage others to do them.

## 8. Rājasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, 'pabbājenti' means banishing from the country. 'Yathāpaccayaṃ vā karonti' means acting according to one's own will or inclination. 'Tatheva pāpakammaṃ pavedenti' means that in whatever manner that person committed an evil deed, they report and reveal it to others in that very same manner.
63:
## 9. Gihisutta-vaṇṇanā

In the ninth sutta, 'saṃvutakammanta' means having closed or restrained actions. 'Ābhicetasikānaṃ' refers to those who depend on the sublime mind. 'Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānaṃ' refers to those who dwell happily in the Dhamma in the present moment, at the very moment of occurrence. 'Ariyakantehi' means by the virtues (sīla) of the Path and Fruit, which are dear to the Noble Ones.

In the phrase "ariyadhammaṃ samādāya," 'ariyadhamma' refers to the Five Precepts. 'Merayaṃ vāruṇiṃ' refers to the four kinds of fermented liquor (meraya) and the five kinds of spirits (surā). 'Dhammañcānuvitakkaye' means one should reflect on the ninefold supramundane Dhamma only by way of recollection (anussati). 'Abyāpajjhaṃ hitaṃ cittaṃ' refers to the mind of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) such as loving-kindness (mettā), which is free from suffering. 'Devalokāya bhāvaye' means one should develop it for the sake of the Brahma world. 'Puññatthဿ jigīsato' refers to one who desires merit, who seeks merit. 'Santesu' refers to the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples (sāvakas). 'Vipulā hoti dakkhiṇā' means the gift thus given is of great fruit. 'Anupubbena' means in sequence, such as the fulfillment of virtue (sīla) and so forth. The remaining terms have the same meaning as stated in the Tika Nipāta.

## 10. Gavesīsutta-vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, "sitaṃ pātvākāsi" means that while traveling on the main road, the Buddha looked at that Sāla grove and considered, "Has any good cause that matures omniscience occurred in this place before?" He then saw the good cause performed by the lay follower named Gavesī during the time of Kassapa Buddha. Then the thought occurred to the Buddha: "This good cause is not manifest to the Saṅgha; it is hidden. Now, I shall make it manifest to the Saṅgha." Stepping off the road and standing in a certain spot, he manifested a smile. He smiled gently, showing the tips of his teeth. Worldly people laugh while striking their bellies, saying "kahaṃ kahaṃ," but the Buddhas do not laugh in that way. The smile of the Buddhas is merely a joyful manner.

What is called laughter (smiling) occurs with thirteen types of consciousness accompanied by joy (somanassa). Among those thirteen types of consciousness, worldly people (puthujjanas) laugh with eight types of consciousness: four from unwholesome consciousness and four from sense-sphere wholesome consciousness. Learners (sekhas) laugh with six types of consciousness, having abandoned the two types of unwholesome consciousness associated with wrong view. Arahants (khīṇāsavas) laugh with five types of consciousness: four rooted functional (sahetuka-kiriya) consciousnesses and one rootless functional (ahetuka-kiriya) consciousness...
64:
(Arahants) laugh with consciousnesses. Among those, when a strong object comes into range, they laugh with two types of consciousness associated with knowledge (ñāṇasampayutta). In the case of a weak object, they laugh with three types of consciousness: two with two roots (duhetuka) and one rootless (ahetuka). In this context, the functional rootless mind-consciousness element (kiriya ahetuka manoviññāṇadhātu) accompanied by joy (somanassasahagata) produces a smile in the Blessed One, which is merely an expression of mirth.

Even such a slight smile became evident to the Venerable Ānanda. How did it become evident? At such a time of smiling, from the four canine teeth of the Tathāgata, rays of light—shining like streaks of lightning descending from the face of a great rain cloud that covers the four continents, and having the size of a great palmyra trunk—emerged, circled the noble head three times clockwise, and disappeared into the tips of the canine teeth themselves. By that sign, the Venerable Ānanda, even though walking behind the Blessed One, knew the manifestation of the smile.

Iddha means prosperous. Phīta means very prosperous, like a tree in full bloom. Ākiṇṇamanussa means crowded with people. Sīlesu aparipūrakārī means one who does not habitually fulfill the five precepts. Paṭidesitāni means those who have declared (confessed) their status as lay followers. Samādapitāni means those who have been established in the refuges. This matter is equal (samasamaṃ) in every respect, not just in part. "I have no practice superior to these donors." The word handa is a particle used in the sense of determination and relinquishment. Atirekāya means for the sake of a special cause or benefit. "Regard me as one who habitually fulfills the five precepts." By this much, those five precepts are said to be undertaken by him. "For what reason shall we not be those who fulfill them?" The remaining words in this sutta are clear.

## (19) 4. The Forest Chapter.

## 1. Commentary on the Āraññika Sutta

In the first sutta of the fourth chapter, mandattā momūhattā means knowing neither the undertaking nor the benefits. One dwells in the forest solely out of ignorance due to one's own dullness and delusion.
65:
One becomes a forest-dweller (āraññaka). Evil desire and being overcome by desire means dwelling in the forest with such an evil desire as: "When I dwell in the forest, they will respect me with the four requisites, saying, 'This is a forest-dweller,' and they will honor me with such qualities as, 'This monk is modest and secluded.'" Being overcome by that very evil desire, one becomes a forest-dweller. A monk who enters and dwells in the forest by the power of madness is called a forest-dweller due to mental distraction (cittakkhepa). "Praised" means one becomes a forest-dweller because this factor of a forest-dweller (āraññakanga) is praised and commended by the Buddhas and their disciples. "Desiring this practice" (idamatthitā) means: because there is benefit in this beautiful practice, it is called idamatthī; the state of such a person is idamatthitā. One becomes a forest-dweller depending only on the desire for that beautiful practice, not depending on any other worldly gain (lokāmisa). The remaining words in this sutta and the following ones have clear meanings.
