## (20) 5. The Brahmin Chapter.

## 1. Commentary on the Soṇa Sutta

In the first sutta of the fifth chapter, brāhmaṇadhamma means the nature of Brahmins. "Among dogs" means it occurs among dogs. "Neither buy nor sell" means they do not buy by taking, nor do they sell by giving. "They consort only with those they love to maintain the lineage" means a loving Brahmin approaches a loving Brahmin woman and engages in consorting to continue the family line. "Filling the belly" means expanding and filling the stomach. "Taking the remainder, they depart" means when they can no longer eat certain food, they pack it up and take it away. In this sutta, only the cycle of suffering (vaṭṭa) is discussed.

## 2. Commentary on the Doṇa Brāhmaṇa Sutta

In the second sutta, "Do you also (claim to be a Brahmin like us)?" is a question: "Do you also profess to be a Brahmin?" "Originators" means those who brought forth (the Vedas). "Of whom" means belonging to those Brahmins. Mantapada refers only to the mantras known as the Vedas. "Sung" means chanted with perfect intonation by the ten ancient Brahmins, such as Aṭṭhaka and others. "Spoken" means told or taught to others. "Collected" means well-assembled or made into a collection.
66:
It means placed in a heap or pile. 'Tadanugāyanti' means that nowadays, Brahmins imitate and sing those Vedas that were sung by the ancient Brahmins such as Aṭṭhaka and others; they imitate and recite them. 'Tadanubhāsanti' means they imitate and speak those Vedas. This word is merely a synonym of the preceding term. 'Bhāsitamanubhāsanti' means they imitate and speak the Vedas spoken by those sages. 'Sajjhāyitamanusajjhāyanti' means they imitate and recite the Vedas recited by those Brahmins. 'Vācitamanuvācenti' means they imitate and teach the Vedas that were taught by those Brahmins to others. 'Seyyathidaṃ' means 'who are those who composed the Vedic texts?' Aṭṭhaka and others are their names. It is said that those Brahmins such as Aṭṭhaka, having looked with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) and without harming or killing others, composed the Vedic texts in alignment with the Dhamma of the Blessed Kassapa Buddha. However, later Brahmins included practices such as killing living beings, corrupted the three Vedas, and made them contrary to the Buddha's words. In the term 'tyāssume', 'assu' is merely a particle. It means those Brahmins designate these five types of Brahmins.

'Mante adhīyamāno' means reciting and learning the Vedas. 'Ācariyadhanaṃ' means the wealth to be offered to the teacher, the teacher's portion. 'Na issatthena' means not seeking wealth through the profession of a warrior or archery. 'Na rājaporisena' means not seeking wealth through royal service. 'Kevalaṃ bhikkhācariyāya' means only through pure alms-gathering. 'Kapālaṃ anatimanyamāno' means not despising the alms-bowl. Indeed, that Brahmin, taking the bowl filled with alms, having washed his head and bathed, stands at the doors of families and begs: "I have practiced the supreme conduct (brahmacariya) since youth for forty-eight years, and I have also learned the Vedas; I wish to give the teacher's fee to my teacher, so give me wealth." Upon hearing those words, people give eight coins, sixteen coins, a hundred, or a thousand coins according to their ability. In this way, having wandered through the entire village, he hands over the wealth obtained to the teacher. Referring to such handing over, this was said. "Doṇa, in this way a Brahmin is equal to Brahma" means that because he is endowed with the divine abidings (brahmavihāra) in this manner, a Brahmin is called one who is equal to Brahma.

'Neva kayena na vikkayena' means neither buying it oneself nor accepting what is given by others through sale. 'Udakūpassaṭṭhaṃ' means given by pouring water. Indeed, when there is a marriageable daughter in a certain family, that Brahmin goes and stands at the door of that house. When asked, "Why are you standing here?", he says, "I have practiced the supreme conduct (brahmacariya) since youth for forty-eight years; I give all that [merit] to you, so give me your daughter." Those parents, having brought the daughter, pour water on the hand of that Brahmin and give her. That Brahmin takes the wife given by pouring water and departs. 'Atimīḷhajo' means...
67:
It is like being born in a very filthy, large heap of dung. That Brahmin's wife is (not for the sake of playing). 'Na davatthā' means not for the sake of playing. 'Na ratatthā' means not for the sake of sensual delight. 'Methunaṃ uppādetvā' means having produced a daughter or a son, and thinking, "Now the lineage will be continued," he leaves the household and goes forth as a monk. 'Sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ' (a happy destination, a heavenly world) is said referring only to the Brahma-world. 'Devasamo hoti' means he is called one who is equal to a god because he is endowed with the divine dwellings (dibbavihāra).

'Tam-eva puttassādaṃ nikāmayamāno' means that upon seeing his own daughter or son, love and delight in the child arise; it refers to living while longing for and desiring that delight. 'Kuṭumbaṃ ajjhāvasati' means establishing wealth and living in the midst of that wealth. The remaining words in this Sutta are quite clear.

## 3. Saṅgārava Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the third Sutta, 'pageva' means right from the start. 'Kāmarāgapariyuṭṭhitena' means one who is overwhelmed and seized by sensual lust. 'Kāmarāgaparetana' means one who is followed by sensual lust. 'Nissaraṇaṃ' means there are three kinds of escape from sensual lust: escape by suppression (vikkhambhana-nissaraṇa), escape by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-nissaraṇa), and escape by eradication (samuccheda-nissaraṇa). Among those three, the first jhāna in the meditation on foulness (asubha) is called escape by suppression. Insight (vipassanā) is called escape by substitution of opposites. The path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga) is called escape by eradication. It means not knowing these three kinds of escape distinctly. In the terms 'attattham-pi' etc., one's own benefit, known as the fruit of Arahantship, is called 'attattha'. The benefit of the donors of the four requisites is called 'parattha'. Both of these together are called 'ubhayattha'. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all instances.

This is the distinction: In the sections such as the escape from ill-will (byāpāda), there are only two kinds of escape: escape by suppression and escape by eradication. Among those, for ill-will, the first jhāna of loving-kindness (mettā) is escape by suppression, and the path of Non-returning (anāgāmi-magga) is escape by eradication. For sloth and torpor (thīnamiddha), the perception of light (āloka-saññā) is escape by suppression, and the path of Arahantship is escape by eradication. For restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca), any kind of calm (samatha) is escape by suppression. Here, for restlessness (uddhacca), the path of Arahantship is escape by eradication, and for remorse (kukkucca), the path of Non-returning is escape by eradication. For doubt (vicikicchā), the defining of phenomena (dhamma-vavatthāna) is escape by suppression, and the first path (pathama-magga) is escape by eradication.

In the similes mentioned in this Sutta, such as "Brahmin, it is like a water bowl mixed with lac," 'udapatto' means a bowl filled with water.
68:
Saṃsaṭṭha means mixed by way of causing discoloration. Pakkuthita means boiling intensely. Ussutita means being steamy (hot water). Sevālapannakapariyonaddha means covered all around with mosses such as sesame-seed-like algae or water-surface algae with the color of a stingray's back. Vāterita means shaken or stirred by the wind. Āvila means unclear or turbid. Luḷita means unsettled (muddy). Kalalībhūta means become like mud. Andhakāre nikkhitta means placed in a dark place without light, such as a storehouse. In this Sutta, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma through three cycles and concluded it with the pinnacle of Arahantship; the Brahmin Saṅgārava, however, was established in the Refuges.

## 4. Commentary on the Kāraṇapālī Sutta
In the fourth, the Kāraṇapālī Sutta, Kāraṇapālī is the name of that Brahmin. He is called Kāraṇapālī because he manages the affairs of the royal family. "Managing affairs" means rising early in the morning to oversee the construction of gates, watchtowers, and walls that have not yet been built, and repairing those that are old and decayed. The Brahmin Piṅgiyānī is a noble disciple (ariya-sāvaka) established in the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala). It is said that he would rise early, take perfumes, garlands, etc., go to the Teacher, pay homage, offer the perfumes and garlands, and then return to the city; this was the Brahmin's daily routine. Kāraṇapālī Brahmin saw Piṅgiyānī returning after performing this routine. Seeing him, he said this: Thinking, "This Brahmin Piṅgiyānī is wise and possesses superior knowledge; where has he gone so early and is now returning?" and recognizing the Brahmin as he approached, he spoke the words beginning with "Well, from where [do you come]?"

Therein, divā divassa means during the day of the day, meaning at the time of midday. Paṇḍito maññe means "Does the venerable Piṅgiyānī consider the ascetic Gotama to be wise, or not?"—this is the meaning here. "Who am I, sir, [to know the ascetic Gotama's proficiency in wisdom]?" means how could someone like me know? "How can I know the ascetic Gotama's proficiency in wisdom? By what reason could I know?" Thus, in every way, he shows his own inability to know. "He who could know the ascetic Gotama's proficiency in wisdom would surely be one like him, who has fulfilled the ten perfections and attained Omniscience." This is the meaning. Indeed, just as one who wishes to measure Mount Sineru, the earth, or the sky needs to obtain a rod or a rope of that same magnitude, so too...
69:
...such a person would be a Buddha alone. Truly, just as one who wishes to measure Mount Sineru, the earth, or the sky must obtain a rod or a rope of that magnitude, so too, he shows that one who wishes to know the wisdom of the ascetic Gotama must obtain Omniscient Knowledge similar to his own knowledge. Here, it is said again out of respect. 'Uḷārāya' means noble, especially excellent. "Who am I, sir?" means "Who am I, sir, in the matter of praising the ascetic Gotama?" "By what reason could I praise the ascetic Gotama?" is the meaning.

'Pasatthappasattha' means he is praised by his own qualities which are above all other qualities and are praised by the whole world. For that Blessed One, there is no need for praise by others. For example, just as a jasmine flower, a blue lotus, a paduma lotus, or red sandalwood are delightful and fragrant by their own color, scent, and splendor, and they do not need to be praised by external colors or scents; and just as a precious gem or the moon's disk shines by its own light and does not need to be illuminated by another light; even so, the ascetic Gotama is praised and extolled by his own qualities which are praised by the whole world, and he has reached the state of being the most excellent in the entire world. For that Blessed One, there is no need for praise by others.

Alternatively, 'Pasatthappasattha' means he is praised by those who are themselves praised. Who are those who are praised? King Pasenadi of Kosala is praised by the inhabitants of Kāsi and Kosala; King Bimbisāra by the inhabitants of Aṅga and Magadha; the Licchavi princes of Vesālī by the inhabitants of the Vajjian territory; the Mallas of Pāvā, the Mallas of Kusinārā, and other various kings are praised by the inhabitants of their respective districts. Brahmins like Caṅkī are praised by groups of Brahmins; lay followers like Anāthapiṇḍika are praised by groups of lay followers; female lay followers like Visākhā are praised by hundreds of female lay followers; wanderers like Sakuludāyī are praised by hundreds of wanderers; great female disciples like the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā are praised by hundreds of bhikkhunīs; great elders like the Elder Sāriputta are praised by hundreds of bhikkhus; gods like Sakka are praised by many thousands of gods; and Brahmas like Mahā Brahma are praised by many thousands of Brahmas. Since all of them extol, laud, and praise the Ten-Powered One, the Blessed One is called 'Pasatthappasattha.' 'Atthavasaṃ' means the benefit or advantage.
70:
Then, that brahmin, wishing to explain the reason for his devotion, said: "Sirs, just as if a man..." and so on. In that statement, 'aggarasaparititta' refers to one who has eaten and drunk to satiety, up to the throat, with the best of flavors, such as the cream of milk among foods, pure honey among drinks, and sugar among sweet flavors. Other inferior flavors compared to the best flavors are called 'aññesaṃ hīnānaṃ'. 'Suttaso' means by way of the Suttas, or in the form of the Suttas. The same method applies to the remaining terms. 'Tato tato' means from those various Suttas and so forth. The doctrines of many other recluses and brahmins are called 'aññesaṃ puthusamanabrāhmaṇappavādānaṃ'. Such a person does not long for those doctrines; even when they are being spoken, he has no desire to listen. 'Jighacchādubbalyapareto' means overcome by hunger and weakness. 'Madhupiṇḍika' refers to a ball of sweets made by mixing roasted Shali rice flour with the four sweet substances (catumadhura), or simply a sweet cake. 'Adhigaccheyya' means one would obtain. 'Asecanaka' refers to a flavor that is naturally delicious and excellent, not needing to be mixed with other flavors to make it sweet.

'Haricandana' refers to golden-colored sandalwood. 'Lohitacandana' refers to red sandalwood. 'Surabhigandha' means having a fragrant scent. Distresses and so forth refer only to the distress, exhaustion, and fever of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). 'Udānaṃ udānesi' means uttering a joyful exclamation. For example, just as oil that a measuring vessel cannot contain and thus overflows is called 'avaseka', and just as water that a lake cannot contain and thus overflows is called 'ogha', even so, when words of joy cannot be contained by the heart and, unable to remain within, come out, they are called 'udāna'. It means he uttered such words filled with joy.

## 5. Piṅgiyānīsutta-vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the fifth sutta, the word 'nīlā' is a term that encompasses all shades of blue. 'Nīlavaṇṇā' and so forth show the different varieties of that blue color. In this context, the natural complexion of the Licchavī princes was not blue, but they are described as such because they were anointed with blue ointments. 'Nīlavatthā' means that their garments, such as cloth and silk, were also blue. 'Nīlālaṅkārā' means they were adorned with blue gems and blue flowers. All their hand ornaments, horse trappings, chariot decorations, curtains, canopies, and tunics were also blue. In this way, the meaning should be understood for all the terms.
71:
"Padumaṃ yathā" means like a red lotus with more than a hundred petals. "Kokanada" is also a synonym for that red lotus. "Pāto" means early, at the time of sunrise. "Siyā" means it would be. "Avītagandhaṃ" means not devoid of fragrance (fragrant). Because rays of light emit from the various parts of the Blessed One's body, he is called "Aṅgīrasa". "Tapantamādiccamivantaliikkhe" means beautiful like the sun shining in the sky, providing light to the four great islands surrounded by two thousand small islands. In saying "Behold Aṅgīrasa," he refers to either himself or the great multitude of people.

## 6. Mahāsupinasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the sixth sutta, the Mahāsupina Sutta, "Mahāsupina" (Great Dreams) are so called because they are dreamt by great men and because they are portents of great benefits. "Pāturahesuṃ" means they became manifest. Regarding the dreaming of dreams, one dreams due to four causes: (1) disturbance of the elements, (2) previous experience, (3) influence of deities, or (4) prophetic signs.

Among these, a person whose elements are disturbed due to causes that agitate the bile and so forth dreams due to the disturbance of the elements. When dreaming thus, one sees various dreams such as falling from a mountain, flying through the sky, or being chased by wild beasts, elephants, or thieves. One who dreams due to previous experience sees objects that were experienced or felt in the past. To one who dreams due to the influence of deities, the deities present various objects, either out of a desire for one's welfare or harm, or for the sake of benefit or detriment. That person sees those objects through the power of those deities. One who dreams due to prophetic signs sees a dream that is a portent of future benefit or harm that is to arise through the power of merit or demerit. For example, the mother of the Bodhisatta dreamt a sign of obtaining a son, or King Kosala dreamt sixteen dreams, or the Blessed One himself, while still a Bodhisatta, dreamt these five great dreams.

Among these dreams, those dreamt due to the disturbance of the elements or previous experience are not true. Those dreamt due to the influence of deities may be true or false (because angry deities, wishing to cause destruction through artifice, may show distorted things). However, a dream dreamt due to prophetic signs is certainly...
72:
A dream seen because of a previous omen is indeed true. Due to the variations of these four root causes, the types of dreams also vary. Only trainees (sekhas) and worldlings (puthujjanas) see these four types of dreams because they have not yet abandoned distortions (vipallāsa); those who are beyond training (asekhas) do not see them because they have abandoned distortions. Does one who sees a dream see it while asleep, while awake, or while neither asleep nor awake? In this matter, if one sees it while asleep, it would contradict the Abhidhamma teachings. This is because one sleeps with the life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅga-citta), and that bhavaṅga-citta does not have objects such as visual signs (rūpa-nimitta) nor is it associated with lust (rāga) and so on. However, such consciousnesses do arise in one who sees a dream. If one sees it while awake, it would contradict the Vinaya teachings. This is because what one sees while awake is seen with conventional consciousness (sabbovahārika-citta). If a transgression is committed with such consciousness, there is no such thing as not being an offense (anāpatti). Yet, even if one who sees a dream commits a transgression, it is definitely not an offense. If one sees it while neither asleep nor awake, one would not be said to 'see' anything at all; if that were the case, would it not mean that dreams do not exist? They do not non-exist. Why? Because one sees a dream when possessed by 'monkey-sleep' (kapimiddha). For it was said: 'Great King, one who is possessed by monkey-sleep sees a dream.'

'Possessed by monkey-sleep' means being endowed with the sleep of a monkey. Just as a monkey's sleep is light and easily disturbed, so too is that sleep which is light and easily disturbed because it is repeatedly interspersed with wholesome and other types of consciousness; one sees a dream when endowed with such sleep, during which there is a repeated emerging from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). Therefore, this dream may be wholesome (kusala), unwholesome (akusala), or indeterminate (abyākata). Among them, it is wholesome for one who dreams of worshipping a shrine, listening to the Dhamma, or preaching the Dhamma. It is unwholesome for one who dreams of killing living beings and so on. Apart from these two sides, the consciousness occurring at the moments of adverting (āvajjana) and registration (tadārammaṇa) should be known as indeterminate. Because the volition (cetanā) in that dream has a weak basis, it is unable to pull towards rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). However, during the course of existence (pavatti), being supported by other wholesome or unwholesome deeds, it gives results. Even if it gives results, the dream-volition is considered non-conventional (abbovahārika) because it arises at an improper time. Regarding the timing of dreams, a dream seen during the day is not true; likewise, dreams seen during the first watch, middle watch, and last watch of the night are not true. However, at the time of a powerful dawn, when the food eaten, drunk, and chewed has been well digested and the essence (ojā) is established in the body, just as the sun is about to rise...
73:
A dream seen [at that time] is true. One who sees a dream with a favorable omen obtains a favorable result, and one who sees a dream with an unfavorable omen obtains an unfavorable result.

However, these five great dreams (mahāsupina) are not seen by ordinary worldly people, nor by great kings, nor by universal monarchs (cakkavatti), nor by chief disciples, nor by Paccekabuddhas, nor by Fully Enlightened Buddhas; only a single Omniscient Bodhisatta sees them. When did our Bodhisatta see these dreams? He saw them at the time of dawn on the fourteenth day of the fortnight, thinking, 'Tomorrow I shall become a Buddha.' Some also say he saw them on the thirteenth day. Having seen these dreams, the Bodhisatta arose, sat down cross-legged, and reflected: 'If I had seen these dreams in the city of Kapilavatthu, I would have told my father, the Great King. If my mother were still alive, I would have told her. But in this place, there is no one who can receive and interpret these dreams; I myself shall receive and interpret them.' Then, having himself interpreted the dreams, thinking, 'This is the precursor for this result; that is the precursor for that result,' he partook of the milk-rice offered by Sujātā in the village of Uruvelā, ascended the Seat of Enlightenment (Bodhimanda), and attained Buddhahood. In due course, while residing at the Jetavana monastery, he addressed the monks to elaborate on the five great dreams he had seen during his time as a Bodhisatta and began this discourse.

In that context, 'Mahāpathavī' refers to the great earth that stands filling the interior of the world-system (cakkavāḷa). 'Mahāsayanaṃ ahosi' means it became a noble bed. 'Ohito' means the [hand] that was placed. That left hand was not placed merely in the water, but should be understood as having gone over the surface of the eastern ocean and rested on the summit of the eastern world-system. The same method applies to the western ocean and the southern ocean. The type of grass called 'tiriyā' refers to dabba grass. 'Rising from the navel and standing touching the sky' means that a red stalk about the size of a plow-pole rose from the navel, and even as he watched, it grew to the size of a span, a cubit, a fathom, sixty fathoms, a quarter-league (gāvuta), half a league, and one league, thus rising and rising until it stood touching the sky for many thousands of leagues. 'Ascending with the feet' means ascending with the feet starting from the tips of the nails. 'Nānāvaṇṇā' means they were of various colors: one was blue-colored, one was yellow-colored, one was red-colored, and one was the color of a pale dried leaf. 'Setā' means they were pure white. 'A great mountain of dung' refers to a mountain of excrement three leagues in height. 'Walks to and fro on the top' means on the very summit...
74:
He walks on the walking path. Long-lived Buddhas, however, appear as if they are seated having entered the Miḷha Mountain, which is three leagues in height.

Having shown the preliminary signs in this many places, he now spoke the words beginning with "Bhikkhave, just as..." in order to show the benefits obtained along with those preliminary signs. In that context, because it bestows all virtues, the Path of Arahantship of the Buddhas is called the Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi). Therefore, seeing the Great Earth of the universe as a glorious bed is the preliminary sign of becoming a Buddha. Seeing Himavanta, the king of mountains, as a pillow is the preliminary sign of the attainment of Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññutañāṇa). Seeing the four feet placed at the ends of the universe is the preliminary sign of the irreversibility of the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka). Seeing himself lying on his back is the preliminary sign of causing beings, who are face down in the three planes of existence, to be face up (with open faces). Appearing as if looking with eyes open is the preliminary sign of the attainment of the Divine Eye (Dibba-cakkhu). Seeing the entire area up to the peak of existence (Bhavagga) becoming a single light is the preliminary sign of Unobstructed Knowledge (Anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa). The remaining words should be understood according to the Pāḷi text.

## 7. Vassa Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta, "nemittā" refers to fortune tellers. "Tejodhātu pakuppati" means a great mass of fire arises. "Pāṇinā udakaṃ sampaṭicchitvā" means taking the water produced by seasonal changes with a hand that is three hundred leagues wide. "Pamattā honti" means they are negligent and lose mindfulness due to their own playing and enjoyment. When the thought "Let us enjoy" arises in the minds of those devas due to their own delight, it rains even if it is not the season; in the absence of that thought, it does not rain. With reference to such non-raining, it is said, "na kālavassaṃ" (it does not rain in season). The eighth and ninth suttas have clear meanings.

## 10. Nissāraṇီya Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, "nissāraṇīyā" means those that have escaped or are disconnected (from opposing states). "Dhātuyo" means natures that are empty of self. "Kāmaṃ manasikaroto" means for one who attends to sense-desire; it refers to one who, having emerged from the meditation on foulness (asubha-jhāna), sends the mind towards sense-desire for the sake of testing, like one who takes medicine and tests the poison. "Na pakkhandati" means it does not enter. "Nappasīdati" means it does not become clear (pleased). "Na santiṭṭhati" means it does not stand firm. "Na vimuccati" means it does not attend (it does not incline). For example, just as a chicken feather or a piece of tendon, when thrown into a fire, shrinks, curls, and twists back, and does not expand, so too...
75:
(The mind) shrinks back and does not expand. "Nekkhamma" (Renunciation) here refers to the first jhāna in the meditations on foulness (asubha) within this Dispensation; for one who attends to that first jhāna, the mind enters (the object). "Tassa taṃ cittaṃ" means that person's foulness-jhāna mind. "Sugataṃ" means well-gone (or well-occurred) because it has reached the proper domain (the object of foulness). "Subhāvitaṃ" means well-developed because it belongs to the part that does not decline. "Suvuṭṭhitaṃ" means well-emerged from sense-desire. "Suvimuttaṃ" means well-freed from sense-desires. "Kāmapaccayā āsavā" refers to the four taints (āsava) that have sense-desire as their root cause. "Vighātā" means sufferings. "Pariḷāhā" means the fevers caused by sensual lust. That person does not experience that sensual feeling, nor the feeling of suffering and fever. This foulness-jhāna is declared as the escape from sense-desires because it has escaped from them. A person who, based on that jhāna, contemplates conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra), reaches the third path (Anāgāmi-magga), and sees Nibbāna through the fruition of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-phala), knows: "There are no more sense-desires." His mind is indeed the absolute escape (accanta-nissaraṇa). In the remaining terms, the method is the same.

However, this is the distinction: In the second turn (vāra), the loving-kindness jhānas (mettā-jhāna) are the escape from ill-will (byāpāda). In the third turn, the compassion jhānas (karuṇā-jhāna) are the escape from cruelty (vihiṃsā). In the fourth turn, the formless jhānas (arūpa-jhāna) are the escape from forms (rūpa). Here, absolute escape should be understood in connection with the Fruition of Arahantship (Arahatta-phala). In the fifth turn, "one who attends to self-identity (sakkāya)" refers to a dry-insight practitioner (sukkha-vipassaka) who, having discerned pure conditioned phenomena and reached Arahantship, emerges from the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) and sends the mind towards the five aggregates of clinging (pañcupādānakkhandhā) for the sake of investigation. This is declared as the escape from self-identity; it refers to the mind of the attainment of the Fruition of Arahantship that arises in a monk who stands having seen Nibbāna through the Path and Fruition of Arahantship, thinking, "There is no more self-identity." Now, wishing to describe the virtues of the Arahant who stands having reached Cessation (Nibbāna), which is the escape from self-identity, he said, "In him, the delight in sense-desire (kāmanandī) no longer underlies," and so on. In that context, "nānuseti" means it no longer arises. "Ananusayā" means because of its non-arising. The remaining words have clear meanings.

## 5. Pañcamapaṇṇāsakaṃ
## (21) 1. Kimilavagga
## 1. Kimilasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the fifth Paṇṇāsaka, 'Kimilāyaṃ' means in the city of this name. 'Niculavane' means in the forest of Nicula trees (Mucalinda forest). 'Etadavoca' (he said this): it is said that this Elder Kimila was the son of a wealthy man in that very city; having ordained in the presence of the Blessed One, he attained the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa). When that elder recollected the continuity of his own past aggregates, he saw that he had ordained during the time when the dispensation of the Kassapa Buddha was declining; when the four assemblies were disrespectful toward the dispensation, he constructed a ladder, climbed a mountain, and practiced the Dhamma of a recluse (samaṇadhamma) there, thus seeing his own past existence. That elder, thinking, "I will approach the Blessed One and ask about the cause [of the disappearance of the dispensation]," spoke the words beginning with "Ko nu kho, bhante" (Who indeed, venerable sir).

'Satthari agāravā viharanti appatissā' means they live without establishing respect or seniority toward the Teacher. The same method applies to the remaining terms. In that regard, disrespect toward the Teacher includes carrying an umbrella or wearing sandals while walking on the grounds of a stupa (cetiya) and such, and speaking various kinds of pointless talk (tiracchānakathā). Sitting in the hall for hearing the Dhamma and falling asleep, as well as speaking various kinds of pointless talk, is called living without respect for the Dhamma. Speaking various kinds of talk while waving one's arms in the midst of the Saṅgha, and not showing respect toward senior, middle-ranking, or junior monks, is called living without respect for the Saṅgha. Not fulfilling the training is called living without respect for the training (sikkhā). Engaging in mutual disputes, quarrels, and so on, is called living without respect for one another. The second sutta has a clear meaning.

## 3. Assājānīyasutta-vaṇṇanā
203-204. In the third sutta, 'ajjavena' means by way of uprightness, not going crookedly. 'javena' means by speed of gait. 'maddavena' means by gentleness of the body. 'khantiyā' means by patience, which is endurance. 'soraccena' means by having pure virtue. In the section on monks (bhikkhuvāra), 'ajjavaṃ' is the upright movement of wisdom. 'javo' is the state of wisdom's movement being courageous.
77:
'maddavaṃ' is the gentleness of virtue. 'khantī' is indeed patience as endurance (adhivāsanakhantī). 'soraccaṃ' is indeed the state of having pure virtue. In the fourth sutta, the five mixed powers (bala) are taught.

## 5. Cetokhila-sutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, 'cetokhila' (mental barrenness) refers to the state of the mind being hardened, being like rubbish, or being like a stump. 'Doubt in the Teacher' means one doubts the physical body or the qualities of the Teacher. Doubting the physical body, one doubts: "Does a body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man really exist, or does it not?" Doubting the qualities, one doubts: "Does omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) capable of knowing the past, future, and present really exist, or does it not?" 'Vicikicchati' (he wavers) means while investigating, he becomes weary, falls into suffering, and is unable to decide. 'Nādhimuccati' (he is not convinced) means he does not obtain the resolution: "This is exactly so." 'Na sampasīdati' (he is not confident) means he is unable to be clear or to be without turbidity through the state of being free from doubt by entering into the qualities. 'Ātappāya' means for the sake of making effort that burns away defilements. 'Anuyogāya' means for the sake of repeated application. 'Sātaccāya' means for the sake of constant action. 'Padhānāya' means for the sake of striving. "This is the first mental barrenness" means this first hardness of mind, known as doubt in the Teacher, has not been abandoned by this monk.

'In the Dhamma' refers to both the Dhamma of scriptures (pariyatti) and the Dhamma of realization (paṭivedha). Doubting the Dhamma of scriptures, one doubts: "They say there is the word of the Buddha called the Tipitaka, consisting of eighty-four thousand Dhamma aggregates; does it really exist, or does it not?" Doubting the Dhamma of realization, one doubts: "They say there is the Path (magga) which is the result of insight (vipassanā), the Fruit (phala) which is the result of the Path, and Nibbāna which is the relinquishment of all conditioned things; do they really exist, or do they not?" 'Doubt in the Saṅgha' means, by way of the words beginning with "practicing rightly" (ujuppaṭipanno), one doubts: "Does the Saṅgha, which is the community of eight persons—the four established in the Path and the four established in the Fruit—who practice such a way, really exist, or does it not?" Doubting the training (sikkhā), one doubts: "They say there is the training in higher virtue (adhisīla), the training in higher mind (adhicitta), and the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā); do they really exist, or do they not?" "This is the fifth" refers to this fifth hardness of mind, rubbish-like state, and stump-like state, known as anger toward fellow practitioners.

## 6. Vinibandha-sutta-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, 'cetosovinibandhā' (mental shackles) are so called because they bind the mind and seize it as if holding it in a fist. 'In sensuality' (kāme) refers to both objective sensuality (vatthukāma) and subjective sensuality (kilesakāma).
78:
"Kāye" means in one's own body. "Rūpe" means in external forms. "Yāvadatthaṃ" means to the extent desired. "Udarāvadehakaṃ" means filling the belly. It is called "udarāvadehakaṃ" because it causes the belly to be full. "Seyyasukkhaṃ" means the happiness derived from sleeping on a couch or bed, or the happiness derived from the season. "Passasukhaṃ" means the happiness that arises on the right or left side for one who is sleeping and turning over. "Middhasukhaṃ" means the happiness derived from drowsiness. "Anuyutto" means living with great exertion. "Paṇidhāya" means having aspired (or having fixed firmly). In the words beginning with "sīlena", "sīlaṃ" means the virtue of fourfold purification (catupārisuddhisīla). "Vataṃ" means the undertaking of vows. "Tapo" means ascetic practice. "Brahmacariyaṃ" means abstinence from sexual intercourse. "Devo vā bhavissāmi" means "I shall become a great deity." "Devaññataro vā" means "I shall become one among the lesser deities."

## 7-8. Yāgusutta-ādi-vaṇṇanā
207-208. In the seventh sutta, "vātaṃ anulometi" means it carries away the wind by regulating it. "Vatthiṃ sodheti" means it cleanses the vessels (channels). "Āmāvasesaṃ pāceti" means if there is any remaining undigested food, it causes that food to be digested. In the eighth sutta, "acakkhussaṃ" means not beneficial for the eyes, or not being able to make the eyes clear.

## 9. Gītassara-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, "āyatakena" means reciting with a long sound, destroying the proper articulation of syllables and the rhythm of the verses. "Sarakuttimpi nikāmayamānassa" refers to one who desires the modulation of the voice, thinking "the singing voice should be made like this." "Samādhissa bhaṅgo hoti" means the destruction of the mind of tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā).

## 10. Muṭṭhassati-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, "dukkhaṃ supati" means sleeping poorly while seeing various kinds of dreams. "Dukkhaṃ paṭibujjhati" means waking up in distress, with trepidation and hair standing on end. In this sutta, mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña) are taught in combination.

## (22) 2. Akkosaka-vagga
## 1. Akkosaka-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the second chapter, 'akkosaka-paribhāsako' refers to one who reviles using the ten grounds of reviling and threatens by showing danger. 'Chinna-paripantho' means one whose dangers are severed because the obstacles to the supramundane path have been cut. 'Rogātaṅko' is called 'affliction of disease' because disease itself brings about a life of hardship.

## 2. Bhaṇḍanakāraka-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, 'adhikaraṇakārako' means one who causes one of the four types of legal issues (adhikaraṇa). 'Anadhigataṃ' refers to the special Dhamma that has not been attained before.

## 3. Sīla-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, 'dussīlo' means one who is immoral or without virtue. 'Sīlavipanno' means one who has failed in virtue or lacks restraint. 'Pamādādhikaraṇaṃ' means due to the cause of negligence. Although this sutta is taught with reference to laypeople, it is also applicable to monastics. This is because if a layperson is negligent in acts such as killing (pāṇātipāta) while earning a living through skills like farming or trade, they cannot complete those tasks in time, and thus their capital is destroyed. Even during times when the king forbids killing, if they commit killing or theft, they suffer great loss of wealth due to royal punishment. An immoral monk, due to negligence, suffers loss of virtue, the Buddha's word, meditative absorption (jhāna), and the seven noble treasures (ariya-dhana).

Among laypeople, a bad reputation spreads in the midst of the fourfold assembly: "This person, though born in such a family, is immoral, of evil nature, has abandoned this world and the next, and does not even give a spoonful of rice." Among monks, a bad reputation spreads: "This monk was unable to guard his virtue or learn the Buddha's word; he lives by medical practice and the like, and is possessed of the six types of disrespect."

'Avisārado' means, for laypeople, approaching with fear, thinking, "In a place where many people gather, if someone knows of my deed, they will punish me or hand me over to the royal family." Such a person sits with an unhappy face, shoulders slumped, looking down and scratching the ground with their big toe. Being devoid of confidence, they are unable to speak. A monk also approaches with fear, thinking, "In a place where many monks gather, if someone knows of my deed, they will prohibit me from Uposatha and Pavāraṇā and expel me from the monkhood." Being devoid of confidence, they are unable to speak. Even if some immoral monks wander about as if they are arrogant, they are inwardly unhappy. Regarding the phrase "sakkaccaṃ kālaṃ karoti", we shall explain it clearly in the Maṇimañjūsā treatise. It becomes evident when one must practice based on the state of being immoral.
80:
He sits with his face turned downwards, scratching the ground with his big toe; he is unable to speak with confidence. Even a monk approaches with fear, thinking, "Many monks have assembled; surely someone will know of my deed. Then they will prevent me from the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā, cause me to fall from monkhood, and expel me." He is unable to speak with confidence. Some immoral person, however, wanders about as if he were proud, yet in his heart, he is indeed dejected.

"He dies confused" means that while that immoral person is lying on his deathbed, the deeds of his immoral life which he undertook and practiced appear before his mind. When he opens his eyes, he sees this world; when he closes them, he sees the next world. The four lower realms appear to him; it is as if he is being struck on the head with a hundred spears. He dies crying out, "Stop it! Stop it!" Therefore, it is said, "He dies confused." The fifth point is quite clear. The talk on the benefits should be understood as the opposite of the faults mentioned.

## 10. Madhurāsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, the Madhurā Sutta, regarding the words "Monks, there are these five disadvantages in Madhurā," the meaning should be understood thus: On one occasion, the Blessed One, wandering on tour accompanied by a large community of monks, arrived at the city of Madhurā and prepared to enter the city. Then, a certain naked female yakkha of wrong view, stretching out both hands and sticking out her tongue, stood before the One of Ten Powers. The Teacher, without entering the city, departed from there and went to a monastery. The multitude of people, taking food, offerings, and honors, went to the monastery and gave gifts to the community of monks headed by the Buddha. The Teacher began this sutta to rebuke (to show the faults of) that city of Madhurā. Therein, "visamā" means having uneven ground. "Bahurajā" means it is as if enveloped by clouds of dust that rise when the wind blows. The rest is clear in all places.

88:
In all terms (it should be understood in this manner): The seeing of elephant-treasures and so forth is not the unsurpassed seeing (dassanānuttariya). However, for a person of established faith, the seeing of the Ten-Powered One (the Buddha), or the Saṅgha of monks, or any one of the meditation objects such as the kasina or the foulness (asubha) signs, through the power of established devotion, is indeed called the unsurpassed seeing.

Hearing the talk of the virtues of kings and so forth is not the unsurpassed hearing (savanānuttariya). However, for a person of established faith, hearing the talk of the virtues of the Triple Gem through the power of established devotion, or hearing the word of the Buddha in the Tipitaka, is indeed called the unsurpassed hearing.

Obtaining gem-treasures and so forth is not the unsurpassed gain (lābhānuttariya). However, obtaining the seven kinds of noble wealth is indeed called the unsurpassed gain.

Learning the elephant-arts and so forth is not the unsurpassed training (sikkhānuttariya). However, fulfilling the three trainings is indeed called the unsurpassed training.

Serving kings and so forth is not the unsurpassed service (pāricariyānuttariya). However, serving the Triple Gem is indeed called the unsurpassed service.

Recollecting the virtues of kings and so forth is not the unsurpassed recollection (anussatānuttariya). However, repeatedly recollecting the virtues of the Triple Gem is indeed called the unsurpassed recollection.

Thus, these six unsurpassed things are taught in terms of the mundane and the supramundane. In the ninth sutta, 'recollection of the Buddha' (buddhānussati) means mindfulness having the qualities of the Buddha as its object. In the remaining terms, the method is the same.

## 10. Commentary on the Mahānāma Sutta

In the tenth sutta, 'Mahānāma' refers to a Sakyan king who was the son of the Buddha's younger paternal uncle. 'Approached the Blessed One' means that after having his breakfast, he went to where the Teacher was, surrounded by his retinue of servants and having them carry perfumes, flowers, and so forth. Because the noble fruit had come to this King Mahānāma, he is called 'one to whom the fruit has come' (agataphala). Because he had understood the teaching of the three trainings, he is called 'one who has understood the teaching' (viññātasāsana). Thus, this king, intending to ask about 'the dwelling of support (nissayavihāra) for a Stream-enterer,' asked and addressed the Buddha in this way.

'His mind is not overwhelmed by lust' means that it is not seized by lust that has arisen and become active. 'It is upright' means it has gone straight into the meditation subject of the recollection of the Buddha. 'Taking the Tathāgata as the object' means taking the qualities of the Tathāgata as the object. 'Atthaveda' is the rapture and gladness that arises based on the Commentary (Atthakatha). 'Dhammaveda' is the rapture and gladness that arises based on the Pali text. 'Dhammūpasañhita' means arising based on both the Pali and the Commentary. 'For one who is glad' means for one who is glad with the two kinds of gladness. 'Rapture arises' means the fivefold rapture is produced. 'The body becomes tranquil' means both the mental body (nāmakāya) and the physical body (karajakāya) become tranquil through the subsiding of distress. 'Happiness' (sukha) refers to both physical and mental happiness. 'He becomes concentrated' means the mind becomes well-established on the object. 'Among a generation that has gone astray' means among beings who have gone astray through lust, hatred, and delusion. 'He has reached evenness' means having reached evenness or peace. 'Accompanied by suffering' means (among beings) who have suffering.
89:
'Entered the stream of Dhamma' (dhammasotaṃ samāpanno) means having reached the stream of Dhamma known as insight (vipassanā). 'Cultivates the recollection of the Buddha' (buddhānussatiṃ bhāveti) means he develops and increases the meditation subject of the recollection of the Buddha. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all sentences. Thus, Mahānāma asked about the dwelling of support for a Stream-enterer. The Teacher also explained that very same thing to him. Thus, in this sutta, only the Stream-enterer is spoken of.

## 2. Sāraṇīya Chapter

## 1. Commentary on the First Sāraṇīya Sutta

In the first sutta of the second chapter, 'sāraṇīyā' refers to those qualities that are fit to be remembered. 'Loving-kindness in bodily action' (mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ) is bodily action to be performed with a mind of loving-kindness. The same method applies to verbal action and mental action. Furthermore, although these come in terms of monks, they are also found among laypeople. For monks, fulfilling the duties of proper conduct (ābhisamācārika) with a mind of loving-kindness is called loving-kindness in bodily action. For laypeople, going for the purpose of worshipping a shrine (cetiya), for the purpose of worshipping the Bodhi tree, or for the purpose of inviting the Saṅgha; seeing monks who have entered the village for alms and going out to welcome them, taking their bowls, preparing seats, and following them—such actions are called loving-kindness in bodily action.

For monks, teaching the training rules known as the regulations of conduct (ācārapannatti), explaining meditation subjects, preaching the Dhamma, and teaching the word of the Buddha which is the Tipitaka with a mind of loving-kindness is called loving-kindness in verbal action. For laypeople, at the time of saying such words as: 'Let us go to worship the shrine, let us go to worship the Bodhi tree, let us listen to the Dhamma, let us make an offering of lamps and flowers, let us undertake and practice the three right conducts, let us give salāka-food and so forth, let us give rainy-season robes, today let us give the four requisites to the Saṅgha, invite the Saṅgha and prepare the food and so forth, prepare the seats, set out the drinking water, go out to welcome and bring the Saṅgha, make them sit on the prepared seats and perform services with enthusiasm'—this is called loving-kindness in verbal action.

For monks, rising early and attending to the body, performing the duties at the shrine courtyard and so forth, and then sitting in a secluded seat and thinking: 'May the monks in this monastery be happy, may they be free from enmity...'
90:
Thinking 'May they be free from ill-will' is called the mental action of loving-kindness (mettā-manokamma). The thought of laypeople, 'May the noble ones be happy, free from enmity, and free from ill-will,' is also called the mental action of loving-kindness.

'Both openly and in private' means in one's presence and in one's absence. Between these two, assisting junior monks in tasks such as robe-making is called bodily action of loving-kindness (mettā-kāyakamma) performed in their presence. All respectful services such as washing the feet of elder monks (Theras) are also called bodily action of loving-kindness performed in their presence. In the absence of both types of monks, taking care of their poorly kept belongings, such as wooden articles, as if they were one's own without showing contempt, is called bodily action of loving-kindness performed in their absence.

Speaking words of praise such as 'Deva Thera, Tissa Thera' is called verbal action of loving-kindness (mettā-vacīkamma) performed in their presence. Inquiring affectionately about a monk who is not in the monastery, saying 'Where is our Deva Thera? Where is our Tissa Thera? When will he return?' is called verbal action of loving-kindness performed in their absence.

Opening the eyes with the moisture of loving-kindness and looking with a clear, pleasant face is called mental action of loving-kindness performed in their presence. Reflecting, 'May Deva Thera and Tissa Thera be free from illness and free from affliction,' is called mental action of loving-kindness performed in their absence.

'Gains' (lābha) refers to obtained requisites such as robes. 'Righteously obtained gains' means gains obtained through the proper practice of alms-gathering, avoiding wrong livelihood such as hypocrisy and the like. 'Even just what is contained in the bowl' refers to even a small amount, such as two or three spoonfuls of alms-food that have entered the bowl.

Regarding 'one who enjoys without dividing,' there are two kinds of dividing: dividing by material things (āmisa-paṭivibhatta) and dividing by person (puggala-paṭivibhatta). Between these two, mentally discriminating, 'I will give this much, I will not give that much,' is called āmisa-paṭivibhatta. Mentally discriminating, 'I will give to this person, I will not give to that person,' is called puggala-paṭivibhatta. One who enjoys without doing either of these is called 'one who enjoys without dividing' (appaṭivibhattabhogī).

Regarding 'one who shares in common with virtuous fellow practitioners (sabrahmacārī),' the characteristic of one who shares in common is this: When he receives excellent requisites, he does not give them to laypeople with the motive of seeking further gains, nor does he enjoy them alone. Even while receiving them, he accepts them with the thought, 'May this be shared with the Saṅgha,' and views them as Saṅgha property to be enjoyed after striking the bell. Who can fulfill this sāraṇīyadhamma, and who cannot? An immoral person cannot fulfill it. This is because virtuous ones do not accept the property of an immoral person. A monk of pure virtue...
91:
...on the other hand, fulfills the sāraṇīya duty without breaking or damaging it. In fulfilling it, this is the practice: If a monk gives specifically to his mother, father, teacher, preceptor, and so on, he is giving what ought to be given. However, for him, it is not the sāraṇīyadhamma; it is called 'tending to impediments' (palibodha-jaggana). The sāraṇīyadhamma is suitable only for a monk who is free from such impediments. A monk who gives in that manner should also give to the sick, those attending the sick, visitors, those departing on a journey, and to a newly ordained monk who does not yet know how to handle the double robe and the bowl. After giving to them, if any food remains, he should give it starting from the elders' seats; whatever amount a monk takes, that much should be given. If no food remains, he should go for alms again, and whatever excellent food he obtains, he should give it starting from the elders' seats and then consume the remainder. Because it is said 'with the virtuous,' it is also proper not to give to an immoral person.

This sāraṇīya practice is easily fulfilled in a well-trained assembly. In a well-trained assembly, a monk who receives from elsewhere does not take it. Even if he does not receive from elsewhere, he takes only what is appropriate in measure, not in excess. This sāraṇīyadhamma is fulfilled in twelve years for a monk who repeatedly goes for alms and gives whatever he receives; it is not fulfilled in less time than that. If, in the twelfth year, a monk fulfilling the sāraṇīya duty places his bowl full of alms-food in the dining hall and goes to bathe, and the elder of the Saṅgha asks, 'Whose bowl is this?' and is told, 'It is the bowl of the monk fulfilling the sāraṇīya duty,' and the elder says, 'Bring it here,' and after distributing and consuming all the alms-food, leaves the empty bowl—if that monk, upon seeing the empty bowl, feels displeasure (domanassa), thinking, 'They have consumed it without leaving anything for me,' his sāraṇīya duty is broken. He must fulfill it again for another twelve years. This is like the probation (parivāsa) of the sectarians; if it is broken once, it must be fulfilled all over again. But if a monk feels joy (somanassa), thinking, 'What a gain for me! How well-obtained for me, that my fellow practitioners consume the food in my bowl even without asking!' then his sāraṇīya duty is said to be fulfilled.

For a monk who has thus fulfilled the sāraṇīyadhamma, neither envy nor stinginess arises. He is loved by humans and loved by non-humans. He obtains the four requisites easily. The food in his bowl does not run out even when being given away. Among items to be distributed, he receives the best items. When danger or famine arrives, the deities take care to assist him.
92:
Regarding the matter of the food in the bowl not being exhausted even when given, and so forth, there are these stories. Elder Tissa, who resided at Senagiri, lived depending on the village named Mahāgiri. While fifty senior elders were traveling to Nāgadīpa to worship the cetiya, they wandered for alms in Giri village but left without receiving anything. As the Elder was entering the village, he saw those elders and asked, "Venerable sirs, did you receive alms?" They replied, "Friend, we have wandered [for them]." Knowing that they had received nothing, he said, "Venerable sirs, please wait right here until I return." They said, "Friend, the fifty of us did not receive even enough to dampen our bowls." He replied, "Venerable sirs, resident monks are capable; even if they do not receive alms, they know the nature of the alms-round routes." The elders waited. The Elder entered the village.

At the very first house, a great female lay devotee had prepared milk-rice and stood looking out for the Elder. As soon as the Elder reached the door of the house, she filled his bowl to the brim. Taking that food, he went to the senior elders and said to the Sangha Elder, "Venerable sir, please accept this." The Sangha Elder thought, "We, being so many, received nothing, yet this monk has brought this so quickly. How can this be?" and looked at the faces of the other monks. Elder Tissa, knowing this by the manner of his looking, said, "Venerable sirs, this food was obtained righteously and fairly. Please accept it without hesitation." Starting from the beginning, he served all the monks as much as they desired, and he himself also ate as much as he desired.

Then, when the meal was finished, the senior elders asked, "Friend, when did you realize the supramundane Dhamma?" He replied, "Venerable sirs, I have no supramundane Dhamma." They asked again, "Friend, then are you an attainer of jhāna?" He replied, "Venerable sir, I do not have this jhāna either." They asked, "Friend, then is this not a miracle?" He said, "Venerable sirs, I have fulfilled the sāraṇīya-dhammas (virtues of social amity). From the time those virtues were fulfilled, even if there were a hundred thousand monks, the food in my bowl is never exhausted." They said, "Sādhu, sādhu, virtuous one! This is appropriate for you." This is the story regarding the food in the bowl not being exhausted.

Furthermore, this same Elder went to the place of giving during the Giribhaṇḍa Great Offering at Cetiyapabbata and asked, "What is the most excellent item in this offering?" They replied, "Venerable sir, it is two cloths." He said, "Those cloths will come to me." Hearing this, a minister informed the King, "A young monk spoke in this way." The King thought, "The young monk has such a mind, but indeed for the senior elders..."
93:
"Fine cloths are suitable for the senior elders," the King said, and he set them aside, intending to offer them to the senior elders. While the Sangha of monks stood in order, as the King was making the offering, those excellent cloths placed at the very top did not come into his hand; only other cloths came. However, at the time of offering to the young monk, those cloths came into his hand. Having placed those cloths in the hand of the young monk and looking at the face of the minister, the King had the young monk sit down, completed the offering, and after the Sangha had departed, he sat near the young monk and said, "Venerable sir, when did you realize this supramundane Dhamma?" That young monk, not wishing to speak of supramundane Dhamma which he did not possess even by way of figurative speech, said, "Great King, I have no supramundane Dhamma." The King asked, "Venerable sir, did you not say previously, 'They will come to me'?" He replied, "Great King, it is true. I am one who fulfills the sāraṇīya-dhammas. From the time those dhammas were fulfilled, the most excellent item reaches me whenever property is distributed." The King said, "Sādhu, sādhu, venerable sir! This is appropriate for you," and then departed. This is the story regarding the phrase, "The excellent item reaches one at the place of distributing property."

During the peril of Brāhmaṇa Tissa, the inhabitants of Bhātaragāma fled without informing Elder Nun Nāgā. At dawn, the Elder Nun said to the young nuns, "The village is exceedingly silent; go and investigate first." They went and saw that everyone had fled, and returning, they informed the Elder Nun. Hearing this, she said, "Do not think about their fleeing. Devote yourselves only to your own recitation of the Pali, inquiry into the commentaries, and wise attention." At the time for alms-round, she robed herself and, together with twelve other nuns including herself, stood at the foot of a banyan tree at the village gate. The deity residing in that tree offered alms-food to all twelve nuns and said, "Ladies, do not go elsewhere; please always come here."

There was an elder named Elder Nāga, who was the younger brother of the Elder Nun. He thought, "The peril is great; it is not possible to subsist here. I will go to the other shore." Departing from his residence with twelve monks including himself, he came to Bhātaragāma, thinking, "I will go after seeing the Elder Nun." The Elder Nun, hearing that the elders had arrived, went to them and asked, "Venerable sirs, what is the matter?" He informed her of the situation. She said, "Stay in the monastery for just this one day and go tomorrow." The elders went to the monastery.

The next day, after wandering for alms at the foot of the tree, the Elder Nun approached the Elder and said, "Please partake of this alms-food." The Elder said, "It would be proper, Elder Nun," and remained silent. She said, "Brother, this alms-food is righteously obtained; partake of it without hesitation..."
94:
“Please partake [of this food],” the Elder Nun requested. “Is it proper for the Elder Nun [to do this]?” the Elder reflected. The Elder Nun then took the alms-bowl and threw it into the air, and the bowl remained suspended in the sky. The Elder said, “Elder Nun, even if it stays at a height of seven palm trees, it is still the food of a nun.” He continued, “Dangers do not exist at all times. When the danger has subsided and I am preaching the Ariyavaṃsa Dhamma, if I am internally reproached with the thought, ‘O alms-food collector, you once spent your time eating the food of a nun,’ I will not be able to maintain my composure. Therefore, O Elder Nuns, be diligent,” and he proceeded on his way.

A tree deity also thought, “If the Elder partakes of the alms-food from the hand of the Elder Nun, I will not stop him. If he does not partake, I will stop him,” and stood watching. Seeing the Elder departing, the deity descended from the tree and said, “Venerable Sir, please give me the bowl.” Taking the bowl, the deity led the Elder to the foot of the tree, prepared a seat, offered alms-food, and after the meal was finished, made him give a promise and then supported twelve nuns and twelve monks for seven years. This is the story regarding the phrase, “Deities strive.” In that story, the Elder Nun was one who fulfilled the Sāraṇīya Dhamma (qualities of concern).

Regarding the terms beginning with “Akhaṇḍāni”: among the seven groups of offenses, if a training rule is broken at the beginning or at the end, that person’s virtue is called “khaṇḍa” (broken), like a cloth with a torn border. If it is broken in the middle, it is called “chidda” (perforated), like a cloth with a hole. If two or three are broken in succession, it is called “sabala” (spotted), like a cow with a different color (such as black or red) appearing on its back or belly. If it is broken at intervals, it is called “kammāsa” (mottled), like a cow variegated with different colored spots here and there. If it is not broken in any way at all, those virtues are called unbroken (akhaṇḍa), unperforated (acchidda), unspotted (asabala), and unmottled (akammāsa).

Furthermore, these virtues are called “bhujissa” (liberating) because they free one from the slavery of craving and make one a free person; “viññuppasattha” (praised by the wise) because they are praised by the Buddha and other wise ones; “aparāmaṭṭha” (untainted) because they are not grasped by craving or wrong view, and because no one can reproachfully say, “You have previously committed such-and-such an offense”; and “samādhisamvattanika” (conducive to concentration) because they lead to access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) or absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi).
96: "Again, ill-will is no more"—thus one sees Nibbāna through the third fruit (anāgāmiphala); the mind of such a person is completely liberated from ill-will. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all instances. "Animittacetovimutti" (signless deliverance of mind) refers to strong insight (balavavipassanā). However, the teachers of the Dīgha Nikāya (Dīghabhāṇakas) say it is the attainment of the fruit of arahantship (arahattaphalasamāpatti). That attainment of the fruit of arahantship is called "signless" (animitta) because of the absence of the sign of lust (rāganimitta), etc., the sign of forms (rūpanimitta), etc., and the sign of permanence (niccanimitta), etc. "Nimittānusārī" means having the nature of following after the various signs mentioned. "Asmi" refers to the conceit "I am" (asmimāna). "This person is I" means viewing within the five aggregates (pañcakkhandhā) that "this particular self is I." By this sequence of words, the declaration of arahantship is made. "Vicikicchākathaṅkathāsalla" is the dart of indecision, which is the doubt "is it thus or is it thus?" "Do not say so" is what should be said to that person. If doubt (vicikicchā), which is to be abandoned by the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga), arises in you, then the declaration of arahantship is false; therefore, one should be restrained by saying, "Do not take up what is not true." "The uprooting of the conceit 'I am'" refers to the path of arahantship (arahattamagga). Indeed, when Nibbāna is seen through the power of the path and fruit of arahantship, the conceit "I am" no longer exists; thus, the path of arahantship is called "the uprooting of the conceit 'I am'." In this way, the subject of false declaration (abhūtavyākaraṇa) is taught in this sutta. ## 4. Bhaddaka Sutta Vaṇṇanā In the commentary on the fourth sutta, "na bhaddakaṃ" means it is not good. In that context, if a person dies in great fear, that person's death is not good. If a person takes rebirth in a woeful state (apāya), that person's death is not a good passing away. In the words "kammārāmo," etc., delight is called "ārāma"; it means great delight (abhirati). Because of delighting in new work (navakamma) such as building a monastery, one is called "kammārāma." Because of being delighted in that very work, one is called "kammarata." Because of being repeatedly devoted to that delight in work, one is called "anuyutta." This method should be understood in all terms. In this sutta, "bhassa" refers to initial talk and repeated conversation (ālāpasallāpa). "Niddā" means sleep. "Saṅgaṇikā" means delighting in company (gaṇasaṅgaṇikā). That socializing should be understood by the method: "for one person there is a second companion, for two persons there is a third," and so on. "Saṃsagga" (association) is the state of being mixed, occurring through the power of seeing, hearing, intimacy, conversing together, enjoying together, and physical contact. "Papañca" (proliferation) is the mental proliferation of defilements (kilesapapañca) which occurs through the power of craving (taṇhā), views (diṭṭhi), and conceit (māna), and which stands in the form of intoxication. "Sakkāya" (identity) refers to the round of existence in the three planes (tebhūmakavaṭṭa). "Sammā dukkhassa antakiriyāya" (for the right ending of suffering) means for the purpose of making a limit or termination of the entire round of suffering through the right cause. "Mago" means like a forest deer. "Nippapañcapade" means in the state of Nibbāna. "Ārādhayi" means one has fulfilled; it means one has accomplished that Dhamma.

## 5. Commentary on the Anutappiya Sutta
In the commentary on the fifth sutta, the Anutappiya Sutta: "Anutappa" refers to things that should be repeatedly grieved over or things that cause repeated remorse. In both these suttas and the verses, the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) are taught.

## 6. Commentary on the Nakulapitu Sutta
In the commentary on the sixth sutta, the Nakulapitu Sutta: "Bāḷhagilāno" means one who is excessively and painfully ill. "Etadavoca" refers to when the wife, being unable to alleviate the husband's illness through medical treatment, now spoke these words beginning with "Mā kho tvaṃ" while sitting nearby, making an Act of Truth (saccakiriya) with a bold speech like a lion's roar to alleviate the disease. "Sāpekkho" means one who has craving (lingering concern). In the phrase "na Nakulamātā," the word "na" should be construed with the following word as "na sakkhati" (not unable, i.e., she is able). "Santharituṃ" means to manage or establish so that there are no gaps or holes. "Veṇiṃ olikhituṃ" means to shear and clear sheep's wool to make it into a braid (spinning).

"Aññaṃ ဃရံ gamissati" means she will take another husband. "Soḷasa vassāni gahaṭṭhakaṃ brahmacariyaṃ samāciṇṇaṃ" means that for sixteen years from now, the holy life as a householder has been practiced. "Dassanakāမတရာ" means having an excessive desire to see (the Buddha). Having made a bold declaration like a lion's roar with these three factors, she made an Act of Truth: "By this true word, may your body be at ease and free from disease."

Now, to make an Act of Truth based on her own virtues such as morality, taking the Blessed One as witness, she said the words beginning with "Siyā kho pana te." In that context, "paripūrakārinī" means one who habitually fulfills. "Cetosamathassa" refers to the power of the meditation of tranquility (samādhi-kammaṭṭhāna). "Ogādhappattā" refers to those who have gained a footing. "Patigādhappattā" refers to those who have reached a firm standing. "Assāsappattā" refers to those who have reached consolation or reliance. "Vesārajjappattā" refers to those who have reached the knowledge of joy (confidence). "Aparappaccayā" means those who are devoid of "parappaccaya," which refers to the faith or conviction dependent on others. Having focused on her own virtues with these three factors, she made the Act of Truth. "Gilānā vuṭṭhito" means rising from illness. "Yāvatā" means as many as. "Tāsaṃ aññatarā" means one among those female lay followers. "Anukampikā" means one who compassionately seeks welfare. "Ovādikā" means one who gives admonition. "Anုသာသိကာ" means one who gives repeated instruction.
98:
## 7. Soppasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the seventh sutta, the Soppa Sutta: "paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito" means rising from solitary contemplation of the Dhamma and from the dwelling of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti-vihāra). "yathāvihāraṃ" means to their respective dwellings. "navā" refers to the newly ordained monks in the Dispensation, of whom there were about five hundred. "kākacchamānā" means making a sound like a crow (snoring) while grinding their teeth. "therā" are the elder monks who have attained a state of firmness. "tena no" is a question: "Is it because of that?" The meanings of terms such as seyyasukha (the pleasure of lying down) are as stated previously. "raṭṭhiko" is one who governs and enjoys a country. "petteṇiko" is one who continues to enjoy the wealth and pleasures enjoyed by his father. "senāpatiko" is a general, the leader of the army. "gāmagāmaṇiko" is a village headman. "pūgagāmaṇiko" is the leader of a group or guild. "avippasako kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ" means being one who does not seek or investigate wholesome states. "bodhipakkhiyānaṃ dhammānaṃ" refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.

## 8. Macchabandhasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the eighth sutta, the Macchabandha Sutta: "macchikaṃ" refers to a fisherman, a killer of fish. "hatthinā yātīti hatthiyāyī" means an elephant-rider because he travels by elephant. The same method of interpretation applies to subsequent terms. "vajjhe" refers to beings that are to be killed. "vadhāyanīte" refers to those led away for slaughter. "pāpakena manasā" means with a wicked, murderous mind. In the Pāḷi text, it is written as "vadhāyupanīte." "māgaviko" is a hunter who kills game. "What need is there to speak of one who looks at a human being with a wicked mind?" means it is unnecessary to mention the loss of wealth and prosperity for one who harbors a wicked mind toward another human. This statement is made to show the undesirable results of wicked, unwholesome kamma. It should be understood that for those who obtain retinue and wealth while performing such unwholesome kamma, it is because wholesome kamma is ripening in dependence on that unwholesome state. However, because it is undermined by that unwholesome kamma, the result does not last long. In this sutta, only the unwholesome side is taught.

## 9. Paṭhamamaraṇassatisutta-vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the ninth sutta, the First Maraṇassati Sutta: "nātike" means in the village of that name. "giñjakāvasathe" means in the brick mansion. "amatogadhā" means plunging into Nibbāna, having Nibbāna as its foundation. "bhāvetha no" is a question: "Do you develop [it]?" "maraṇassatiṃ" refers to the meditation subject of mindfulness of death. "aho vatā" is a particle used in the sense of a wish. "If only I have done much in the Teacher's Dispensation..."
99:
"assa" means "If only my duty in your Dispensation were much accomplished." "tadantaraṃ" refers to that moment, that opportunity. In the phrase "assasitvā vā passasāmi," the in-breath is called "assāsa," and the out-breath is called "passāsa." Thus, this monk, desiring to live only as long as the in-breath goes out or the out-breath comes in, speaks in this way. "dandhaṃ" means slow, heavy, and not moving quickly. "āsavānaṃ khayāya" means for the sake of the fruit of Arahantship. In this sutta, mindfulness of death is taught leading up to the attainment of Arahantship.

## 10. Dutiyamaraṇassatisutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta: "patigatāya" means when reached (or practiced). "iti paṭisañcikkhati" means he reflects thus. In the phrase "so mamassa antarāyo," there are three kinds of obstacles: the obstacle to life, the obstacle to the monk's practice, and for worldlings, the obstacle to heaven and the obstacle to the Path when they die. He speaks thus with reference to all of these. "byāpajjeyya" means it might be disturbed or afflicted due to indigestion and so forth. "adhimatto" means powerful or intense. "chando" is the desire to act (kattukamyatā-chanda). "vāyāmo" is energy called effort (payoga-vīriya). "ussāho" is energy called exertion (ussāpana-vīriya). "ussoḷhī" is energy called accomplishment (sampādana-vīriya). "appaṭivānī" means non-weariness and non-regression. The remaining words have clear meanings in all places.

## The Second Chapter: Sāraṇīya Vagga
## 3. Anuttariya Vagga
## 1-2. Sāmagāmasutta-ādi-vaṇṇanā
21-22. In the first sutta of the third chapter: "sāmagāmake" means in the small village of that name, so called because of the abundance of sāmaka grass. "pokkharaṇiyāyaṃ" means in the monastery named Pokkharaṇiyā. "abhikkantāya rattiyā" means when the first watch of the night has passed and the middle watch has arrived. "abhikkantavaṇṇā" means of surpassing beauty. "kevalakappaṃ" means entirely (all around without remainder). "pokkharaṇiyaṃ obhāsetvā" means having illuminated the great monastery named Pokkharaṇiyā with his own radiance. "samanuñño" means having equal approval, having a similar mind. "dovacassatā" is the state of being difficult to speak to. "pāpamittatā" is the state of having evil friends.
100:
Having evil friends (lāmakamittatā). In this sutta, only the factors leading to decline are taught. In the second sutta, the factors leading to non-decline are taught, mixed with supramundane states.

## 3. Bhaya Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, 'kāmarāgarattāya' means this person is stained by sensual lust. 'Chandāragavinibaddho' means bound by desire and lust. 'Bhayā' means because of the fear known as mental terror. 'Paṅkā' means because of the mire of defilements. 'Saṅgo paṅko ca ubhayaṃ' means both these two: attachment and mire. 'Ete kāmā pavuccanti, yattha satto puthujjano' means in which attachment and mire the worldling is attached, entangled, and obstructed. 'Upādāne' means in the four kinds of grasping. 'Jātimaraṇasambhave' means in the cause that is the origin of birth and death. 'Anupādā vimuccanti' means they are liberated without grasping. 'Jātimaraṇasaṅkhaye' means they are liberated by the liberation that has Nibbāna as its object, which is called the destruction of birth and death. In this context, having turned away from the round of rebirth, this monk has reached only the fruit of Arahantship. Now, wishing to praise that one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), he said 'te khemappattā' and so forth. In that passage, 'khemappattā' means those who have reached the state of safety. 'Sukhino' means those who are happy with supramundane happiness. 'Diṭṭhadhammābhinibbutā' means those who are cooled even in the present life because of the absence of defilements within. In this sutta, only the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) is taught, while in the verses, both the round and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) are taught.

## 4. Himavanta Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, 'padāleyya' means one should break or destroy. 'Chavāya' means low or inferior. 'Samādhissa samāpattikusalo hoti' means one is skilled, expert, capable, and competent in entering concentration after attending to suitable food and suitable climate. 'Samādhissa ṭhitikusalo' means one is skilled in the steadiness of concentration, meaning one is able to maintain concentration. 'Samādhissa vuṭṭhānakusalo' means one is skilled in emerging from concentration, meaning one is able to emerge according to the predetermined time. 'Samādhissa kallitakusalo' means one is skilled in the readiness of concentration, meaning one is able to make the mind of concentration joyful and ready. 'Samādhissa gocarakusalo' means one who avoids states that are unsuitable and unhelpful to concentration and frequents states that are suitable and helpful, and also... 'This concentration...'
101:
"...one who knows, 'This concentration has a sign as its object; this concentration has a characteristic as its object,' is also called one skilled in the range of concentration (gocarakusala). One who is able to direct the concentration of the first absorption (jhāna) and so forth for the purpose of attaining higher and higher attainments is called one skilled in the direction of concentration (abhinīhārakusala). That person, having emerged from the first absorption, enters the second absorption; having emerged from the second absorption, enters the third absorption; having emerged from the third absorption, enters the fourth absorption.

## 5. Anussatiṭṭhāna Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta: Anussatiṭṭhāna means the causes of recollection (anussati). The terms beginning with 'Itipi so bhagavā' have already been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. 'Monks, having made this recollection of the Buddha the object' means making this meditation subject of the recollection of the Buddha the object. 'They are purified' means they reach Nibbāna, which is the supreme purity. The remaining words have clear meanings in all places. In this sutta, it should be understood that the six bases of recollection are taught in a mixed manner.

## 6. Mahākaccāna Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta: 'In the crowded place' (sambādhe) means the crowdedness of the five cords of sensual pleasure. 'Attaining the opportunity' (okāsādhigamo)—here, the six bases of recollection are called 'opportunity' (okāsa); it is the attainment of those opportunities. 'For purification' means for the benefit of purification. 'To overcome sorrow and lamentation' means for the benefit of surpassing sorrows and lamentations. 'For the ending' means for the benefit of reaching the end. 'To attain the right path' means for the benefit of attaining the path together with insight (vipassanā). 'To realize Nibbāna' means for the benefit of personally realizing Nibbāna, which is free from conditions.

'In every way' (sabbaso) means by all modes. 'Like the sky' (ākāsasamena) means with a mind like the sky because of the meanings of non-attachment and non-obstruction. 'Vast' (vipulena) means with a mind that is not small. 'Reached the state of greatness' (mahaggatena) means with a mind that has reached a great state, or a mind practiced by the noble disciples who are great. 'Measureless' (appamāṇena) means with a mind that is measureless because of the measurelessness of its pervasion. 'Without enmity' (averena) means with a mind free from the enmity of unwholesome states and the enmity of persons. 'Without ill-will' (abyāpajjhena) means with a mind free from the suffering caused by anger. All these words are spoken with reference only to the mind associated with the recollection of the Buddha. In the subsequent recollections, the method should be understood in the same way. 'Purifying states' (visuddhidhammā) means states that have the nature of purification. In this sutta also, the six bases of recollection are taught only in a mixed manner.
102:
## 7. Commentary on the First Samaya Sutta
In the seventh sutta, regarding the word "manobhāvanīyassa," it is called manobhāvanīya because it causes the mind, which takes Nibbāna (the state of safety) as its object, to develop and increase. "Dassanāya" means for the sake of seeing. "Nissaraṇaṃ" means escape or peace. "Dhammaṃ deseti" means teaching the meditation on foulness (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna) for the purpose of abandoning sensual lust.
