In the second instance and so forth, it should be understood that he teaches the Dhamma by: teaching the meditation on loving-kindness (mettā-kammaṭṭhāna) to abandon ill-will; teaching either a discourse that abandons sloth and torpor, or the perception of light (āloka-saññā), or one of the grounds for initiating effort (vīriyārambhavatthu) to abandon sloth and torpor; teaching the meditation on tranquility (samatha-kammaṭṭhāna) to abandon restlessness and worry; and teaching the virtues of the Triple Gem to abandon doubt. "Āgamma" means depending on or because of. "Manasikaroto" means for one who applies the mind (attends) by way of the object. "Anantarā āsavānaṃ khayo hoti" means the destruction of the taints (āsavas) occurs without interval (immediately).

## 8. Commentary on the Second Samaya Sutta
In the eighth sutta, "maṇḍalamāḷe" means in the dining hall. "Cārittakilamatho" means the fatigue arising from the alms round. "Bhattakilamatho" means the distress or fatigue caused by food. "Vihārapacchāyāyaṃ" means in the shade near the monastery. "Yadevassa divā samādhinimittaṃ manasikataṃ hoti" means if that person has applied his mind to (attended to) a certain sign of tranquility (samatha-nimitta) during the earlier part of that day. "Tadevassa tasmiṃ samaye samudācarati" means that very object of tranquility appears in the mind-door of that person while he is sitting in the monastery during the day-rest at that evening time. "Ojaṭṭhāyī" means standing or established by way of essence (ojā). "Phāsukassa hoti" means there is comfort for him. "Sammukhā" means in the presence of the Blessed One who is teaching. "Sutaṃ" means heard with the ear. "Paṭiggahitaṃ" means received with the mind.

## 9. Commentary on the Udāyī Sutta
In the ninth sutta, "Udāyiṃ" refers to the Elder Lāḷudāyī. "Suṇomahaṃ, āvuso" means "Friend, I am not deaf; I hear the words of the Blessed One, but I am investigating the problem." "Adhicittaṃ" means the mind of tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā). "Idaṃ, bhante, anussatiṭṭhānaṃ" means this basis of recollection, which is described as the three jhānas. "Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārāya saṃvattati" means it leads to a happy dwelling in this very life. "Ālokasaññāṃ" means the perception that arises regarding the sign of light. "Divā saññāṃ adhiṭṭhāti" means he establishes the perception of day. "Yathā divā tathā ratti" means just as this practitioner attends to the perception of light, etc., during the day, in the same way, he attends to that very perception of light during the night. "Yathā rattiṃ tathā divā" means just as this practitioner attends to the perception of light, etc., during the night, in the same way, he attends to that very perception of light during the day. "Vivaṭaṃ" means open and clear. "Apariyonaddhaṃ" means not enveloped (not covered) by the hindrances (nīvaraṇas). "Suppabhāsaṃ cittaṃ bhာဝေတိ" means he develops the insight-mind along with radiance for the sake of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). Furthermore, the statement "ālokasaññāṃ manasikaroti" is said with reference to the perception of light that abandons sloth and torpor. The divine eye...
103:
...the rest of the words are omitted. "As in the day, so at night" means just as this practitioner attends to the perception of light during the day, he attends to that very perception of light in the same way during the night. "As at night, so in the day" means just as this practitioner attends to the perception of light during the night, he attends to that very perception of light in the same way during the day. "Vivaṭa" means clear (open). "Apariyonaddha" means not enveloped (not covered) by the hindrances. "Develops a mind with radiance" means increasing the mind along with radiance for the sake of attaining the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). It should be understood that the statement "attends to the perception of light" is said with reference to the perception of light that abandons sloth and torpor, and not with reference to the light of the divine eye. "For the attainment of knowledge and vision" means for the sake of attaining the knowledge and vision called the divine eye.

In the passages beginning with "this very body," everything that should be said has been explained in detail in all its aspects in the Visuddhimagga, in the section on the meditation of mindfulness directed to the body (Kāyagatāsati-kammaṭṭhāna). "For the sake of abandoning sensual lust" means for the purpose of abandoning the lust that occurs in the five cords of sensual pleasure. "As if one were to see" means just as one would see. "Sarīra" refers to a dead corpse. "Discarded in a cemetery" means a corpse left in a cemetery. A corpse that has been dead for one day is called ekāhamata; for two days, dvīhamata; for three days, tīhamata. A corpse that has become bloated like a leather bag due to wind is called uddhumātaka. Or it is called uddhumātaka because it is loathsome. A corpse that is discolored and dark-blue is called vinīlaka. Or it is called vinīlaka because it is loathsome. This is a designation for a corpse that is red in fleshy parts, white in parts where pus has accumulated, and generally blue-black, like one covered with a blue cloth. A corpse from which pus is flowing from the ruptured parts or from the nine openings is called vipubbaka. Or it is called vipubbaka because it is loathsome. The state of having reached such a condition of flowing pus is called vipubbakajāta.

"That monk [compares] this very body" means that monk compares his own body with that dead corpse by means of knowledge. How does he compare? He reflects: "This body of mine also is of such a nature, it will become like this, it cannot escape this nature." The meaning is: as long as these three things—life-faculty (āyu), heat (usmā), and consciousness (viññāṇa)—exist, this body is capable of standing, walking, and so forth. But when these things are gone, this body also is of such a nature as to be putrid. "It will become like this" means it will become bloated and so forth. "Cannot escape this" means it cannot transcend the state of being bloated and so forth.
104:
Khajjamāna refers to a corpse that is being pecked and eaten by crows, vultures, and so on, which sit on parts such as the belly and pluck out the flesh of the belly, the lips, and the eye sockets. Samaṃsalohita refers to a corpse that is still joined with the remaining flesh and blood. Nimmaṃsalohitamakkhita refers to a corpse where the flesh is gone but the blood has not yet dried up. Aññena means being scattered in another direction. Hatthaṭṭhika refers to the sixty-four types of hand bones being scattered individually. The same method should be understood for the foot bones and so on. Terovassikāni refers to bones that are more than a year old. Pūtīni refers to bones that have rotted after more than a year due to exposure to wind, sun, and rain while lying in the open. However, bones that are underground remain for a longer time. Cuṇṇakajātāni refers to bones that have become powder and are scattered. In all sentences, the connection should be made according to the method mentioned above, through the power of khajjamāna and so on.

Asmimānasamugghātāya means for the purpose of eradicating the ninefold conceit that arises as 'I am.' Anekadhātupaṭivedhāya means for the purpose of penetrating and knowing many elements. Sato va abhikkamati means going only while being endowed with mindfulness and wisdom. Sato va paṭikkamati means returning only while being endowed with mindfulness and wisdom. The same method should be understood for the remaining terms. Satisampajaññāya means for the sake of mindfulness and knowledge. Thus, in this sutta, mindfulness and knowledge are taught in combination.

## 10. Anuttariyasutta Vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, uccāvacaṃ means anything great or small, or high or low. Hīnaṃ means a lowly thing. Gammaṃ means the vision (practice) of those living in a village. Pothujjanikaṃ means the property (practice) of worldlings. Anariyaṃ means not noble, not excellent, not pure. Anatthasaṃhitaṃ means not connected with benefit. Na nibbidāya means not for the purpose of disenchantment with the suffering of the round of rebirths. Na virāgāya means not for the purpose of the fading away of lust and so on. Na nirodhāya means not for the purpose of the cessation of lust and so on, so that they do not arise again. Na upasamāya means not for the purpose of the calming of lust and so on. Na abhiññāya means not for the purpose of knowing with higher knowledge. Na sambodhāya means not for the purpose of penetrating the four path-knowledges called enlightenment (sambodhi). Na nibbānāya means not for the purpose of realizing Nirvana.

Niviṭṭhasaddho means one with established faith. Niviṭṭhapemo means one with established love. Ekantagato means one who has reached the absolute, meaning one who has reached an unwavering state. Abhippasanno means one who is extremely devoted. Etadānuttariyaṃ means this supreme thing, such as seeing the Buddha and his disciples. 'He also learns elephant-craft' means (learning elephant-craft and so on are also uccāvaca [various/lowly]).
105:
He learns elephant-craft, which is to be learned through signs related to elephants. The same method applies to the remaining terms. 'Uccāvacaṃ' means learning crafts that are great or small.

'Upaṭṭhitā pāricariyā' means being present for service. 'Bhāvayanti anussatiṃ' means they develop supreme recollection. 'Vivekappatisaṃyuttaṃ' means doing so by relying on Nirvana. 'Khemaṃ' means being free from danger. 'Amatagāminaṃ' means they develop the Noble Path, which is the way to reach the Deathless (Nirvana). 'Appamāde pamoditā' means they rejoice and are happy in diligence (appamāda), which is called the non-absence of mindfulness. 'Nipakā' means they are endowed with wisdom. 'Sīlasaṃvutā' means they are restrained and protected by virtue. 'Te ve kālena paccenti' means those monks know at the appropriate and suitable time. 'Yattha dukkhaṃ nirujjhati' means those monks know that Great Nirvana, the state free from death, where all the suffering of the round of rebirths ceases. In this sutta, the six supreme things (anuttariya) are taught in combination.

## The Supreme Group (Anuttariyavagga), the Third.

## 4. The Deities Group (Devatāvagga)

## 1. Sekhasutta Vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the fourth group, 'sekhassa' refers to the seven types of noble learners (sekha). Regarding worldlings, there is nothing to be said. 'Parihānāya' means for the purpose of declining from higher and higher qualities (the paths and fruits).

## 2-3. Aparihānasutta-dvaya Vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, 'satthugāravatā' means showing respect to the Teacher (the Buddha). 'Dhammagāravatā' means showing respect to the ninefold supramundane Dhamma. 'Saṅghagāravatā' means showing respect to the Saṅgha. 'Sikkhāgāravatā' means showing respect to the three trainings. 'Appamādagāravatā' means showing respect to diligence. 'Paṭisanthāragāravatā' means showing respect to the two kinds of hospitality: Dhamma hospitality and material hospitality. Because he is one who respects the Teacher, he is called 'satthugaru.' Because he is one who respects the Dhamma, he is called 'dhammagaru.' 'Tibbagāravo' means having intense reverence.
106:
One who has respect for hospitality is called 'paṭisanthāragārava'. In the third sutta, 'sappatisso' means one who has a superior or one who is respectful. In this sutta, hiri (shame) and ottappa (fear of wrongdoing) are taught in combination.

## 4. Mahāmoggallānasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, the monk named Tissa is simply the co-resident (saddhivihārika) of the Elder. He is called 'mahiddhika' (of great power) because he possesses great psychic power in the sense of accomplishment. He is called 'mahānubhāva' (of great majesty) because he has great influence in the sense of pervasiveness. "Friend Moggallāna, it has been a long time since you made this turn [to come here]"—this is a common expression of affection in the world. Worldly people, upon seeing a pleasant person who has come after a long time or who has never come before, say things like, "Where has the venerable one come from? It has been a long time since the venerable one came. How did you know the way to come here? Did you lose your way?" and so on. This Tissa Brahma said this only because [the Elder] had come before. For the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna used to go to the Brahma world from time to time. In that context, 'pariyāyamakāsi' means he made a turn or visit. 'Yadidaṃ idhāgamanāya' means it is said that he took a long time to make this turn of coming here. "This seat has been prepared"—he said this after preparing a costly Brahma-couch (brahmapallaṅka). 'Aveccappasādena' means with the unwavering confidence in the Path that has been attained. In this sutta, the knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga-ñāṇa) is taught.

## 5. Vijjābhāgiyasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, 'vijjābhāgiya' refers to those states that belong to the category of knowledge (vijjā). 'Aniccasaññā' is the perception arising in the knowledge of contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā-ñāṇa). 'Anicce dukkhasaññā' is the perception arising in the knowledge of contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā-ñāṇa). 'Dukkhe anattasaññā' is the perception arising in the knowledge of contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā-ñāṇa). 'Pahānasaññā' is the perception arising in the knowledge of contemplation of abandonment (pahānānupassanā-ñāṇa). 'Virāgasaññā' is the perception arising in the knowledge of contemplation of dispassion (virāgānupassanā-ñāṇa). 'Nirodhasaññā' is the perception arising in the knowledge of contemplation of cessation (nirodhānupassanā-ñāṇa).
107:
## 6. Vivādamūlasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, 'vivādamūlāni' means the roots of dispute. 'Kodhana' means one endowed with anger, characterized by being angry. 'Upanāhī' means one endowed with grudging, characterized by not relinquishing enmity. 'For the harm and suffering of devas and humans'—how does the dispute between two monks lead to the harm and suffering of devas and humans? Just as in the Kosambaka-khandhaka, when two monks fall into dispute, their resident pupils in that monastery also dispute. The community of nuns (bhikkhunī-saṅgha) who receive their instruction also disputes. Then their lay supporters (upāsakas) dispute. At that time, the guardian deities of the humans split into two factions. Likewise, the guardian deities of those who speak according to the Dhamma (dhammavādī) become Dhamma-speakers, and the guardian deities of those who speak what is not Dhamma (adhammavādī) become non-Dhamma-speakers. Then the terrestrial deities (bhummā devā), who are friends of the guardian deities, split. In this way, through a succession up to the Brahma world, excluding the noble disciples (ariya-sāvaka), all devas and humans split into two factions. However, those who speak what is not Dhamma are much more numerous than those who speak according to the Dhamma. Therefore, they follow what is taken up by the majority, which is adhamma (non-Dhamma). Abandoning the Dhamma, the majority take up adhamma. Living with adhamma at the forefront, they are reborn in the states of deprivation (apāya). Thus, the dispute between two monks leads to the harm and suffering of devas and humans. 'Ajjhattaṃ vā' means within your internal assembly; 'bahiddhā' means in the assembly of others.

'Makkhī' means one endowed with smearing (makkha), characterized by depreciating the virtues of others. 'Paḷāsī' means one endowed with spite (paḷāsa), characterized by rivalry. 'Issukī' means one endowed with envy (issā), characterized by envying the respect and so on received by others. 'Maccharī' means one endowed with stinginess (macchariya) regarding dwellings and so on. 'Saṭho' means one who is deceitful. 'Māyāvī' means one who conceals one's own faults. 'Pāpiccho' means one of evil desires who is immoral and wishes to be praised for virtues one does not possess. 'Micchādiṭṭhī' means a nihilist (natthika-vādī), an accidentalist (ahetuka-vādī), or one who denies the efficacy of action (akiriya-vādī). 'Sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī' means one who firmly grasps only one's own views. 'Ādhānaggāhī' means one who tends to hold on tightly. 'Duppaṭinissaggī' means one who is unable to be made to relinquish what has been grasped. In this sutta, only the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) is taught.

## 7. Dānasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta, 'Veḷukaṇḍakī' means a resident of the city of Veḷukaṇḍaka. 'Chaḷaṅgasamannāgataṃ' refers to a gift endowed with six factors. 'Dakkhiṇaṃ patiṭṭhāpeti' means one gives a gift. 'Pubbeva dānā sumano' means being glad even before giving; [thinking] "I will give" from a month or half a month beforehand.
108: From the moment one intends to give, one attains joy. Herein, the preliminary volition (pubbacetanā) is obtained by one who, from the time the thought 'I will give' arises, thinks, 'When I rise from this place, I will give,' starting with the acquisition of the field and so forth. The volition during the act of giving (muñcacetanā), described as 'one clarifies the mind while giving,' is obtained only at the time of giving. The subsequent volition (aparacetanā), described as 'having given, one is glad,' is obtained by one who recollects the gift repeatedly. Vītarāgā refers to Arahants whose lust is gone. Rāgavinayāya vā paṭipannā refers to those practicing the path for the removal of lust. This is an exalted teaching. Indeed, not only is a gift given to Arahants endowed with the six factors, but a gift given to Anāgāmīs, Sakadāgāmīs, Sotāpannas, and even to a young novice (sāmaṇera) in charge of stores who has gone forth on that very day, is also endowed with the six factors. For that novice has gone forth for the sake of the fruit of the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga). Yaññassa sampadā means the fulfillment of the gift. Saññatā refers to those restrained by the restraint of virtue (sīla). Sayaṃ ācamayitvāna means having personally washed one's hands and feet and rinsed one's face. Sakehi pāṇibhi means with one's own hands. There is also a variant reading sayehi. Saddho means one who has faith in the qualities of the Triple Gem. Muttena cetasā means with a mind liberated from stinginess regarding gains and so forth. Abyāpajjhaṃ sukhaṃ lokaṃ means the celestial world which is free from suffering and possesses noble happiness and joy. ## ၈။ အတ္တကာရီသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ In the eighth sutta, addasaṃ vā assosiṃ vā means 'let me not see with eyes opened,' 'let me not hear that he lives in such and such a place,' or 'let me not hear the words of one who speaks.' Kathañhi nāma means 'for what reason?' Ārambhadhātu is energy (vīriya) characterized by the exertion of effort. Nikkamadhātu is energy characterized by emerging from laziness. Parakkamadhātu is energy characterized by progressive crushing (of defilements). Thāmadhātu is energy characterized by strength. Ṭhitidhātu is energy characterized by persistence. Upakkamadhātu is energy characterized by endeavor. All these names are just names for energy functioning in various modes. ## ၉-၁၀။ နိဒါနသုတ္တာဒိဝဏ္ဏနာ ၃၉-၄၀။ In the ninth sutta, kammānaṃ means of the actions (kamma) that lead to the round of rebirth. Samudayāya means for the sake of accumulation. Nidānaṃ means cause. Lobhajena means born of greed.
109:
'Na paññāyanti' means they are not seen as 'being produced by such kamma.' 'Sukkapakkhe kammānaṃ' refers to actions leading to the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa). Thus, in this Sutta, the round (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) are discussed. In the tenth Sutta, 'niculavane' means in the Great Mucalinda forest. 'Saddhamma' refers to the True Dhamma of the Dispensation (sāsana).

## 11. Dārukkhandha Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the eleventh Sutta, 'having attained mastery over the mind' (cetovasippatto) means having reached the state of being able to make the mind follow one's will. 'One should perceive it only as earth' means one should note the hard characteristic as the earth element (pathavīdhātu). 'Depending on which' means depending on the evident hard characteristic of the earth element, one should perceive this log only as 'earth,' meaning the earth element exists in this log. In this manner, the remaining terms should also be understood. Just as the earth element exists in that log as the hard characteristic, so too do the liquid characteristic as the water element (āpodhātu), the heat characteristic as the fire element (tejodhātu), and the supporting characteristic as the air element (vāyodhātu). In the red-colored heartwood, there is the beautiful element (subhadhātu) like the color of a lotus flower. In the decayed powder, sapwood, and bark, there is the unbeautiful element (asubhadhātu) which has an unattractive color. Depending on that unbeautiful element, one should perceive and note this log only as 'unbeautiful.' In this Sutta, the mixed abiding (missakavihāra) is discussed.

## 12. Nāgita Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the twelfth Sutta, 'one who dwells in a village-outskirt monastery' (gāmantavihāriṃ) means one who lives in a dwelling near a village. 'Sitting in concentration' (samāhitaṃ nisinnaṃ) means sitting having attained concentration in that village-outskirt dwelling. 'Now this person' (idāni imaṃ) refers to this individual at this time. 'Will cause him to waver from concentration' means will cause him to rise from concentration. 'I am not pleased' means it is not according to one's own mind. 'Nodding off' (pacalāyamānaṃ) means one who is drowsy. 'Oneness' (ekattaṃ) means one will direct the mind only to the perception of the forest (araññasaññā) which has a single nature and a single object. 'Will protect' (anurakkhiyyati) means will support. 'Will liberate the unliberated mind' means it will now liberate the mind, which was not liberated from defilements at other times, through the five kinds of liberation (vimutti). 'Abandons' (riñcati) means avoids or lets go. 'Having removed' (paṭipaṇāmetvā) means having discarded or cast away. 'For the purpose of defecation and urination' means for the sake of discharging excrement and urine. By this much, the Teacher has praised the forest dwelling. The matters to be said in the first part of the Sutta should be understood as already stated below.

## Devatāvaggo Catuttho.
110:
## 5. Dhammika Vagga
## 1. Commentary on the Nāga Sutta

In the first sutta of the fifth chapter, the phrase "with the Venerable Ānanda" (āyasmata ānandena saddhiṃ) is stated because the Teacher set out after calling the Elder Ānanda, saying, "Come, Ānanda." However, it should be understood that the Teacher went there surrounded by no less than five hundred monks. "He approached" (tenupasaṅkami) means he approached while being surrounded by those same five hundred monks. The word "having bathed" (parisincitvā) is a common usage meaning "having washed."

"Restoring [the body] to its original state" (pubbāpayamāno) means that after putting on the red double-layered undergarment and holding the upper robe with both hands, he stood with his back to the western world-element and faced the eastern world-element, making his limbs as they were before by cleansing them with water. The community of monks also descended at various places, bathed, and upon emerging, stood surrounding the Teacher. At that time, the sun, like a red-gold earring falling from the sky, entered the western world-element. The moon, like a pure silver disc, rose from the eastern world-element. In the center, the Fully Enlightened One, surrounded by five hundred monks, stood adorning the world at the bank of the Pubbakoṭṭhaka River, emitting the six-colored Buddha rays.

At that time... "the elephant named Seto" (seto nāma nāgo) refers to a noble elephant that received this name because of its white color. "With the grand playing of musical instruments" (mahātūriyatāḷitavāditetena) means with the great striking and blowing of instruments. Among these, the initial striking is called "tāḷita," and the subsequent blowing is called "vādita." "The people" (jano) refers to the great multitude of people who had gathered to see the elephant. "Seeing [it], they spoke thus" (disvā evamāha) means that after seeing that great elephant—whose limbs had been rubbed and washed, who had been brought up to the bank, whose body had been dried, and who was adorned with elephant ornaments—they spoke words of praise: "Sirs, how beautiful indeed!"

"Endowed with a [perfect] body" (kāyupapanno) means endowed with physical excellence; it means having complete major and minor limbs. "The Venerable Udāyī" (āyasmā udāyī) refers to the Elder Kāḷudāyī, who had attained the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). "He said this" (etadavoca) means that upon seeing the multitude praising the appearance of the elephant, he thought: "These people are speaking of the beauty of an elephant born of rootless rebirth (ahetuka-paṭisandhi), not of the Buddha-Elephant. I shall now speak of the beauty of the Buddha-Elephant by making a comparison with this noble elephant," and thus he addressed [the Buddha] with these words.
111:
Venerable Udāyī, intending to praise the virtues of the Buddha, spoke the words beginning with, "Venerable Sir, is this merely an elephant?" In that context, "great" (mahanta) refers to being endowed with height. "Immense" (brahanta) refers to being endowed with girth. "Spoke thus" (evamāha) means he said this. Then, because the word 'Nāga' is used for elephants, horses, bulls, snakes, trees, and humans, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with, "Even an elephant..."

"Evil" (āgu) refers to base, inferior, unwholesome states. "I call him a Nāga" (tamahaṃ nāgo brūmi) means: I call that person a 'Nāga' because he does not commit the ten unwholesome paths of action or the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness through the three doors [of action]. Indeed, such a person is called a 'Nāga' in the sense that he does not commit evil (na āguṃ karoti). "I rejoice with these verses" means: I rejoice and delight with these sixteen verses consisting of sixty-four lines (pādas).

"Become human" (manussabhūta) means being truly human without having transitioned to the state of a deva or others. "Self-tamed" (attadanta) means tamed by oneself alone, not brought to discipline by others. For the Blessed One, through the discipline of the Path produced by himself, is tamed at the eye-door, and also at the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind doors. Being thus tamed, peaceful, calmed, and fully extinguished in these six areas, he is called "self-tamed."

"Concentrated" (samāhita) means being firm through the two types of concentration. "Dwelling" (iriyamāna) means living or staying. "The Noble Path" (brahmapatha) means the excellent path, the deathless path, the path to Nibbāna. "Delighting in the tranquility of the mind" (cittassūpasame rata) means having stilled the five hindrances through the first jhana, vitakka and vicāra through the second jhana, rapture (pīti) through the third jhana, and pleasure and pain (sukha-dukkha) through the fourth jhana; it is the state of greatly delighting in such mental tranquility.

"They pay homage" (namassanti) means they pay homage through body, speech, mind, and through practice in accordance with the Dhamma; they show respect and honor. "One who has gone to the far shore of all dhammas" (sabbadhammānapāragu) means one who has reached the far shore, the summit, and the pinnacle of all dhammas—aggregates, sense bases, and elements—through the sixfold arrival at the far shore: higher knowledge (abhiññā), full understanding (pariññā), abandoning (pahāna), development (bhāvanā), realization (sacchikiriyā), and attainment (samāpatti).

"Even the devas pay homage to him" means that even the devas from the ten thousand world systems, including those like the young deva Subrahma who have reached suffering and those who have reached happiness, all pay homage to you. "Thus I heard from the Arahant" (iti me arahato sutaṃ) indicates: "Thus I have heard in the presence of you, who have received the designation 'Araha' (Arahant) due to four reasons."
112:
‘Sabbasaṃyojanātīta’ refers to a person who has transcended all ten fetters. ‘Vanā nibbanamāgata’ means having emerged from the forest of defilements and reached Nibbāna, which is free from the forest of defilements. ‘Kāmehi nekkhammarata’ means that because of emerging from the two types of sensuality—sensual objects (vatthu-kāma) and sensual defilements (kilesa-kāma)—monkhood, the eight attainments, and the four Noble Paths are called ‘renunciation’ (nekkhamma), and He greatly delights in those states. ‘Muttaṃ selāva kañcana’ means being like pure gold released from a block of raw stone.

‘Sabbe accaruci’ means possessing an exceedingly brilliant radiance (or delight) that arises by surpassing all beings. Because of the delight that arises by surpassing the eighth person (one on the path of stream-entry), a Stream-enterer is called ‘accaruci’. Because of surpassing the Stream-enterer, the Once-returner is so called; likewise, by successively surpassing the Non-returner, the Arahant, and the Paccekabuddha, the Blessed One is called ‘accaruci’ (one with exceedingly brilliant majesty). ‘Himavāvaññe siluccaye’ means that just as the Himavanta, the king of mountains, is beautiful by surpassing other mountains, so too He is exceedingly beautiful. ‘Saccanāma’ means having a true name, a factual name. Just as He is called ‘Nāga’ because of not committing evil (āgu), thus He has an unfailing name.

‘Soracca’ refers to pure virtue (sīla). ‘Avihiṃsā’ refers to compassion (karuṇā) and the states that are precursors to compassion. These two states are the two front legs of the Great Elephant, the Buddha.

‘Tapa’ refers to the undertaking of ascetic practices (dhutaṅga). ‘Brahmacariya’ refers to the virtue associated with the Noble Path. These two states are the other two hind legs of the Great Elephant, the Buddha. ‘Saddhāhattha’ means being endowed with the trunk of faith (saddhā). ‘Upekkhāsetadantavā’ means being endowed with the white tusks of six-factored equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā).

‘Sati gīvā’ means that just as the neck is the support for the network of veins in the major and minor limbs of a great elephant, so too mindfulness (sati) is the support for the states such as gentleness (soracca) of the Great Elephant, the Buddha. Therefore, it is said, ‘Mindfulness is the neck.’ ‘Siro paññā’ means that just as the head of a great elephant is the supreme limb, so too the omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) of the Great Elephant, the Buddha, is the supreme limb. Since He knows all things through that knowledge, it is said, ‘Wisdom is the head.’ ‘Vīmaṃsā dhammacintanā’ means that just as the tip of the trunk of a great elephant is called ‘vīmaṃsā’ (investigation), and that elephant investigates with the tip of its trunk what is hard or soft, what is edible or inedible, and then discards what should be discarded and takes what should be taken; even so, the reflection on the Dhamma, known as the knowledge that distinguishes the groups of Dhamma of the Great Elephant, the Buddha, is called ‘vīmaṃsā’. Through that knowledge, He knows those who are capable (bhabba) and those who are incapable (abhabba). Therefore, it is called ‘vīmaṃsā’.
113:
Reflection on the Dhamma (dhammacintanā) means: just as a great elephant investigates with the tip of its trunk what is hard or soft, what is edible or inedible, and then discards what should be discarded and takes what should be taken; even so, the reflection on the Dhamma, known as the knowledge that distinguishes the groups of Dhamma of the Great Elephant, the Buddha, is called ‘vīmaṃsā’ (investigation). Through that investigative wisdom, He knows the states to be cultivated and the states not to be cultivated. Therefore, it is called ‘vīmaṃsā dhammacintanā’.

In the term ‘dhammakucchisamātapo’, the concentration of the fourth jhāna is called ‘Dhamma’. Since the belly itself is the support for good practice (samātapa), it is called ‘kucchisamātapo’. ‘Samātapa’ means the place or support for good practice. Because the state called the fourth jhāna concentration is the support for good practice like a belly, it is called ‘dhammakucchisamātapo’. For the person established in the fourth jhāna concentration, various states such as the modes of psychic power (iddhividha) are fulfilled; therefore, that fourth jhāna is called ‘kucchisamātapa’.

‘Viveko’ refers to physical seclusion (kāya-viveka), mental seclusion (citta-viveka), and seclusion from the substrates of existence (upadhi-viveka). Just as the tail of a great elephant wards off flies, even so the seclusion of the Blessed One wards off laypeople and monastics. Therefore, that seclusion is called ‘vāladhī’ (the tail).

‘Jhāyī’ means one who habitually enters meditative absorption through the two types of jhāna. ‘Assāsarato’ means: just as a great elephant has inhalation and exhalation, the Great Elephant, the Buddha, has the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti), and He delights in that attainment of fruition. It means that just as one cannot exist without inhalation and exhalation, He does not exist without that attainment of fruition. ‘Sabbattha saṃvuto’ means restraint in all sense doors. ‘Anavajjānī’ refers to meals obtained through right livelihood. ‘Sāvajjānī’ refers to meals obtained through the five types of wrong livelihood.

‘Aṇuṃthūlaṃ’ means small and large. ‘Sabbaṃ chetvāna bandhanaṃ’ means having cut all ten fetters. ‘Nupalippati lokena’ means not being smeared by the world with the smears of craving, conceit, and views. ‘Mahāginī’ means a great fire. In this context, ‘viññūhi desitā’ means that only the Elder Kāḷudāyī, who reached the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), is the wise and learned one (viññū); it means it was shown by that Elder. ‘Viññassanti mahānāgā, nāgaṃ nāgena desitaṃ’ means that other Arahant-elephants will understand the Buddha-elephant taught by the Udāyī-elephant.

‘Sarīraṃ vijahaṃ nāgo, parinibbissati’ means that having attained Nibbāna through the extinction of defilements at the throne of enlightenment, He will attain Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element without remainder between the twin Sāla trees. In this way, the Elder Udāyī, who had reached the analytical knowledges, concluded the teaching by praising the virtues of the Possessor of Ten Powers (Dasabala) with 16 verses and 64 lines. The Blessed One rejoiced. At the end of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings drank the nectar of Nibbāna.

## 2. Migasālā Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, ‘kathaṃ kathaṃ nāma’ means ‘for what reason?’. ‘Aññeyyo’ means ‘to be known’. ‘Yatra hi nāma’ means ‘in which Dhamma’.
114:
'Samasama-gatikā' means those who have an equal destination through an equal state. 'Bhavissanti' means they will be. 'Sakadāgāmi-patto tusitaṃ kāyaṃ upapanno' means that having become a Once-returner, he was reborn only in the Tusita heaven. 'Kathaṃ kathaṃ nāma' is an inquiry: For what reason? Knowing what did he teach, or did he teach without knowing? The Elder Ānanda, not knowing the reason, said, "Sister, the Blessed One has answered this matter in this way."

'Ammakā ammakapaññā' refers to one who, being a woman, is endowed only with the perception of a woman. In the phrase 'ke ca purisapuggala-paropariyañāṇe', the 'knowledge of the higher and lower states of persons' refers to the knowledge that understands the maturity or immaturity of the faculties (indriya) by way of their sharpness or dullness. Therefore, who is the foolish Migasālā, and who are the Fully Enlightened Buddhas whose knowledge of the maturity and immaturity of the faculties of persons is unobstructed? The summary here is that these two are far apart, very far apart.

Now, wishing to show Migasālā's distance from the truth, the Buddha taught, "Ānanda, these six persons," and so on. 'Sorato hoti' means one who well refrains from evil. There is also a variant reading 'surato'. 'Abhinandanti sabrahmacārī ekatta-vāsena' means that fellow practitioners rejoice and are pleased by living together with that person. There is also a variant reading 'ekanta-vāsena', which means by living constantly. 'Savane-napi akataṃ hoti' means that what ought to be heard has not yet been heard. In the phrase 'bāhusaccena-pi akataṃ hoti', 'bāhusacca' (great learning) here refers to energy (vīriya); it means that what ought to be done with energy has not yet been done. 'Diṭṭhiyā-pi appaṭividdhaṃ hoti' means that the Dhamma which ought to be penetrated by wisdom has not yet been penetrated. 'Sāmāyikampi vimuttiṃ na labhati' means not obtaining the joy and gladness that arises based on hearing the Dhamma from time to time. 'Hānagāmī-yeva hoti' means one who only goes towards decline.

'Pamāṇikā' are those who take measures or judge persons. 'Paminanti' means they attempt to compare or weigh. 'Eko hīno' means one person is low in qualities. 'Eko paṇīto' means one person is excellent in qualities. 'Taṃ hi' refers to that act of measuring.

'Abhikkantataro' means one who is better. 'Paṇītataro' means one who is more excellent. 'Dhamma-soto nibbahati' means the stream of Dhamma, which is insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) arising courageously, carries one away (leading one to the stage of the Noble Ones).
115:
It leads one to the stage of the Noble Ones (ariya-bhūmi). 'Tadantaraṃ ko jāneyya' means who else besides the Tathāgata could know that interval or that reason?

'Kodhamāno' refers to anger and conceit. 'Lobbhadhammā' is simply the nature of greed. 'Vacīsaṅkhārā' refers to words in the sense of conversation and talk. 'Yo vā panassa mādiso' means only another Fully Enlightened Buddha like me could exist; only such a Buddha could take the measure of (judge) persons. 'Khanyatī' means reaching the destruction of one's qualities. "Ānanda, these six persons" refers to: two who are gentle/patient, two who are not yet free from anger, conceit, and greed, and two who are not yet free from anger, conceit, and verbal formations—these are the six persons. 'Gatiṃ' refers to the course of knowledge (ñāṇa-gati). 'Ekanga-hīnā' means they are each lacking one factor of quality. Purāṇa was distinguished by virtue (sīla), while Isidatta was distinguished by wisdom (paññā). Purāṇa's virtue stood in the place of Isidatta's wisdom, and Isidatta's wisdom stood in the place of Purāṇa's virtue.

## 3. Commentary on the Iṇa Sutta

In the third sutta, 'dāliddiyaṃ' means poverty. 'Kāmabhogino' refers to a being who enjoys sense pleasures. 'Assako' means one who has no possessions of his own. 'Anāḷhiko' means one who is not wealthy. 'Iṇaṃ ādiyati' means being unable to make a living, he takes a debt. 'Vaḍḍhiṃ paṭissuṇāti' means being unable to pay, he promises to pay interest. 'Anu-carantipi naṃ' means they follow him closely, harassing him in the midst of an assembly or a group by exposing him to the sun or throwing dust on him. 'Saddhā natthi' means there is not even a trace of conviction or faith. 'Hirī natthi' means there is not even a trace of the sense of shame regarding evil. 'Ottappaṃ natthi' means there is not even a trace of the fear of wrongdoing. 'Vīriyaṃ natthi' means there is not even a trace of bodily energy. 'Paññā natthi' means there is not even a trace of the wisdom that knows one is the owner of one's actions (kammassakatā-paññā). 'Iṇādānasmiṃ vadāmi' means He teaches this as taking a debt. 'Mā maṃ janyū' means "May they not know me."

'Dāliddiyaṃ dukkhaṃ' means poverty in wealth is suffering. 'Kāmalābhābhijappinaṃ' refers to those who long to obtain sense pleasures. 'Pāpakamma-vinibbayo' is that which increases evil deeds. 'Saṃsappati' means he trembles or wavers. 'Jānaṃ' means knowing. 'Yassa vippaṭisārajā' means those (suffering) states born of remorse for that person...
116:
For that person, there are (suffering states) arising from remorse (*vippaṭisāra*). '*Yonimaññataraṃ*' refers to one of the animal births. The donor gives while clarifying the mind. '*Kaṭaggāha*' means taking victory or taking faultless clothes and so on. '*Gharamesino*' refers to one who seeks a household life or one who lives in a house. '*Cāgo puññaṃ pavaḍḍhati*' means the merit called generosity increases. There is also a reading '*cāgā puññaṃ*'. '*Patiṭṭhitā*' refers to the established faith of a Stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*). '*Hirimano*' is one who has a mind associated with a sense of shame (*hiri*). '*Nirāmisa sukha*' is the happiness arising based on the three *jhānas*. '*Upekkhā*' is the equanimity associated with the fourth *jhāna*. '*Āraddhavīriya*' is one who has fully exerted energy. '*Jhānāni upasampajja*' means having attained the four *jhānas*. '*Ekodi nipako sato*' means being one with a unified mind, endowed with knowledge of the ownership of deeds (*kammassakatā-ñāṇa*) and mindfulness.

It means knowing this matter according to its true nature. '*Sabbasaṃyojanakkhaya*' occurs in Nibbāna. '*Sabbaso*' means in every way. '*Anupādāya*' means without clinging (through craving and views). '*Sammā cittaṃ vimuccati*' means that in Nibbāna, which is the destruction of all fetters, without clinging in any way, the path-mind (*magga-citta*) is rightly liberated through the appropriate means. In the Pali, it is also written as '*etaṃ ñatvā yathābhūtaṃ sabbasaṃyojanakkhayaṃ*'. The meaning of that Pali is: having known that Nibbāna, which is the destruction of all fetters, according to its true nature. However, that Pali phrase does not connect well with the preceding and following sentences.

'*Tassa sammā vimuttassa*' refers to that Arahant who is rightly liberated. '*Ñāṇaṃ hoti*' means that reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa*) arises. '*Tādino*' refers to one who is established in such a nature. '*Akuppā*' is the unshakeable (liberation) because it takes the unshakeable Nibbāna as its object and because of the absence of defilements which are the causes of shaking. '*Vimutti*' refers to both the liberation of the Path (*magga-vimutti*) and the liberation of the Fruit (*phala-vimutti*). '*Bhavasaṃyojanakkhaye*' refers to Nibbāna, which is the destruction of the fetters of existence, or the (liberation) that arises at the end of the fetters of existence. '*Etaṃ kho paramaṃ ñāṇaṃ*' means this knowledge of the Path and Fruit is called the supreme knowledge. '*Sukhamanuttaraṃ*' means only this happiness of the Path and Fruit is called the unsurpassed happiness. '*Āṇaṇyamuttamaṃ*' means since the Arahant is the supreme debt-free person among all those free from debt, the Fruit of Arahantship is called the supreme freedom from debt (*āṇaṇya*). In this way, the Buddha took the Fruit of Arahantship as the climax of the teaching. In this Sutta, only the round of rebirth (*vaṭṭa*) is discussed, but in the verses, both the round (*vaṭṭa*) and the cessation of the round (*vivaṭṭa*) are discussed.
117:
## 4. Commentary on Mahācunda Sutta
In the fourth Sutta, the Mahācunda Sutta, '*cetiyesu*' means in the Ceti country. '*Sahajātiyaṃ*' means in the market town named Sahajāti. '*Mahācunda*' refers to the Elder Mahācunda, the younger brother of the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta. Because those monks possess the scriptural Dhamma (*pariyatti*) which is repeatedly practiced, they are called '*dhammayogā*' (those devoted to the Dhamma). This is a name for the Dhamma preachers. Because they contemplate, they are called '*jhāyī*' (meditators). '*Apasādenti*' means they disparage or harm. '*Jhāyanti*' means they contemplate. '*Upajjhāyanti*', '*anupajjhāyanti*', '*pajjhāyanti*', '*nijjhāyanti*', etc., are expansions made by the power of prefixes. The word '*jhāyanti*' is used when questioning: "What Dhamma do these people contemplate?", "For what benefit do they contemplate?", "For what reason do they contemplate?".

'Touching the Deathless element with the body and dwelling' means that the monks, dwelling while taking up a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) with the aim of the Deathless Nibbāna element, gradually touch it with the mental body (*nāma-kāya*) and dwell. 'Deep meaning' refers to the hidden and profound meanings of the aggregates (*khandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and so on. 'Seeing by penetrating with wisdom' means seeing by penetrating with the Path-wisdom (*magga-paññā*) along with insight (*vipassanā*). In this context, not only the wisdom of investigation and penetration but also the wisdom of learning and inquiry is appropriate.

## 5-6. Commentary on the Two Sandiṭṭhika Suttas
47-48. In the fifth Sutta, 'that which is clearly present within oneself' means existing within one's own internal continuity. By the terms such as 'greed' (*lobha*), the three unwholesome roots are shown. By the terms such as 'states of greed' (*lobhadhammā*), the states associated with that greed, etc., are shown. In the sixth Sutta, '*kāyasandosa*' is the manner of corruption of the body-door. In the remaining two terms as well, the method is the same. In both of these Suttas, only reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇā*) is taught.

## 7. Commentary on Khema Sutta
In the seventh Sutta, '*vusitavā*' means one who has lived and practiced the noble holy life of the Path. '*Katakarṇīyo*' means one who stands having done what was to be done by the four Paths. '*Ohitabhāro*' means one who stands having laid down the burden of the aggregates, the burden of defilements, and the burden of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*). '*Anuppattasadattho*' means one who has reached their own goal, which is the Fruit of Arahantship. '*Parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano*' means one whose fetters of existence are exhausted. '*Sammadaññā vimutto*' means one who is liberated from defilements having known rightly through reason and cause.

For that Arahant, there is no longer such conceit as "I am superior," etc. By such words, the three types of conceit are shown to be abandoned. Indeed, for an Arahant, the conceit "There is one superior to me, there is one equal to me, there is one inferior to me" does not arise. By the words "There is no one superior to me," etc., those same conceits are abandoned. In an Arahant, the kind of conceit such as "I alone am superior, I am equal, I am inferior, there are no others who are superior, etc." does not arise. '*Acirapakkantesu*' means when they have departed not long after declaring the Fruit of Arahantship. 'They declare another meaning' refers to the declaration of the Fruit of Arahantship. 'It seems they declare another meaning while smiling' means...
118:
Only those prides are abandoned. Indeed, for an Arahant, such pride as "I alone am superior, I am equal, I am inferior, there are no others superior etc." does not occur.

*Acirapakkantesu* means shortly after they have departed after declaring Arahantship. *Aññaṃ vyākaronti* means they speak of Arahantship. *Hasamānakā maññေ aññaṃ vyākaronti* means they speak as if they are laughing. *Vighātaṃ āpajjanti* means they undergo suffering.

"Not among the superior, nor the inferior, nor the equal are they led"—in this verse, *Ussa* refers to the exalted, superior persons. *Oma* refers to the inferior persons. *Samatta* refers to the equal persons. Thus, among these three types—superior, inferior, and equal—Arahants are not led by pride, they do not lead, and they do not approach (pride). *Khīṇā jāti* means their rebirth is exhausted. *Vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ* means the holy life of the Path has been lived. *Caranti saṃyojanavippamuttā* means they live and move about being liberated from all fetters. In both the Sutta and the verse, only the Arahant is spoken of.

## 8. Commentary on the Indriyasaṃvara Sutta

In the eighth sutta, *hatūpanisaṃ hoti* means having a destroyed basis. *Sīlavipannassa* means for one whose virtue is ruined. *Yathābhūtañāṇadassanaṃ* means tender insight knowledge. In the phrase *nibbidāvirāgo*, *nibbidā* is powerful insight, and *virāgo* is the Noble Path. In the phrase *vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ*, *vimutti* is the fruit of Arahantship, and *ñāṇadassanaṃ* is reviewing knowledge. *Upanissayasampannaṃ hoti* means having a complete basis. In this sutta, the restraint of the senses (indriyasaṃvara) which is the protection of virtue is taught.

## 9. Commentary on the Ānanda Sutta

In the ninth sutta, *kittāvatā* means by how much or by what means. *Assutañceva* means never heard before at another time. *Na sammosaṃ gacchanti* means they do not go to destruction. *Cetaso samphuṭṭhapubbā* means previously touched by the mind. *Samudācaranti* means they occur at the mind-door. *Aviññātañca vijānāti* means one knows a matter not known at another time. *Pariyāpuṇāti* means one uses or speaks. *Deseti* means one shows (expounds). *Paraṃ vāceti* means one makes another learn.
119:
*Āgatāgama* means those to whom any of the traditions (āgama) such as the Dīgha Nikāya etc. have come. *Dhammadhara* means those who bear the Suttanta Piṭaka. *Vinayadhara* means those who bear the Vinaya Piṭaka. *Mātikādhara* means those who bear the two Pātimokkhas. *Paripucchati* means asking about the sequence of what precedes and follows. *Paripañhati* means weighing or defining, thinking "I will ask this and that." "Venerable sir, how is this? Venerable sir, how is the sequence of what precedes and follows?"—thus one asks. "What is the meaning of this spoken word?"—thus one asks. *Aviwaṭa* means a matter not yet revealed. *Vivaranti* means making clear. *Kaṅkhāṭhāniyesu* means in things that are causes for doubt. Therein, whatever thing doubt arises in, that very thing should be known as a ground for doubt (*kaṅkhāṭhāniya*).

## 10. Commentary on the Khattiya Sutta

In the tenth sutta, *bhogādhippāyā* means (kings) who have the desire or the arising disposition for the purpose of accumulating wealth. *Paññūpavicārā* means they have a preoccupation for the sake of wisdom, thinking "May we be wise." For those kings, this very preoccupation occurs close to the mind. *Balādhiṭṭhānā* means (kings) who have the army as their support. For when they have obtained the army, they are called those who have obtained a support. *Pathavībhinivesā* means they have a mental fixation for the sake of the earth, thinking "May we be lords of the earth." *Issariyapariyosānā* means having the royal consecration as their end. For when they reach the consecration, they are called those who have reached the end. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all sentences.

As for the remaining terms, this is the intention: First, Brahmins are called those who have obtained a support when they have obtained the Vedas; householders when they have obtained some craft; women when they have obtained a son who is the heir to the family; thieves when they have obtained some weapon; and monks are called those who have obtained a support when they are fulfilled in virtue. Therefore, the words "supported by mantras" (*mantādhiṭṭhānā*) etc. were spoken.

For Brahmins, the mind is fixed on "We will perform a sacrifice," and they are called those who have reached the end when they reach the Brahma-world. Therefore, it was said of those Brahmins: "fixed on sacrifice, ending in the Brahma-world." For householders, the mind is fixed on performing work; therefore they are called "fixed on work." When the work is finished, they are called those who have reached the end; therefore they are called "ending in finished work."

*Purisādhippāyā* means (women) who have a desire for men. For those women, the mind is preoccupied for the sake of adornment; therefore they are called "preoccupied with adornment." Being without a co-wife...
120:
"I wish to live alone in the house"—because her mind is fixed in this way, it is called *asapattībhinivesā* (fixation on having no co-wives). Because they are said to have reached the end when they obtain sovereignty over household duties, they are called *issariyapariyosānā* (having sovereignty as the end).

Because those thieves desire to take the property of others, they are called *ādānādhippāyā* (having the intention to take). Because the minds of those thieves roam in the forest, which is their hiding place, they are called *gahanūpavicārā* (roaming in the thicket). Because the minds of those thieves are fixed for the purpose of darkness, they are called *andhakārābhinivesā* (fixation on darkness). Because they are said to have reached the end when they reach the state of not being seen by others, they are called *adassanapariyosānā* (having invisibility as the end).

Because those monks desire patience (*khanti*) and pure conduct (*soracca*), they are called *khantisoraccādhippāyā* (having the intention for patience and gentleness). Because the minds of those monks are fixed on the state of having no possessions and being unrestrained, they are called *ākiñcaññābhinivesā* (fixation on having nothing). Because they are said to have reached the end when they reach Nibbāna, they are called *nibbānapariyosānā* (having Nibbāna as the end).

## 11. Appamādasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eleventh sutta, "*samadhiggayha*" means having taken well. "*Jaṅgalānaṃ pāṇānaṃ*" refers to creatures with feet that move on the ground. "*Padajātāni*" refers to footprints. "*Samodhānaṃ gacchanti*" means they come together or are included. "*Aggamakkhāyati*" means it is said to be the foremost. "*Pabbajalayako*" is one who reaps *pabbaja* grass. "*Odhunāti*" means shaking with the face turned downwards. "*Nidhunāti*" means shaking from both sides. "*Nicchādeti*" means striking with the arm or against a tree. "*Ambapiṇḍiyā*" occurs in a cluster of mangoes. "*Vaṇṭūpanibandhanāni*" are things bound to the stalk or situated on the stalk. "*Tadanvayāni bhavanti*" means they follow the stalk; it also means they follow the stem of the mango cluster. "*Khuddarājāno*" refers to minor kings or ordinary kings.

## 12. Dhammikasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the twelfth sutta, "*sabbaso*" means in all [ways]. "*Sattasu vihāresu*" refers to the seven precincts. "*Paribhāsati*" means to abuse or threaten with danger. "*Vihiṃsati*" means to harm. "*Vitudati*" means to prick or pierce. "*Roseti vācāya*" means to offend or strike with words. "*Pakkammanti*" means they go away to various directions. "*Na saṇṭhahanti*" means they do not remain stable.
121:
"*Riñcanti*" means they abandon or release. "*Pabbājeyyāma*" means we should expel. "*Handa*" is an exclamation (*nipāta*) used in the sense of connection (*vavassagga*). "*Alaṃ*" means it is appropriate to expel. "*Kiṃ te iminā*" means what benefit is there for you by living like this in your birthplace? "*Tīradassiṃ sakuṇaṃ*" refers to a shore-sighting bird, a direction-crow (*disākāka*). "*Muñcanti*" means they release it to look for a direction. "*Sāmantā*" means in a place not far away. There is also a variant reading "*samantā*," which means from all around. "*Abhiniveso*" is the location of branches that have spread out and remained. "*Mūlasantānakānaṃ*" is the location of the roots.

"*Āḷhakathālikā*" is a rice pot for cooking one *āḷhaka* of rice. "*Khuddaṃ madhu*" is a honeycomb with a stick made by small bees. "*Anelakaṃ*" is pure honey. "*Na ca sudaṃ aññamaññassa phalāni hiṃsanti*" means they do not destroy the fruits on the branches belonging to each other's portion. There is no such thing as cutting the roots, bark, or leaves from one's own portion; they only consume the fruits that have fallen beneath their own branches. Even if a fruit rolls from another's portion into their own, they do not eat it, knowing, "This is not a fruit from our branch." "*Yāvadatthaṃ bhakkhitvā*" means having eaten to one's fill, up to the throat. "*Sākhaṃ bhañjitvā*" means having broken off a leaf the size of an umbrella to make shade and then departing. "*Yatra hi nāma*" means "for indeed." "*Pakkamiṣṣatī*" means he has departed. "*Nādāsi*" means he did not take the fruit due to the power of a deity. That deity made a resolution not to take the fruit.

"*Tenupasaṅkami*" means the country folk went and said, "Great King, the tree does not bear fruit; is it our fault or yours?" The King thought, "There is no fault in me, nor in the country folk; there is no injustice in our kingdom. For what reason does the tree not bear fruit? I will go and ask Sakka, the Lord of Devas," and thus he approached Sakka. "*Pavattesi*" means he turned it around. "*Ummūlamakāsi*" means he turned the roots upward. "*Api nu tvaṃ*" means "of yours." "*Aṭṭhitāyeva*" means simply not remaining. "*Sacchavīni*" means having the same color, situated in their natural place. "*Na paccakkosati*" means he does not revile in return. "*Rosantaṃ*" means one who offends or oppresses. "*Bhaṇḍantaṃ*" means one who strikes.

"*Sunetto*": Eyes are called '*netta*'; because those eyes are beautiful, he is called '*Sunetta*' (Beautiful-eyed). "*Titthakaro*" is one who makes a landing place for descending into the happy realms. "*Vītarāgo*" means...
122:
One is free from lust through the power of abandonment by suppression (vikkham bhana-pahāna). 'Pasavati' means he obtains. 'Diṭṭhisampannaṃ' refers to a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) who is endowed with the Path of Stream-entry (dassana). 'Khanti' means the digging up or destruction of one's own virtues. The phrase "yathāmaṃ sabrahmacārīsu" means that the Buddha does not refer to the inability to endure such things as the verbal abuse and threats directed at this Stream-enterer among his fellow monks, which would destroy his virtues. In the phrase "na no samasabrahmacārīsu," the term 'samajano' refers to one's own retinue. Therefore, the meaning here is that our minds will not become malicious toward our fellow monks who are our own retinue.

Regarding Jotipāla and Govinda, he was Jotipāla by name and Mahāgovinda by rank or position. 'Sattapurohita' means he was the chaplain to seven kings, such as King Reṇu. "Ahimsakā atītaṃse" means these six teachers were non-violent toward others in the past. 'Nirāmagandhā' is so called because they were free from the impurity (āmagandha) of anger. 'Karuṇāvimuttā' means they were those inclined toward the meditative absorption of compassion (karuṇā-jhāna); they were established in compassion and in the preliminary stages of compassion. 'Yete' means "these people," or this is the actual reading. One should not harm (or offend) a virtuous person. 'Diṭṭhiṭṭhānappahāyinaṃ' refers to one who has abandoned the sixty-two types of wrong views.

'Sattamo' (the seventh) refers to the person who is the seventh when counting from the fruit of Arahantship. 'Avītarāgo' means one who is not free from lust. By this word 'avītarāgo,' the status of being a Non-returner (Anāgāmī) is excluded. "The five faculties are tender" means the five faculties of insight (vipassanā-indriya) are weak. For that Stream-enterer, those faculties are called tender when compared to a Once-returner (Sakadāgāmī). 'Vipassanā' is the knowledge that comprehends formations (saṅkhāra). "Harmed from the very beginning" means being harmed at the earliest stage. 'Akkhato' means being uninjured and unharmed by the destruction of virtues. The remaining words are clear in meaning in all places.

## 5. Dhammika Vagga
## The First Fifty (Paṭhama Paṇṇāsaka) is finished.
123:
## 2. Dutiya Paṇṇāsakaṃ
## 6. Mahāvagga
## 1. Soṇasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the first sutta of the sixth chapter, 'Soṇa' refers to the very delicate Elder Soṇa. 'Sītavana' refers to the cemetery of that name. It is said that in that Sītavana cemetery, five hundred ambulatory (caṅkama) cells were created in succession; among them, the Elder took a suitable ambulatory path for himself and practiced the recluse's Dhamma. As he walked in meditation with aroused energy, the soles of his feet broke open. When he walked on his knees, his knees and even the palms of his hands broke open, and sores appeared. Although he lived with such aroused energy, he was unable to manifest even a sign of light (obhāsa-nimitta). To show the thought that arose in that Elder, whose body was exhausted by his exertion, as he sat on a stone slab at the edge, the passage beginning with "Atha kho āyasmato" was spoken. Therein, 'āraddhavīriyā' means those with fully exerted energy. Regarding the phrase "na anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimuccati," he thought: "If I were a person of quick intuition (ugghaṭitaññū), or one who understands through elaboration (vipañcitaññū), or one who is guidable (neyya), surely my mind would be liberated from the defilements. But I am certainly one for whom the word is the maximum (padaparama); that is why my mind is not liberated." Having made this resolution, he pondered the passage beginning with "Saṃvijjanti kho panā." Therein, the word 'bhogā' is a nominative case used in the sense of the accusative.

'Pāturahosi' (manifested) means that the Buddha, knowing the Elder's thought, thought: "Today, this Soṇa is sitting on the ground of exertion in the Sītavana cemetery and is thinking this thought. I will go, take up his thought along with its meaning, and teach him the meditation subject using the simile of the lute (vīṇā)." Thus, he appeared clearly before him. 'Paññatte āsane' (on the prepared seat) means that monks who practice meditation usually prepare whatever seat is available for the Blessed Buddha who comes to their dwelling to advise them, and only then do they continue their meditation. If they find no other seat, they spread old leaves and lay their outer robe (saṅghāṭi) on top. The Elder also prepared a seat before practicing meditation. It is in reference to this preparation of the seat that it is said, "paññatte āsane."

'Taṃ kiṃ maññasi' (What do you think?) means the Teacher thought: "This monk has no need for other meditation subjects. This Soṇa is skilled and proficient in the art of the lute; in his own field..."
124:
Thinking, 'He will be able to quickly understand the Dhamma being taught,' the Buddha spoke the words beginning with 'What do you think?' to teach the simile of the lute. 'Skill in the sound of the lute strings' means proficiency in playing the lute, and Venerable Soṇa was skilled in that art. His parents had thought, 'If our son learns other arts, he will be physically exhausted; but this art of the lute can be learned even while sitting on a bed,' and so they had him learn only the Gandhabba art (the art of the lute). For that Elder—

The 7 notes, the 3 scales, the 21 modulations,
The 49 locations—these are the saramandala (the circle of notes).

All such Gandhabba arts were already mastered by him. 'Accāyatā' means excessively tight kharamūcchanā (harsh tuning). 'Saravatī' means being endowed with sound. 'Kammaññā' means being fit for work, suitable. 'Atisithilā' means excessively loose mandamūcchanā (soft tuning). 'Same guṇe patiṭṭhitā' means being tuned and played at a medium pitch.

'Accāraddha' means excessively strenuous effort. 'Uddhaccāya saṃvattati' means it leads to restlessness. 'Atilīna' means excessively lax. 'Kosajjāya' means it leads to laziness. 'Vīriyasamathaṃ adhiṭṭhaha' means establish tranquility (concentration) conjoined with energy; the meaning is to join energy with concentration. 'Indriyānañca samataṃ paṭivijjha' means establish the equality of the faculties such as faith and so on. In that balancing, by joining faith with wisdom, wisdom with faith, energy with concentration, and concentration with energy, the equality of the faculties is said to be established. Mindfulness, however, is a factor useful in all circumstances and should be strong at all times. The method of joining these faculties is already explained in the Visuddhimagga. If the faculties are thus balanced, just as a reflection of a face appears in a mirror, the signs of tranquility (samatha-nimitta), insight (vipassanā-nimitta), the path (magga-nimitta), and the fruit (phala-nimitta) should be grasped (brought into being). Thus the Teacher taught the meditation subject to Venerable Soṇa, directing him toward the fruit of Arahantship.

In that teaching, 'nimittaṃ aggahesi' means he grasped the sign of tranquility and the sign of insight. 'Cha ṭhānāni' means the six causes. 'Adhimutto hoti' means he stands having penetrated and realized. 'Nekkhammādhimutto' and so on are all spoken solely in terms of the fruit of Arahantship. For the fruit of Arahantship is called 'nekkhamma' (renunciation) because it has emerged from all defilements; it is called 'paviveka' (seclusion) because it is secluded from them; it is called 'abyāpajjha' (non-ill will) because of the absence of malice; at the end of the destruction of craving...
125:
...because it arises at the end of the destruction of craving, it is called 'taṇhākkhaya' (destruction of craving). Because it arises at the end of the destruction of clinging, it is called 'upādānakkhaya' (destruction of clinging). Because of the absence of confusion, it is called 'asammoha' (non-delusion).

'Kevalaṃ saddhāmattakaṃ' means mere faith alone, devoid of penetration (paṭivedha) and unmixed with the wisdom of penetration. 'Paricayaṃ' means increase through repeated practice. 'Vītarāgattā' means because lust has been removed through the penetration of the Path, he stands having penetrated and realized Arahantship, which is called renunciation (nekkhamma); he dwells in the attainment of the fruit (phala-samāpatti), and his mind is solely inclined toward that Arahantship. This is the method for the remaining terms as well.

'Lābhasakkārasilokaṃ' means the acquisition of the four requisites, their excellence, and the speaking of praise. 'Nikāmayamāno' means desiring or longing for. 'Pavivekādhimutto' means inclined toward seclusion, meaning he declares the attainment of Arahantship.

'Sīlabbataparāmāsaṃ' means merely grasping onto precepts and practices by misinterpreting them. 'Sārato paccāgacchanto' means knowing them as the essence. 'Abyāpajjhādhimutto' means declaring Arahantship, which is called non-ill will. The meaning should be understood in all places according to this same method. Furthermore, in this context, some teachers say, 'In this term nekkhammādhimutto, Arahantship is spoken of, while in the remaining five terms, Nibbāna is spoken of.' Others say, 'In this term asammohādhimutto, Nibbāna is spoken of, while in the remaining terms, Arahantship is spoken of.' However, the essence here is that in all those terms, both Arahantship and Nibbāna are indeed spoken of.

'Bhusa' means powerful objects that are like divine forms. They are unable to overwhelm the mind of that Arahant and remain there. This is because defilements, when they arise, are said to overwhelm the mind. 'Amissīkataṃ' means defilements mix the mind with the object; because of the absence of those defilements, the Arahant's mind is unmixed. 'Ṭhitaṃ' means firmly established. 'Āneñjappattaṃ' means having reached imperturbability. He sees both the arising and the passing away of that mind. 'Bhusa vātavuṭṭhī' means a powerful mass of wind. It means being unable to move it to one side. It means being unable to shake it from all sides like a pillar. It means being unable to make it fall by shaking it and shaking it violently.
126:
“Nekkhammaṃ adhimuttassa” refers to an Arahant who has penetrated and stands in the fruit of Arahantship. In the remaining terms as well, only the fruit of Arahantship is spoken of. In the phrase “upādānakkhayassa ca,” the genitive case (sāmi-vibhatti) is used in the sense of the accusative (upayogattha). “Asammohañca cetaso” refers to the inclination towards the non-delusion of the mind (the fruit of Arahantship). “Disvā āyatanuppādaṃ” means having seen the arising and passing away of the sense bases (āyatanas). “Sammā cittaṃ vimuccati” means the mind is liberated through right reason and method, both by this practice of insight (vipassanā) and by the power of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti); it inclines towards the object of Nibbāna. Alternatively, this passage speaks of the practice of an Arahant. For that Arahant, having seen the arising and passing away of the sense bases, the mind is well liberated from all defilements through the power of the Noble Path attained by this insight. For one who is thus well liberated... (and so on), there is no further task to be done. Among those words, “santacittassa” means one whose mind is peaceful, with defilements stilled. The meaning of the remaining words is quite clear.

## 2. Phagguna Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, “samadhosi” shows the manner of rising. “Paṭikkamanti” means they decline. “No abhikkamanti” means they do not increase. “Sīsaveṭhanaṃ dadeyya” refers to wrapping the head and twisting it with a stick. “Indriyāni vippasīdiṃsu” means that at the time of death, the six faculties became exceptionally clear. “Atthupaparikkhāya” means investigating what is beneficial and what is not, what is a cause and what is not. “Anuttare upadhisaṅkhaye” refers to Nibbāna. “Avimuttaṃ hoti” means it is inclined towards the fruit of Arahantship.

## 3. Chaḷabhijāti Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, “chaḷabhijātiyo” means the six classes (births). “Tatridam” means “among those six, this class.” “Luddā” means they are cruel. “Bhikkhū kaṇṭakavuttikā” refers to the monks (ascetics) who live in the forest like thorns. “Ekasaṭakā” are those who cover themselves in front with only a single piece of cloth. “Akāmakassa bilaṃ olaggeyyuṃ” refers to when ox-merchants are traveling and an ox dies; while they divide and eat the meat to get the value of the ox, they say to one who does not wish to eat the meat, “You must eat this meat and you must pay the price,” and thus forcibly place that portion of meat into his hand. “Akhettaññunā” means by one who does not know the field or scope of the designation of classes (abhijāti). “Taṃ suṇāhi” means “listen to that designation of mine.” “Kaṇhābhijātiko” is one of a dark class. “Kaṇhaṃ dhammaṃ abhijāyati” means being of a dark nature, one is born or arises; or it means one is born into a dark class.
127:
“Nibbānaṃ abhijāyati” means one reaches Nibbāna, or is born with the nature of Nibbāna known as the Noble ground.

## 4. Āsava Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, “saṃvarā pahātabbā” means they are to be abandoned by the restraint of the faculties such as the eye. In the remaining terms as well, this is the method. “Idha” means in this Dispensation (Sāsana). “Pဋိသင်္ခါ” (Paṭisaṅkhā) means having known, having reflected. “Yoniso” means by wise means or method. Here, “yoniso paṭisaṅkhā” should be understood as reflecting on the danger of non-restraint. That reflection should be understood through the teaching of the Ādittapariyāya Sutta, such as: “Monks, it would be better for the eye-faculty to be struck by a red-hot iron pin, glowing, blazing, and radiant, than to grasp the signs (nimitta) and features (anubyañjana) of forms cognizable by the eye.”

“Cakkhundriyasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharati”: in this passage, the eye itself is a faculty (indriya), thus it is called the “eye-faculty.” It is called “restraint” (saṃvara) because it guards, because it shuts or closes. This term “restraint” is a designation for mindfulness (sati). Restraint in the eye-faculty is “eye-faculty restraint.” Although this restraint arises in the impulsion (javana), it is called “eye-faculty restraint” because it prevents the arising of defilements at that door. “Saṃvuto” means endowed with that restraint. Indeed, in the Vibhaṅga of the phrase “pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto,” it is said: “He is endowed with... possessed of... this Pātimokkha restraint.” Alternatively, “saṃvuta” means by way of “saṃvarī,” meaning he closed or shut. “Cakkhundriyasaṃvarasaṃvuto” means he closed or shut the door-leaf of mindfulness, known as eye-faculty restraint, at the eye-door, just like a door-leaf at the door of a house. This meaning is particularly good here. Indeed, this very meaning is seen in the phrases “for one dwelling without restraint of the eye-faculty” and “for one dwelling with restraint.”

In the phrase “yaṃ hissa” and so on, it means for that monk who dwells without restraining or closing that eye-faculty. Alternatively, the letter “ye” is changed to “yaṃ,” meaning “those taints for him.” “Āsavā vighātapariဠာဟာ” (Āsavā vighātapariḷāhā) refers to the four taints as well as other distress-causing defilement-fevers or resultant-fevers. For one who enjoys and delights in a pleasant object that has come into range at the eye-door by the power of sensual enjoyment, the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava) arises. For one who enjoys with the longing for existence, thinking “I will obtain such a pleasant object in another happy realm of existence,” the taint of existence (bhavāsava) arises.
128:
Bhavāsava arises. For one who grasps [the notion] of a 'being' or 'belonging to a being', diṭṭhāsava arises. Unknowing (aññāṇa) that is co-nascent with all [taints] is called avijjāsava. Thus, the four taints arise. Other defilements that cause distress and fever, which are associated with these four taints, or their future results, are said to arise for one who dwells without restraint. "Thus they [are] to him" (evaṃsa te) means that by this means they do not occur to him, and not otherwise. The same method applies to the sentences beginning with "Reflecting wisely, he is restrained with the restraint of the ear-faculty," and so on. These are called taints to be abandoned by restraint. In these six doors, by taking four [taints] for each, it is meant that twenty-four taints are to be abandoned by restraint (saṃvara).

Everything that should be said regarding the sentences beginning with "Reflecting wisely, [he uses] the robe," has already been stated in the Sīlakathā of the Visuddhimagga. "Whatever to him" (yaṃ hissa) refers to whichever one of the requisites, such as robes or almsfood, he possesses. "By not using" (appaṭisevato) means for one who does not use them after reflecting wisely [taints arise]. In this section, the arising of kāmāsava should be understood for one who either longs for requisites like robes not yet obtained, or relishes those already obtained. For one who relishes them with a longing for existence, thinking, "I shall obtain such things in another happy state of existence," bhavāsava arises. For one who clings with the perception of self (attasaññā), thinking, "I obtain, I do not obtain," or "This is mine," diṭṭhāsava arises. The arising of the four taints, together with avijjāsava which is co-nascent with all taints, should be understood as the arising of distress and fever, and also by the production of new feelings. Monks, these taints are to be abandoned by using (paṭisevanā). This means that by taking four taints for each of the four requisites, sixteen taints are to be abandoned by using them after reflection, which is known as restraint by knowledge (ñāṇasaṃvara).

"Reflecting wisely, he is one who endures cold" means that having reflected by the proper means, he becomes an endurer of cold. He endures and tolerates cold; he does not, like a man lacking energy, shake and tremble at even a little cold and give up his meditation subject. The same method applies to heat and so on. Here, it should be understood that the word (vacana) itself is the "pathway of speech" (vacanapatha). In the terms beginning with "painful" (dukkhānaṃ), they should be understood as: "painful" (dukkha) because they are hard to endure; "intense" (tibba) because of their strength; "harsh" (khara) because of their roughness; "sharp" (kaṭuka) because of their pungency; "disagreeable" (asāta) because they lack pleasure; "unpleasant" (amanāpa) because they do not increase [the joy of] the mind; and "life-taking" (pāṇahara) because they are capable of taking life. "Whatever to him" (yaṃ hissa) means if any one of these factors like cold exists for him. "By not enduring" (anadhivāsato) means for one who does not endure [taints arise].
129:
For one who does not endure (the arising of taints should be understood). Here, the manner in which the taints arise should be understood thus: for one who, being afflicted by cold, longs for heat, kāmāsava arises; the same applies in all cases. For one who longs for existence, thinking, "There is no cold or heat in a happy state of existence," bhavāsava arises. The grasping, "I am cold, I am hot," is diṭṭhāsava. Avijjāsava is associated with all of them. "These are said [to be abandoned]" means that many taints, taking four for each of the factors like cold and heat, are to be abandoned by endurance (adhivāsanā), which is known as restraint by patience (khantisaṃvara).

"Reflecting wisely, he avoids a fierce elephant" means that thinking, "I am a recluse," one should not stand near a fierce elephant. Because of that standing near, there might be death or suffering equal to death; thus, reflecting by this proper method, he avoids and turns away from a fierce elephant. This method is the same everywhere. "Fierce" (caṇḍa) means a wicked and wild beast. "Stump" (khāṇu) means a stump of a catechu tree and so on. "Thorny place" (kaṇṭakaṭṭhāna) means a place where thorns might prick. "Pit" (sobbha) means a precipice broken on all sides. "Precipice" (papāta) means a precipice broken on one side. "Cesspool" (candanika) means a place for discarding waste water, filth, and so on. "Slop-basin" (oḷigalla) means a place where the mud of that same filth flows. Such a place is filled with impure things up to the knees. Both these places are frequented by non-human beings and should therefore be avoided.

In the word "unsuitable seat" (anāsana), an improper seat is called anāsana; in meaning, it should be understood as a secluded and hidden seat that is the basis for an indefinite (aniyata) offense. In the word "unsuitable resort" (agocara), an improper resort is called agocara. It is of five kinds, such as courtesans and so on. "Bad friends" (pāpake mitte) means those who are inferior, immoral, and false friends who are actually enemies. "In bad [things]" (pāpakesu) means in inferior things. "Would suspect" (okappeyyuṃ) means they would believe or conclude, "Surely this venerable one has done [this] or will do [it]." "Whatever to him" (yaṃ hissa) means if any one of these things like an elephant exists for him.

Here, the manner in which the taints arise should be understood thus: for one who, being afflicted by the suffering caused by an elephant and so on, longs for happiness, kāmāsava arises. For one who longs for existence, thinking, "There is no such suffering in a happy state of existence," bhavāsava arises. The grasping, "An elephant is treading on me, a horse is treading on me," is diṭṭhāsava. Avijjāsava is associated with all of them. "These are said [to be abandoned]" means that many taints, taking four for each of the factors like an elephant and so on, are to be abandoned by this avoidance (parivajjana), which is known as restraint by virtue (sīlasaṃvara).

"Reflecting wisely, he does not endure an arisen sensual thought" means (reflecting): "For this reason, this thought is unwholesome; for this reason, it is blameworthy; for this reason, this thought has a painful result." This is the meaning. Reflecting wisely, he does not endure an arisen sensual thought.
130:
“It leads to my own affliction,” etc. (M. Ni. 1. 207-208). By this method, one reflects on the danger in sensual thoughts with wise consideration. One does not tolerate the sensual thought that has arisen regarding various objects; one does not keep it in the mind, nor does one allow it to dwell within. This is the meaning. What does one do when not tolerating it? One abandons it. Is it like throwing out rubbish with a basket? No, rather, one dispels it, prods it, pierces it, and removes it. Is it like prodding an ox with a goad? No, rather, one brings it to an end, makes it have a complete end, so that not even a trace as small as a fragment remains within. How does one make it not remain?
