One causes it to reach a state of non-existence, repeatedly causes it to reach non-existence, and acts so that it is well-suppressed through abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhanappahāna). This same method applies to the remaining two types of thoughts (thoughts of ill-will and thoughts of cruelty).

“Uppannuppanna” means those that arise again and again, or those that have just arisen. It does not mean that after dispelling it once, one is indifferent when it arises a second time; even if it arises a hundred times, one dispels it every time it arises. “Evil unwholesome states” refers to those very sensual thoughts and so on, or all nine great thoughts (mahāvitakka). Among those nine, three have been taught (sensual thought, thought of ill-will, and thought of cruelty). The remaining six are: “thought of relatives (ñātivitakka), thought of the countryside (janapadavitakka), thought of immortality (amarāvitakka), thought connected with sympathy for others, thought connected with gain, honor, and fame, and thought connected with not being despised by others.” “Yaṃ hissa” means if any one of these thoughts should arise in that monk. Here, sensual thought is indeed the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava); other thoughts are the taint of existence (bhavāsava); the thought associated with that is the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava); and ignorance in all thoughts is the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava). Thus, the arising of the taints should be understood. “These taints” means the taints mentioned by way of sensual thoughts and so on, which are to be abandoned by dispelling, known as restraint through energy (vīriyasaṃvara), accompanied by the reflection on the danger in those various thoughts.

“Reflecting, he develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor with wise consideration” means reflecting on the danger of not developing it and the benefit of developing it through the proper means and path, he develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor. This same method applies everywhere. The development of the enlightenment factors has been explained in detail below. “Yaṃ hissa” means if any one of these enlightenment factors should arise in that monk. Here, regarding the arising of taints, because these enlightenment factors associated with the Noble Path have not been developed, those taints such as the taint of sensual desire might arise; for the monk who develops them thus...
131:
“Those taints do not occur”—this method should be understood. “These taints are said” means these taints such as the taint of sensual desire are to be abandoned by this development of the supramundane enlightenment factors. Desiring to praise the monk whose taints are destroyed through these six ways, He said, “Yato kho bhikkhave,” and so on. There, “yato” is the suffix “-to” used in the sense of the genitive case; it means “yassa” (of whom). However, the ancient teachers explain it as “yamhi kāle” (at which time). “Those taints which are to be abandoned by restraint, those taints are abandoned by restraint” means those taints that must be abandoned by restraint are indeed abandoned by restraint; it does not mean that one perceives them as abandoned when they are not yet abandoned.

## 5. Dārukammikasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, the Dārukammika Sutta: “Dārukammiko” refers to a lay follower who made his living by selling wood. “Kāsikacandanaṃ” refers to fine sandalwood. “Aṅgena” means by an attribute that is not a virtue (on the unwholesome side), or by an attribute that is a virtue on the side of the bright (wholesome) side. “Nemantaniko” is one who accepts invitations. “Saṃghe dānaṃ dassāmi” means “I will give an offering to the Saṅgha of monks.” Having spoken thus and paid homage to the Teacher, that donor departed. Later, five hundred monks who used to frequent his house returned to the lay life. When it was said, “Those monks who frequent your house have disrobed,” he said, “What is that to me?” and did not show even a slight change in his mind. Referring to this, the Teacher said, “Your mind will be clear while giving that gift to the Saṅgha.”

## 6. Hatthisāriputtasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta: “Abhidhammakathaṃ” means a talk mixed with Abhidhamma. “Kathaṃ opāteti” means interrupting the talk of those elders and speaking his own words. In the phrase “therānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ,” the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental; it means “together with the elder monks.” It means that this person is also able to speak the talk mixed with Abhidhamma that the elders speak. “Cetopariyāyaṃ” means the range of the mind (the mental process). “Idha” means in this world. “Soratasorato” means like one who is very gentle, like one endowed with gentleness of conduct. “Nivātanivāto” means like one who is very humble, like one who has a humble habit. “Upasantupasanto” means like one who is very peaceful...
132:
He is calm like one who is peaceful. "Vapakassateva satthārā" means being distant from the Teacher. "Saṃsaṭṭhassa" refers to the state of one who is associated with the five types of association. "Vissaṭṭhassa" refers to the state of one who is loose or released. "Pākatassa" refers to the state of one with manifest (undisciplined) faculties.

"Kiṭṭhādo" refers to one who eats crops in the field. "Antaradhāpeyya" means one should destroy. "Gopasu" refers to cows and goats. "Sippisambukaṃ" refers to mussels and snails. "Sakkharakaṭhalaṃ" refers to gravel and potsherds. "Ābhidosikaṃ" refers to spoiled kudrūsaka rice with obvious defects. "Nacchādeyya" means one should not be pleased with. In the phrase "yadetāṃ purisaṃ bhuttāvi," the accusative case (upayogavacana) is present; that accusative case should be understood in the sense of the genitive (sāmī-attha). "Amum hāvuso purisaṃ" means "Friend, that person."

"Sabba-nimittānaṃ" means all signs such as the sign of permanence (nicca-nimitta), etc. "Animittaṃ cetosamādhiṃ" means strong insight concentration (vipassanā-samādhi). "Cīrikasaddo" is the sound of a cricket (cicada). "Sarissati nekkhammassa" means he will remember the benefits of renunciation (becoming a monk). "Arahatam ahosi" means he became one of the Arahants among the Buddha's disciples. This elder became a layman seven times and ordained seven times. For what reason? It is said that during the time of Kassapa Buddha, this elder once spoke in praise of the lay life to a monk. Due to that karma, even though he possessed the strong supporting condition (upanissaya) for Arahantship, he cycled between lay life and monkhood seven times, and upon his seventh ordination, he attained Arahantship.

## 7. Commentary on the Majjhe Sutta

In the seventh sutta, "Pārāyane Metteyyapañhe" means in the question of the youth Metteyya in the Pārāyana assembly. "Ubho ante viditvāna" means having known the two ends (two parts). In the phrase "majjhe mantā na lippati," "mantā" refers to wisdom; having known the two ends with that wisdom, one is not smeared in the middle, not smeared in the central position. "Sibbinimaccagā" means one who has transcended craving, which is called the seamstress (sibbinī). "Phasso" (Contact): Because it arises through the power of contact, this individual existence (attabhāva) is called one end. "Phassa-samudayo" (Arising of contact): Because contact is the cause of that future existence, it is called the arising of contact; the future existence that arises due to the cause of contact associated with kamma performed in this existence is called the second end. "Phassa-nirodho" (Cessation of contact) is Nibbāna. "Majjhe" (In the middle): Nibbāna is called the middle because it cuts craving, the seamstress, and creates two separate parts. Craving...
133:
...indeed sews him; craving sews or joins the two states of existence known as contact and the arising of contact. For what reason? For the sake of the production of various existences. If craving did not sew them together, the production of those various existences would not occur. In this context, the analogy of the ends and the middle is used. Indeed, when two pieces of cloth are brought together and sewn in the middle with a thread, it is called "the ends and the middle." When the thread is cut, the two pieces fall to either side. In this analogy, the two ends mentioned earlier should be understood as the two pieces of cloth; craving should be understood as the thread that remains after sewing; and just as the two pieces fall to either side when the thread is cut, when craving ceases, the two ends also cease. "Ettāvatā" (By this much): By knowing these two ends and by not being smeared in the middle by craving, one is said to fully know the four noble truths that should be known through higher knowledge (abhiññā). One is said to fully understand the two mundane truths (lokiya sacca) that should be understood through the full understanding of investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā) and the full understanding of abandoning (pahāna-pariññā). "Diṭṭheva dhamme" (In this very life) means in this very existence. "Dukkhassantakaro hoti" (He is one who makes an end of suffering) means he is one who makes an end to the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha), one who defines its limit.

In the second turn, the analogy should be understood by way of three pieces of cloth. Indeed, when three pieces are sewn together with a thread, when the thread is cut, the three pieces fall in three places. In this analogy, the past, future, and present aggregates (khandhas) should be understood as the three pieces of cloth, and craving as the thread. For craving sews the past with the present, and the present with the future. Just as the three pieces fall in three places when the thread is cut, when craving ceases, the past, future, and present aggregates also cease.

In the third turn, "neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is the middle" means it is the middle because it stands between the two feelings. Indeed, pleasure is not the interval of pain, nor is pain the interval of pleasure. "Craving is the seamstress (sibbinī)" means that the delight and lust (nandi-rāga) for feelings prevents the cutting off of feelings, and thus it is said to sew them.

In the fourth turn, "consciousness is the middle" means that both rebirth-linking consciousness and the remaining consciousness are called the middle of name-and-form because they arise due to the condition of name-and-form.

In the fifth turn, "consciousness is the middle" means kamma-consciousness is the middle. Alternatively, because kamma is grasped by the mind-base (manāyatana) among the internal bases, any consciousness here is called the middle. Or, because the advertence (āvajjana) at the mind-door depends on an internal base, the impulsion consciousness (javana-viññāṇa) is called the middle.

In the sixth instance, 'sakkāya' refers to the round of existence (vaṭṭa) occurring in the three realms. 'Sakkāyasamudaya' refers to the truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca). 'Sakkāyanirodha' refers to the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca). 'Pariyāyena' means it occurs only through various reasons. The remaining terms should be understood in the same manner as previously stated in all places.

## 8. Purisindriyañāṇa Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, 'aññataro' refers to a certain person belonging to Devadatta's faction. 'Samannāharitvā' means having reflected or considered. That person asks with the intention: "Did the Blessed One speak having known, or without knowing? Did He speak categorically (ekaṃsika) or analytically (vibhajja)?" 'Āpāyiko' refers to one who will be reborn in the lower realms (apāya). 'Nerayiko' refers to one who is headed for hell (niraya). 'Kappaṭṭho' refers to one who will remain for an aeon because of having performed kamma that lasts for an aeon. 'Atekiccho' refers to one who is incurable. 'Dvejjhaṃ' refers to a state of duality (dvidhābhāva). 'Vālaggakoṭinittudanamattaṃ' refers to the measure of a mere prick of a hair-tip or the measure of the fall of a hair-tip. 'Purisindriyañāṇāni' means the knowledges that understand the sharpness or dullness of the faculties (indriya) of individuals.

"Wholesome states that exist, and unwholesome states that exist" means "I, the Buddha, know that there are this many wholesome states and this many unwholesome states." 'Antarahitā' refers to states that have gone to invisibility (disappeared). 'Sammukhībhūtā' refers to states that have become manifest through habitual practice (samudācāra). 'Kusalamūlaṃ' refers to the wholesome inclination (kusalajjhāsaya). 'Kusalā kusalaṃ' means that from that wholesome inclination, another wholesome state will also arise. 'Sāradāni' refers to those whose essence has been taken, or crops produced in the month of Sarada (autumn). 'Sukhasayitāni' refers to things that are well-accumulated. 'Sukhette' means occurring in a good field. 'Nikkhittāni' means sown or planted. 'Sappaṭibhāgā' refers to things having a similar nature. 'Abhido addharattaṃ' means when approaching the time of midnight. 'Bhattakālasamaye' means at the time known as the mealtime of kings. Regarding "one of a nature to decline," whom did the Blessed One know as such? It was King Ajātasattu. For he, depending on a bad friend (Devadatta), declined from the paths and fruits. The Blessed One also knew others such as Suppabuddha and Sunakkhatta. Regarding "one of a nature not to decline," whom did the Blessed One know as such? It was Susīma the wanderer and others of such nature. Regarding "one who will attain Parinibbāna," whom did the Blessed One know as such? It was the Great Minister Santati and others of such nature.

## 9. Nibbedhika Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the ninth (Nibbedhika) Sutta, it is called 'Nibbedhika-pariyāya' (the method of penetration) because it penetrates and destroys the mass of greed and so on, which have not been penetrated or destroyed before. It means the cause of penetration. 'Nidānasambhava': it is called 'nidāna' (source/cause) because it is capable of producing or cleansing the sensual defilements. It is called 'sambhava' (origin) because it arises from there. The source that cleanses is itself the cause of arising, thus it is called 'nidānasambhava'. 'Vemattatā' means diversity or differentiation.

'Kāmaguṇa' (strands of sensual pleasure): they are called 'kāma' in the sense of being desired, and 'guṇa' in the sense of binding, as in the term 'antaguṇa' (mesentery/small intestines). 'Cakkhuviññeyyā' refers to things to be seen by eye-consciousness. 'Iṭṭha' means desirable objects (iṭṭhārammaṇa), whether they are sought after or not. 'Kantā' means lovely things. 'Manāpā' means things that increase [the pleasure of] the mind. 'Piyarūpā' means things of an endearing nature. 'Kāmūpasañhitā' means things connected with the sensual defilement that arises by taking them as an object. 'Rajanīyā' means things that are the cause for the arising of lust (rāga). "Nete kāmā" means these objects such as forms are not called 'kāma' in the sense of desiring. 'Saṅkapparāgo' is lust that arises by the power of thought/intention. 'Kāmo' refers to this very 'saṅkapparāga' which must be abandoned by those practicing for the abandonment of sensual defilements. They are called 'kāma' in the sense of desiring. 'Citra' refers to variegated or diverse objects.

'Phasso' refers to co-nascent contact. 'Kāmayamāno' refers to one desiring desire. "Tajjaṃ tajjaṃ" refers to things appropriate to that desire. 'Puññabhāgiya' (merit-sharing/wholesome portion): the individual existence (attabhāva) of a being reborn in the deva world due to the fulfillment of good conduct, having aspired for celestial pleasures, is called 'puññabhāgiya'. The individual existence of a person reborn in the lower realms due to the fulfillment of bad conduct is called 'apuññabhāgiya'. "Monks, this is called the result (vipāka) of desires" means these two types of existence are called the result of desires because they arise depending on the longing for desires. "He [knows] this penetrating..." means that monk knows this noble practice (seṭṭhacariya) of penetrating in thirty-six places. 'Kāmanirodha' (cessation of desire) is the Noble Path which has received this name because of the cessation of desires. In this context, only the Noble Path, referred to as the holy life (brahmacariya), is called 'kāmanirodha'.

'Sāmisa' refers to things connected with the bait (āmisa) of defilements. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all places. Furthermore, 'vohāravepakka' means the result (vipāka) of conventional expression. For conventional expression (vohāra), known as speech, is the result of perception (saññā). In the phrase "yathā yathā naṃ," the word "naṃ" is merely a particle. Therefore, in whatever way one perceives...
136: One speaks of having such a perception in such and such a manner; therefore, it means having the result of conventional usage (vohāra-vepakka). Avijjā refers to the dense ignorance that is non-knowledge in the eight instances. It is called nirayagamanīya because it leads to hell; it means the condition for rebirth in hell. The same method applies to the remaining terms. Cetanāhaṃ means 'I [say] volition.' Here, the coordinating volition (saṃvidahana-cetanā) that encompasses all wholesome and unwholesome states is taken. Cetayitvā means volition occurring at the sense doors. Manasā means with a mind associated with volition. Nirayavedanīyaṃ means [kamma] that yields results in hell. The same method applies to the remaining terms. Adhimattaṃ means intense suffering. Dandhavirāgī means suffering that is heavy, not quick, and fades away slowly. Urattāḷiṃ kandati means weeping while beating one's breast. Pariyeṭṭhiṃ means seeking. Ekapadaṃ dvipadaṃ means 'who knows the mantra of one line or two lines?' Sammohavepakkaṃ means having the result of delusion. The delusion of suffering is called the result of natural consequence (nissanda-vipāka). The same method applies to the second term. For seeking is also the natural consequence of that suffering. In this sutta, the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) are taught. ## ၁၀။ သီဟနာဒသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ In the tenth sutta, āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ means the noble and unshakable position. Sīhanādaṃ means the fearless cry, the supreme cry. Brahmacakkaṃ means the supreme wheel of knowledge, namely, the knowledge of penetration (paṭivedha-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of teaching (desanā-ñāṇa). Ṭhānañca ṭhānato means [knowing] the cause as cause. Yampi means by which knowledge. Idampi tathāgatassa means this knowledge of what is possible and impossible (ṭhānāṭhāna-ñāṇa) is also called a Power of the Tathāgata (tathāgatabala). Thus, the meaning should be understood in all terms. Kammasamādānānaṃ means [knowing the result] of wholesome and unwholesome kammas performed after undertaking them; or kamma itself is called kammasamādāna. Ṭhānaso hetuso means by way of condition (paccaya) and by way of root cause (hetu). Therein, destination (gati), physical body (upadhi), time (kāla), and effort (payoga) are the 'stations' (ṭhāna) of the result, while kamma is the 'root cause' (hetu). Jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattīnaṃ means [knowing the result] of the four jhānas, the eight liberations (vimokkha), the three concentrations (samādhi), and the nine successive attainments (anupubba-samāpatti). Saṃkilesaṃ means states partaking of decline. Vodānaṃ means states partaking of distinction. Vuṭṭhāna refers to the mastered jhānas and the life-continuum fruition attainments (bhavaṅga-phala-samāpatti), as it is said: 'Purification (vodāna) is also emergence (vuṭṭhāna); emerging from this or that concentration is also emergence.' A lower mastered jhāna is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for a higher one; therefore, it is said 'Purification is also emergence.' By means of the life-continuum...
137:
'Jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattīnaṃ' refers to the four jhānas, the eight liberations (vimokkha), the three concentrations (samādhi), and the nine successive attainments (anupubba-samāpatti). 'Saṃkilesa' means states partaking of decline, and 'vodāna' means states partaking of distinction. 'Vuṭṭhāna' (emergence) refers to purification and also to emerging from various concentrations. The mastered jhānas and the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) fruit attainments occur. A mastered jhāna at a lower level is the proximate cause for a jhāna at a higher level. Therefore, purification is also called emergence.

By means of the life-continuum mind (bhavaṅga-citta), there is emergence (vuṭṭhāna) from all jhānas. By means of fruit attainment (phala-samāpatti), there is emergence from the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). With reference to that emergence, it is said: 'Emergence from various concentrations is emergence'. The words beginning with 'anekavihitaṃ' have already been explained in the Visuddhimagga. The knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa) has the same meaning as stated below. If one desires a detailed explanation of the group of the three preceding knowledges, one should look at the commentary on the Mahāsīhanādasutta in the Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā.

'Samāhitassa' means of one who has a concentrated mind. 'Samādhi maggo' means concentration is the means for attaining these knowledges. 'Asamādhi' means the state of not being concentrated. 'Kummaggo' means the wrong path (micchā-magga). In this sutta, the power of the Buddha's knowledge is taught.

## 1-5. Commentary on the first Piyasuutta and others

1-5. In the first sutta of the Book of Sevens, "anavaññattikāmo" means desiring the state of not being known or recognized by others. In the third sutta, "yoniso vicine dhammaṃ" means one investigates the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths by wise means. ## 7. Commentary on Uggasutta

In the seventh sutta, "uggo rājamahāmatto" refers to the great minister of King Pasenadi of Kosala. "Upasaṅkami" means he approached after having eaten his breakfast. "Aḍḍho" means rich with wealth stored in the ground. "Migāro rohaṇeyyo" refers to the banker Migāra, who was the grandson of the banker Rohaṇa. "Mahaddhano" means having great wealth in terms of usable riches. "Mahābhogo" means having great possessions due to the abundance of goods for use and consumption. "Hiraññassa" refers to gold only. Indeed, for that minister, gold alone amounted to tens of millions. "Rūpiyassa" means there is no need to even mention the extent of other utensils such as bowls, rugs, and clothing (as they were so numerous).
147:
...but his taints are destroyed, having seen [the four noble truths] with wisdom. This person is called one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta).

He is called a 'body-witness' (kāyasakkhī) because he has realized [the liberations] by touching them. That 'kāyasakkhī' person first touches the contact of jhāna, and later realizes Nibbāna, which is the cessation of phenomena. That 'kāyasakkhī' person is of six types, starting from one established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphalaṭṭha) up to one established in the path of Arahantship (arahattamaggaṭṭha). Therefore, it is said: 'Here, a certain person dwells having touched the eight liberations with the mental body, and some of his taints are destroyed, having seen them with wisdom. This person is called a body-witness.'

He is called 'one attained to vision' (diṭṭhippatta) because he has reached the four noble truths that have been seen. The brief characteristic of the term 'diṭṭhippatta' is: one who has known, seen, clarified, realized, and touched with wisdom that 'formations are suffering, and Nibbāna, the cessation of phenomena, is bliss.' In detail, that 'diṭṭhippatta' person is also of six types, just like the 'kāyasakkhī'. Therefore, it is said: 'Here, a certain person understands as it really is, "This is suffering"... "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering." The four noble truths taught by the Buddha are well seen by his noble wisdom and well explored by his noble wisdom... This person is called one attained to vision.'

He is called 'one liberated by faith' (saddhāvimutta) because he is liberated from defilements through faith. That 'saddhāvimutta' person is also of six types in the same manner as mentioned. Therefore, it is said: 'Here, a certain person understands as it really is, "This is suffering"... "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering." The four noble truths taught by the Buddha are well seen by his noble wisdom and well explored by his wisdom... but not [as quickly] as the taints are destroyed for one attained to vision. This person is called one liberated by faith.' Indeed, for that 'saddhāvimutta' person, the destruction of defilements occurs at the moment of the preliminary insight path (vipassanāmagga) as if believing, as if entering into, and as if resolving. For the 'diṭṭhippatta' person, at the moment of the preliminary insight path, the knowledge that cuts defilements arises without hesitation, sharply and courageously. Therefore, for example, for one who cuts a banana tree with a sword that is not very sharp, the cut surface is not smooth, the sword does not move quickly, a sound is heard, and especially great effort must be made; the development of the preliminary insight path of the 'saddhāvimutta' person is of such a nature. However, for one who cuts a banana tree with a well-sharpened sword, the cut surface is smooth, the sword moves quickly, and no sound is heard...
148:
There is no longer the task of strenuous exertion; the development of the path of insight in the preliminary stage of such a person liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta) should be understood.

One is called a Dhamma-follower (dhammānusārī) because one follows the Dhamma. 'Dhamma' refers to wisdom; the meaning is that one develops the path preceded by wisdom. The same principle applies to the faith-follower (saddhānusārī). Both of these are only those standing on the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimaggaṭṭha). Thus it has been said: "For which person, practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, the faculty of wisdom is predominant, and who develops the noble path led by wisdom, carried by wisdom—this person is called a Dhamma-follower. For which person, practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, the faculty of faith is predominant, and who develops the noble path led by faith, carried by faith—this person is called a faith-follower" (Puggalapaññatti). This is a brief explanation here; for a detailed account, the discussion on those liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta) and so forth is stated in the section on the development of wisdom in the Visuddhimagga. Therefore, it should be understood according to the method stated in that text.

## 5. Commentary on the Udakūpama Sutta

In the fifth sutta, 'the water simile' (udakūpama) refers to individuals compared to water by taking the modes of sinking and so forth. 'Sinks once' means sinking only a single time. 'With those who are entirely black' (ekantakāḷakehi) is said with reference to fixed wrong view (niyata micchādiṭṭhi). 'Emerges' means rising up. 'Good' (sādhu) means a beautiful or good person. 'Only declines' means declining just like water poured on a walkway. 'Emerges and looks around' means rising up and looking at the direction to be gone (Nibbāna). 'Swims' means swimming towards the direction to be gone. 'One who has reached a foothold' means, after emerging, looking, and swimming, reaching a place to stand; staying there, one does not return. 'One who has crossed over, reached the far shore, and stands on dry land' means one who has crossed the flood of all defilements, gone to the other shore, and stands on the dry land of Nibbāna. In this sutta, the round of suffering (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) are discussed.

## 6. Commentary on the Aniccānupassī Sutta

In the sixth sutta, one is called 'a contemplator of impermanence' (aniccānupassī) because one repeatedly contemplates with wisdom, pervading with the thought 'it is impermanent.' One is 'percipient of impermanence' (aniccasaññī) because one has such a perception of impermanence. One is 'experiencing impermanence' (aniccapaṭisaṃvedī) because one has a state that is clearly known by knowledge as 'impermanent.' 'Constantly' (satataṃ) means at all times. 'Continuously' (samitaṃ) means the manner in which the preceding consciousness and the succeeding consciousness are joined, approached, and connected; it refers to such uninterrupted occurrence.
149:
Just as the preceding consciousness and the succeeding consciousness are joined, approached, and touched, so it is here. 'Unadulterated' (abbokinna) means not mixed with another consciousness, without interval. 'Resolving with the mind' (cetasā adhimuccamāno) means deciding with the mind. 'Penetrating with wisdom' (paññāya pariyogāhamāno) means entering into it with insight knowledge.

'Neither before nor after' (apubbaṃ acarimaṃ) means occurring at the same moment, not before and not after. In this context, the 'equal-headed' (samasīsī) individual is discussed. That samasīsī individual is of four types: the disease-equal-headed (roga-samasīsī), the feeling-equal-headed (vedanā-samasīsī), the posture-equal-headed (iriyāpatha-samasīsī), and the life-equal-headed (jīvita-samasīsī). Among these four, for a person afflicted by a certain disease, the subsiding of the disease and the destruction of the taints occur at the same stroke; this person is called a disease-equal-headed one. For one experiencing a certain feeling, the subsiding of the feeling and the destruction of the taints occur at the same stroke; this person is called a feeling-equal-headed one. For one who is endowed with one of the postures such as standing and is practicing insight, the end of the posture and the destruction of the taints occur at the same stroke; this person is called a posture-equal-headed one. For one who, either through effort or naturally, the exhaustion of the life faculty and the destruction of the taints occur at the same stroke; this person is called a life-equal-headed one. In this context, this life-equal-headed individual is intended. In saying so, because the destruction of the taints occurs with the path-consciousness and the exhaustion of the life faculty occurs with the death-consciousness, there is actually no such thing as both occurring at the same moment. However, since for that person the exhaustion of the life faculty occurs immediately after the stage of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇavāra) as soon as the taints are destroyed, and the interval is not apparent, it is spoken of in this way (as being simultaneous).

'One who attains Nibbāna in the interval' (antarāparinibbāyī) is the name for a person who, having been reborn in any of the five Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa), reaches Arahantship either at the moment of rebirth, or after a short time has passed, or while staying in the middle of the lifespan. 'One who attains Nibbāna after landing' (upahaccaparinibbāyī) is the name for a person who reaches Arahantship in that same Pure Abode after passing the middle of the lifespan. 'One who attains Nibbāna without exertion' (asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī) is the name for those individuals who exhaust the defilements without prompting and with little effort. 'One who attains Nibbāna with exertion' (sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī) is the name for one who exhausts the defilements with prompting and with effort. 'One who goes upstream to the Akanittha realm' (uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī) is the name for one who, having been reborn in any of the four lower Pure Abodes and having passed away from there, gradually takes birth in the Akanittha realm and reaches Arahantship.

17-19. In the seventh sutta, 'dukkhanupassī' means contemplating repeatedly as suffering in the sense of oppression. ## 10. Commentary on the Niddasavatthu Sutta

In the tenth sutta, 'niddasavatthūni' refers to the reasons for the term 'niddasa' and so on. These are the reasons for saying 'a niddasa monk, nibbīsa, nittiṃsa, niccattālīsa, nippaññāsa.' It is said that this question arose within the views of the outsiders (titthiyas). The outsiders call a Nigaṇṭha who dies at the age of ten 'niddasa' (one who is no longer ten). That deceased Nigaṇṭha cannot become ten years old again. Not only ten years, he cannot become nine years or one year old either. In this same way, they call a Nigaṇṭha who dies at the age of twenty and so on 'nibbīsa, nittiṃsa, niccattālīsa, nippaññāsa.'

The Venerable Ānanda, while wandering in the village, heard that talk, and upon returning to the monastery, he informed the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, this is not a designation for the outsiders; it is a designation for an Arahant (khīṇāsava) in my teaching. For when an Arahant attains Parinibbāna at the age of ten, he does not become ten years old again. Not only ten years, but nine years ... one year old he does not become. Not only one year, but even one who is eleven months ... one month ... or even one moment (muhutta) old, he does not become." Why? Because there is no further rebirth (paṭisandhi). The same method applies to nibbīsa and the others. Thus, the Blessed One, having said, "In my teaching, this is a designation for an Arahant," began this discourse to show the reasons why one is called niddasa.

In that discourse, 'idha' means in this teaching. 'Sikkhāsamādāne tibbachando hoti' means having a strong desire in fulfilling the three trainings. 'Āyatiñca sikkhāsamādāne avigatapemo' means being endowed with unfailing love for fulfilling the training in the future, such as on the following day and so on. 'Dhammanisantiya' means investigating and reflecting on the teachings. This is a designation for insight (vipassanā). 'Icchāvinaye' means in the removal of craving (taṇhā). 'Paṭisallāne' means in solitude. 'Vီရိယာရမ္ဘေ' (vīriyārambhe) means in the [initiation] of energy that occurs in the body and mind...
151:
...in fulfilling energy. 'Satinepakke' means in mindfulness and in the state of prudence (nepakka). 'Diṭṭhipaṭivedhe' means in the penetration and seeing of the Path (magga). The rest of the words are clear in meaning everywhere.

## 3. The Chapter on the Seven Conditions of the Vajjis (Vajjisattakavagga).

## 1. Commentary on the Sārandada Sutta

In the first sutta of the third chapter, 'Sārandada Cetiya' refers to the monastery of that name. It is said that before the Tathāgata appeared, there was a shrine (cetiya) at that place which was the dwelling of a yakkha named Sārandada. Then, they built and offered a monastery for the Blessed One at that place. That monastery became known simply as the Sārandada Cetiya. 'Yāvakīvañca' means for as long a time. 'Abhiṇhaṃ sannipātā' means that if they assemble three times a day or at various intervals, it is indeed frequent assembly. 'Sannipātabahulā' means assembling many times without falling back, not thinking, "We assembled yesterday and the day before yesterday; why should we assemble again today for what purpose?"

"The Vajjī Licchavis can expect only growth, not decline" means that if they do not assemble frequently, they will not hear the news coming from various directions. Because they do not hear it, they will not know, "The boundaries of such-and-such a village or market town are in disorder; thieves have arisen in such-and-such a place." The thieves, knowing that "the kings are negligent," will attack the villages and market towns and destroy the countryside. In this way, decline occurs for the kings. But if they assemble frequently, they hear that news and can crush the enemies by sending the military forces. The thieves, knowing that "the kings are diligent; we cannot wander about in groups," will break up and flee. In this way, growth occurs for the kings. Therefore, it was said, "The Vajjī Licchavis can expect only growth, not decline."

In the words "in harmony" (samaggā) and so on, the decision should be understood thus: When the assembly drum is sounded, the Licchavi kings who are distracted, making excuses such as "Today I have business, I have a ceremony," are not said to assemble in harmony. But those who, upon hearing the drum sound, come to assemble even while eating, decorating themselves, or dressing, even if only half-finished, are said to assemble in harmony. After assembling, if they do not rise together after deliberating, consulting, and doing what should be done, they are not said to rise in harmony. For when they rise in harmony like this, such a thought does not occur to the Licchavi kings who go first...
152:
The thought arises: "We have heard only external talk; now it will be a talk of decision." Only those kings who rise up together are said to rise in unity.

In another way, upon hearing, "In such a place, the boundaries of the village or the boundaries of the town are in disorder, and robbers have risen up in revolt," when it is asked, "Who will go and crush the enemy?" those kings who go saying, "I will go first, I will go first," are also said to rise in unity. Furthermore, when the affairs of one king are declining, the remaining kings send their sons and brothers to support his affairs; and when a visiting king arrives, they do not differentiate by saying, "Let him go to such a king's house, let him go to that king's house," but all together they welcome him; and when a wedding, an illness, or any other such matter of happiness or sorrow arises for one king, all go there as companions—such kings are said to perform the duties of the Vajjis in unity.

Regarding the terms beginning with "appaññattaṃ," the decision is as follows: Kings who forcibly collect customs duties, taxes, or fines that were not previously established are said to enact what was not enacted by former kings. Kings who fail to collect only those taxes that have come down through ancient tradition are said to abolish what was enacted. When someone is caught and presented as a "thief," those kings who, without careful investigation, pass sentences of mutilation or execution are said not to live according to the ancient Vajji Dhamma.

In the reign of those who enact what was not enacted, people oppressed by new customs duties and the like, thinking, "We are being greatly persecuted; who would want to live in the realm of these kings?" enter the border regions and, becoming either robbers or associates of robbers, destroy the countryside. For those kings who abolish what was enacted and do not collect the traditional customs duties and the like, the treasury declines. Due to the decline of the treasury, the elephant troops, horse troops, the assembly of soldiers, and the retinue of the harem, not receiving their regular allotted maintenance, decline in strength and power. They become capable neither of fighting in war nor of serving the king. In the realm of kings who do not live according to the ancient Vajji Dhamma, people become angry, saying, "They have accused our sons, fathers, and brothers of being thieves when they were not, and have killed and oppressed them," and entering the border regions, they become robbers or associates of robbers and destroy the countryside. Thus, the decline of kings occurs.

However, in the reign of kings who do not enact what was not enacted, people are joyful and satisfied, thinking, "The kings act only according to ancient tradition," and they fully carry out their affairs such as agriculture and trade. For those kings who do not abolish what was enacted and collect the traditional customs duties and the like, the treasury increases. Because the treasury increases, the elephant troops, horse troops, the assembly of soldiers, and the retinue of the harem, receiving their regular allotted maintenance, become endowed with strength and power, and are capable of both fighting in war and serving the king. Ancient...
153:
People do not criticize those kings who live by undertaking the laws of the Vajjis. Thinking, "The kings act according to ancient tradition; surrounded by the eight classes of ministers, the general, and the viceroy, and having themselves consulted and had the Book of Precedents read out, they inflict only appropriate punishment; there is no fault in these kings, the fault lies only in us," they perform their duties without negligence. In this way, the prosperity of the kings occurs.

"Sakkariissanti" means that in performing any act of honor toward those kings, they will do it well. "Garuṃ kariissanti" means they will act by establishing a sense of reverence. "Mānessanti" means they will cherish them with their minds. "Pūjessanti" means they will honor them with the four requisites. "Sotabbaṃ maññissanti" means that going to serve them two or three times a day, they will consider that the words of those kings should be listened to and believed. Among them, if any junior kings do not perform such acts of honor toward the elder kings, or do not go to serve them for the sake of receiving advice, they are abandoned by the elders and, receiving no advice, they become devoted to play and decline from their kingship. But those who conduct themselves in that way (with respect) are told the ancient traditions by the elder kings, saying, "This should be done, this should not be done." Even when they reach the battlefield, the elders show them the strategy, saying, "Thus one should enter, thus one should exit." Those junior kings, receiving advice from them and practicing according to that advice, are able to maintain the royal lineage. Therefore, it is said, "Only growth is to be expected for the Licchavis of the Vajjis."

"Kulitthiyo" refers to the housewives of the clans. "Kulakumāriyo" refers to their unmarried daughters. "Okassā" or "pasayhā" are names for the manner of using force or violence. Some also read it as "okāsā." Therein, "okassā" means dragging away by force, and "pasayhā" means overwhelming and oppressing; this is the meaning of the words. In the realm of kings who act thus (toward women), the people, becoming angry and saying, "These kings have forcibly taken and kept in their own houses our daughters whom we raised in our homes along with their brothers, even removing their saliva and mucus with our own mouths," enter the border regions and become robbers or associates of robbers and destroy the countryside. However, in the realm of kings who do not do so, the people, being without anxiety and performing their own works, increase the royal treasury. Thus, in this matter, prosperity and decline should be understood.
154:
Regarding the Vajjīs, 'Vajjī-cetiyāni' refers to the dwelling places of yakkhas in the Vajjian country of the Vajjī kings, which have acquired the name 'cetiya' in the sense of being honored. 'Abbhantarāni' means those situated inside the city. 'Bāhirāni' means those situated outside the city. 'Dinnapubbaṃ katapubbaṃ' refers to the offerings and honors that were previously given and performed in the past. 'No parihāpessanti' means they will not allow those offerings to decrease but will perform them exactly as they have been traditionally carried out.

Deities do not provide well-arranged protection to those who decrease the righteous offerings (dhammika bali). Even if they cannot cause new suffering to arise, they increase existing diseases such as coughs and headaches. When a battle is reached, they do not become companions. However, for those who do not decrease the offerings, deities provide well-arranged protection. Even if they cannot cause new happiness to arise, they remove existing diseases such as coughs and headaches. They also become companions on the battlefield. Thus, in this context, growth and decline should be understood.

In the phrase 'dhammikā rakkhāvaraṇagutti', it is called 'rakkhā' (protection) itself; it is called 'āvaraṇa' (defense) because it prevents undesired things from coming; it is called 'gutti' (guarding) because it guards so that desired things are not destroyed. In this regard, guarding by surrounding with an army is not called righteous protection, defense, and guarding for monks. However, when people do not cut down trees in the grove of the monastery, when hunters do not kill animals, and when they do not catch fish in the ponds—acting in this way is called righteous protection, defense, and guarding. 'Kinti' means for what reason.

In that context, those kings who do not desire the coming of Arahants who have not yet arrived are those without faith and without devotion. When monks arrive, they do not go out to welcome them, they do not go to see them, they do not engage in polite conversation, they do not ask questions, they do not listen to the Dhamma, they do not give gifts, they do not listen to the words of appreciation (anumodanā), and they do not arrange a place to stay. Then, the ill-repute of those kings spreads: "Such and such a king has no faith, is not devoted, does not welcome arriving monks... and does not arrange a place to stay." Hearing this, even when monks pass by that king's city gate, they do not enter the city. Thus, there is the non-arrival of Arahants who have not yet come. As for those who have already arrived, because there is no comfortable living, even those who arrived without knowing the situation, having come thinking "We will stay," depart, thinking "Who can stay with this kind of behavior from these kings?" Thus, when those who have not come do not arrive, and those who have come live in discomfort, that fault results in the place being uninhabitable for monks. Consequently, there is no protection from deities. When there is no protection from deities, non-human beings...
155:
...find an opportunity. These non-human beings (amanussā), having gained the opportunity, cause diseases to arise that had not yet occurred. The merit based on seeing virtuous monks, asking questions, and so on, does not arise. Conversely, the occurrence of the bright side (the side of wholesomeness), which is the opposite of the aforementioned dark side (the side of unwholesomeness), happens in a perverted way. Thus, in this context, growth and decline should be understood.

## 2. Vassakārasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, 'abhiyātukāmo' means desiring to go for the purpose of overwhelming or oppressing. 'Vajjī' refers to the Vajjī kings. 'Evaṃ-mahiddhike' means endowed with such great royal power. By this, their state of unity is spoken of. 'Evaṃ-mahānubhāve' means endowed with such great royal majesty. By this, their state of being trained in elephant-craft and so on is spoken of. Referring to that state of being trained, it is said (in the Saṃyutta Nikāya): "Indeed, these Licchavī youths are trained; indeed, these Licchavī youths are well-trained, in that they can shoot arrows through a fine keyhole one after another without missing." 'Ucchecchāmi' means I will cut off and destroy. 'Vināsessāmi' means I will make them disappear (bring to non-visibility). 'Anayavyasanaṃ' refers to non-prosperity and the ruin of kinsmen. 'Āpādessāmi' means I will cause them to reach [this ruin].

It is said that King Ajātasattu used to speak only this talk of war while standing, sitting, and so on. He also commanded his army, "Be ready to go." Why? It is said that based on a port village near the Ganges River, half a league (yojana) was the territory of Ajātasattu, and half a league was the territory of the Licchavīs. There, valuable goods would descend from the foot of the mountain. Hearing of this, while Ajātasattu was still arranging, saying "I will go today, I will go tomorrow," the Licchavīs, being united and harmonious, would arrive earlier and take everything. Ajātasattu, arriving later and learning of that event, would return in anger. They did the same in subsequent years as well. Then, he became filled with intense resentment and acted in this way.

Then he thought: "War with a group (the Licchavīs) is a heavy matter; among them, there is not even a single vain blow (missed shot). If I act after consulting with a wise man, I will be blameless. And there is no wise man equal to the Teacher (the Buddha). The Teacher is staying in a nearby monastery. Now, I will send [someone] to ask. If to me..."
156:
Now I shall send [him] to ask; if there is any benefit for me, the Blessed One will remain silent. If there is no benefit, he will say, 'What benefit is there for the Great King in going to that battle?' Thus he thought. That King Ajātasattu sent the Brahmin named Vassakāra. Having gone, the Brahmin Vassakāra informed the Blessed One of the King's intention to wage war against the Vajjis. Therefore, it is said: 'Atha khō rājā ... āpādessāmi vajjī.'

'Bhagavantaṃ vījayamāno' means the Elder Ānanda, taking his duty as the primary focus, was fanning the Blessed One; however, the Blessed One felt neither cold nor heat. When the Blessed One heard the words of the Brahmin Vassakāra, wishing to discuss with the Elder instead of discussing directly with the Brahmin, he said: 'Ānanda, what have you heard?' and so on. That statement has the same meaning as previously explained.

The Blessed One spoke these words, 'Ekamidāhaṃ,' to make it clear that he had previously taught these seven conditions of non-decline (aparihāniya dhamma) to the Vajjis. 'Akaraṇīyā' means not to be done, not to be taken. 'Yadidant' is merely a particle (nipāta). 'Yuddhassa' uses the genitive case in the sense of the instrumental; it means that it is impossible to conquer [the Vajjis] by direct warfare. 'Aññatra upalāpanāya' means except by persuasion. Persuasion (upalāpanā) means sending and offering gifts such as elephants, horses, chariots, gold, and silver, saying, 'Enough of quarreling, let us be united now.' It means that only after becoming familiar through such support can [the Vajjis] be taken over. 'Aññatra mithubhedā' means except by sowing discord among them. By this, it is shown that they can be conquered by causing division among one another. Thus, the Brahmin Vassakāra spoke after obtaining a method from the Blessed One's words.

Did the Blessed One know that the Brahmin would obtain a method from these words? Yes, he knew. Knowing this, why did he speak? Out of compassion. It is said that the Blessed One had this thought: 'Even if I do not speak, [Ajātasattu] will go and capture them all within a few days. But if I speak, while he tries to divide those who are united, he will only be able to capture them after about three years. Living for this much longer is indeed better; while living for this long, those kings will be able to perform meritorious deeds which are their refuge.' 'Abhinanditvā' means rejoicing in the mind, and 'anumoditvā' means expressing appreciation verbally, saying, 'Venerable Gotama, these words are very good indeed.' 'Pakkāmi' means he returned to the presence of the King. King Ajātasattu also sent that same Brahmin, and only after causing division among all [the Vajjis] did he go and bring them to ruin.

## 3. Commentary on the First Sutta of the Sevens (Paṭhamasattakasutta)

In the third sutta, the words 'Abhiṇhaṃ sannipātā' (frequent assemblies) are the same as what was said regarding the seven conditions of non-decline of the Vajjis. In this Dispensation (Sāsana) as well, if they do not assemble frequently, they will not hear the news arriving from various directions.
157:
Because they do not assemble in that way, they do not know such matters as: 'In such-and-such a monastery, the boundary (sīmā) is confused; the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies have stopped; in such-and-such a place, monks are practicing medicine, acting as messengers, and so on; being full of requests, they make a living by giving flowers and so forth.' Evil monks, knowing that 'the Saṅgha is negligent,' gather in groups and cause the Dispensation to decline. However, when they assemble frequently and constantly, they hear of those events. Having heard, they send a group of monks to rectify the boundary, they cause the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā to be maintained, they send monks who preach the Ariyavaṃsa (Noble Lineage) to places where wrong livelihood is prevalent and have them preach the Ariyavaṃsa, and they have the masters of discipline (vinayadhara) restrain the evil monks. The evil monks, too, realizing that 'the Saṅgha is vigilant; it is no longer possible for us to go about in factions,' break up and flee. Thus, growth and decline in this matter should be understood.

Regarding the words 'Samaggā' (united) and so on: when the drum or bell is struck with the desire to establish a pact for repairing a pagoda, or for roofing a Bodhi-tree house or an Uposatha hall, those monks who make excuses and create distractions, saying, 'I have a robe to sew, I have a bowl to fire, I have new work to do,' are not said to assemble in unity. Only those monks who, putting aside all their own work, assemble at once, saying, 'I will assemble first, I will assemble first,' are said to assemble in unity. After assembling, if they do not rise together after deliberating, discussing, and performing what needs to be done, they are not said to rise in unity. For among those who rise in this [disunited] way, those who leave first might think, 'We have only heard external talk; only now will the talk of decision take place.' Only when they rise at the same time are they said to rise in unity. Alternatively, when they hear, 'In such-and-such a place, the monastery boundary is confused, the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā have stopped, and evil monks who practice medicine and so on are prevalent,' and it is asked, 'Who will go and restrain them?', those monks who go saying, 'I will go first, I will go first,' are also said to rise in unity.

When they see a visiting monk, without saying, 'Go to this compound, go to that compound, who is this person?', if all monks perform the duties [of hospitality]; or seeing one with worn-out bowl and robes, if they seek a bowl and robes for him through the duty of alms-round; or if they seek medicine for a sick monk; or if they look after a helpless sick monk in their own compound without driving him away by saying, 'Go to such-and-such a compound'; if one...
158:
When the scriptures are declining, by supporting a wise monk and having him teach those scriptures, they are said to perform the duties of the Saṅgha in harmony.

Regarding the terms beginning with "Appaññattaṃ" (what is not prescribed): those monks who adopt new, unrighteous agreements or training rules are said to prescribe what is not prescribed, like the monks in Sāvatthī regarding the matter of old rugs (purāṇasanthata). Those who present what is not the Sutta or Abhidhamma, or what is not the Vinaya, as the Teaching (Sāsana) are said to abolish what has been prescribed, like the Vajjiputta monks of Vesālī a hundred years after the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna. Those monks who intentionally transgress minor and very minor offenses do not live according to the training rules as they were prescribed, like the monks Assaji and Punabbhasuka. However, those monks who do not act in that way—such as the Venerable Upasena, the Venerable Yasa Kākaṇḍakaputta, and the Venerable Mahākassapa—do not prescribe what is not prescribed and do not abolish what is prescribed, but live according to the training rules as they were prescribed. "Vuddhiyeva" means only growth through virtues such as morality (sīla), not decline.

"Thera" (Elder) refers to those who have reached a state of stability and are endowed with the qualities that make one an elder. They are called "Rattaññū" because they have known many nights. They are called "Cirapabbajita" because they have been ordained for a long time. They are called "Saṅghapitu" (Fathers of the Saṅgha) because they stand in the position of a father to the Saṅgha. Because they stand in the position of a father, they lead the Saṅgha; being leaders, they guide others in the three trainings (sikkhā), and thus they are called "Saṅghapariṇāyaka" (Leaders of the Saṅgha).

Those junior monks who do not show respect and so forth to these great elders, and do not go to attend on them two or three times to receive advice—those great elders also do not give them advice, do not speak of the traditional lineage, and do not teach them the Dhamma-discourses that are of the essence. Being neglected by those elders, those junior monks decline from the groups of Dhamma such as morality (sīla) and from the seven noble wealths (ariya-dhana), and so forth. Those junior monks who show respect and so forth to those great elders and go to attend on them—those great elders give them advice such as "In this way you should progress," speak of the traditional lineage, and teach them the Dhamma-discourses that are of the essence, instructing them with the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) and the ten subjects of discourse (kathāvatthu). Abiding by the advice of those great elders and growing in virtues such as morality, those junior monks gradually attain Arahatship, which is the fruit of recluseship (sāmaññattha). Thus, decline and growth should be understood in this context.

Because it has the nature (sīla) of giving rise to a new birth, it is called "Ponobbhavika"; it means "productive of new existence." Regarding the phrase "they will not fall under the power of that craving which leads to new existence" (ponobbhavikāya): those monks who, for the sake of the four requisites, follow closely in the footsteps of donors and wander from village to village...
159:
Those monks are said to fall under the power of that craving. Others do not. In this matter of following or not following, decline and growth are indeed evident.

"Āraṇyakesu" refers to forest dwellings that are at least five hundred bow-lengths away. "Sāpekkhā" means having regard (or longing). In village-vicinity monasteries, even if one attains a meditative absorption (jhāna), as soon as one emerges from that jhāna, one hears the sounds of men, women, boys, girls, and so forth; because of hearing those sounds, even the special attainment one has reached declines. In a forest dwelling, even if one is asleep, as soon as one wakes up, one hears the sounds of lions, tigers, peacocks, and so forth; because of hearing those sounds, one gains joy (pīti) in the forest and, by contemplating that very joy, one becomes established in the highest fruit, Arahatship. Thus, the Blessed One praises even a monk sleeping in the forest more than a monk sitting in meditative absorption in a village-vicinity monastery. Therefore, for the sake of that special benefit, He said: "They will have regard for forest dwellings."

"They will establish mindfulness within themselves" means they will establish mindfulness within their own internal continuity. "Pesalā" means those who have dear virtue. In this Dispensation, resident monks who do not desire the arrival of fellow practitioners lack faith and are not confident. They do not perform duties for the monks who arrive at the monastery, such as going out to meet them, receiving their bowls and robes, preparing seats, or offering fans. Then, an ill report about those monks spreads: "The monks living in such-and-such a monastery lack faith and are not confident; they do not even perform minor duties for the monks who enter the monastery." Hearing that report, even when monks pass by the gate of the monastery, they do not enter. Thus, those who have not yet come simply do not come. As for those who have already arrived, since there is no comfortable living, even those who arrived without knowing say: "We came thinking we would stay, but with this kind of behavior from these resident monks, who could stay?" and they depart. In this way, that monastery becomes a place where other monks do not reside. Because other monks do not reside there, the resident monks do not get the opportunity to see virtuous monks, and thus they do not get to dispel their doubts, learn the training in conduct, or hear the sweet Dhamma. For those monks, learning the Dhamma they have not yet learned and reciting the Dhamma they have already learned do not happen. Thus, for them, there is only decline, not growth.

However, those monks who desire the arrival of fellow practitioners have faith and are confident. They perform duties such as going out to meet the arriving fellow practitioners and preparing seats for them.
160:
They provide (lodging and resting places). They take those arriving monks and enter the village for alms. They dispel their doubts. They obtain the opportunity to hear the sweet Dhamma. Then, the reputation of those resident monks spreads: "The monks living in such-and-such a monastery are thus faithful, devoted, accomplished in their duties, and hospitable." Hearing this news, monks come even from afar. The resident monks perform duties for those visiting monks; they approach and pay homage to the visiting elders and sit down. They take a seat near the junior visiting monks and, having sat down, ask: "Will you stay in this monastery or will you go?" If they say, "We will go," they say, "The lodging is suitable, alms are easy to obtain," and so on, and do not allow them to leave. If the visitor is a bearer of the Vinaya, they recite the Vinaya in his presence. If he is a bearer of the Suttas and so on, they recite that respective Dhamma in his presence. Those resident monks, established in the advice of the visiting elders, reach Arahantship along with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). The visiting monks also tend to say: "We came thinking we would stay for only a day or two, but because of the pleasantness of living with these resident monks, we have stayed for ten or twelve years." Thus, in this context, decline and growth should be understood.

## ၄။ ဒုတိယသတ္တကသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ

In the fourth sutta, "na kammārāmā" means those monks who spend the whole day only making robes, waistbands, water filters, water-strainers, brooms, foot-scrubbers, and so on; this prohibition is intended for those monks. However, if a monk performs those tasks like robe-making only at the proper time, takes up the lesson at the time for lessons, recites at the time for recitation, performs the duties at the stupa terrace at the time for those duties, and applies mental attention at the time for mental attention, he is not called one who delights in work (kammārāma).

The monk who spends the day and night only engaging in conversation about the appearance of women, the appearance of men, and so on, and does not make a limit to such talk, is called one who delights in talking (bhassārāma). However, the monk who teaches the Dhamma or answers questions throughout the day and night is indeed one of few words and one who makes a limit to speech. Why? Because it was said: "Monks, when you have gathered, there are two things to be done: Dhamma talk or noble silence."

The person who, whether standing, walking, or sitting, is overcome by sloth and torpor (thīna-middha) and is only sleeping, is called one who delights in sleep (niddārāma). For the monk whose mind...
161:
...descends into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) due to physical illness, this is not delighting in sleep. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Aggivessana, I know that in the last month of the summer season, after returning from the alms round after the meal, I would spread out the outer robe (saṅghāṭī) fourfold and lie down on the right side, mindful and clearly comprehending, and fall asleep."

The person who lives only in association, thinking "two for one, three for two, four for three," and does not find pleasure alone, should be called one who delights in company (saṅgaṇikārāma). The person who finds pleasure alone in all four postures is not one who delights in company.

Those without virtue who are possessed of the desire to be esteemed for qualities they do not possess are called those of evil desires (pāpicchā). Those who have evil associates because of going about together in all four postures, and those who are inclined, leaning, and bent towards those evil associates, are called those with evil friends, evil associates, and evil companions (pāpamitta, pāpasahāya, pāpasampavaṅka).

"Oramattakena" means by a low measure, by a small measure. "Antarā" means in this interval before reaching Arahantship. "Vosānaṃ" means a retreat, considering it finished, thinking "this much is enough." This is what is meant: as long as the monks do not reach a standstill, thinking they have finished with a mere measure of any of these—purity of virtue, jhāna, insight, or the state of a stream-enterer and so on—only growth is to be expected for the monks, not decline.

## ၇။ သညာသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ
In the seventh sutta, perceptions such as the perception of impermanence (aniccasaññā) are perceptions accompanied by the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) and so on.

## ၈။ ပဌမပရိဟာနိသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ
In the eighth sutta, they are called "bhāravāhino" (burden-bearers) because they carry the burden by completing the duties of the Saṅgha that have arisen. Those elders will be known by that—by those duties appropriate to their status as elders. "Engaging in them" means applying effort; it means starting to perform those duties oneself.
162:
## 9. Dutiyaparihānisuttavaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the ninth sutta, the Second Sutta on Decline, the phrase "bhikkhudassanaṃ hāpeti" means neglecting to go for the purpose of seeing the Saṅgha of monks (not going). "Adhisīle" refers to the higher virtue consisting of the five precepts and the ten precepts. "Ito bahiddhā" means outside of this Dispensation (Sāsana). "Dakkhiṇeyyaṃ gavesati" means seeking those worthy of offerings. "Tattha ca pubbakāraṃ karoti" means giving first to those titthiyas (outsiders) who are outside the Dispensation, and only afterwards giving to the monks. The remaining explanations are clear in all sentences.

## Vajjisattakavaggo Tatiyo.
The Third Chapter, the collection of the seven principles taught to the Vajjians, is finished.

## 4. Devatāvaggo
## 5. Paṭhamamittasuttavaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the fifth sutta of the fourth chapter, the First Sutta on Friends, "duddadaṃ" means giving precious possessions that are difficult to give away. "Dukkaraṃ karoti" means performing a task that is not easy to do. "Dukkhamam khamati" means enduring what is difficult to endure for the sake of a friend. "Guyhamassa āvikaroti" means revealing one's own secrets to that friend. "Guyhamassa pariguyhati" means concealing the friend's secrets without telling others. "Khīṇena nātimaññati" means not despising the friend because of the exhaustion of their wealth; it means not regarding that person as inferior nor regarding oneself with excessive conceit.

## 6. Dutiyamittasuttavaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the sixth sutta, the Second Sutta on Friends, "vattā" means being skilled in giving advice. "Vacanakkhamo" means being patient with words of advice and following the advice given. "Gambhīraṃ" refers to profound matters, such as talk related to secrets, or talk based on jhāna, insight (vipassanā), the Path (magga), Fruition (phala), and Nibbāna.

## 7. Paṭhamapaṭisambhidါသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ
In the commentary on the seventh sutta, the First Sutta on Analytical Powers, "idaṃ me cetaso līnattaṃ" means that when sluggishness of mind arises, one knows it according to its true nature: "This is the sluggishness of my mind." "Ajjhattaṃ saṅkhittaṃ" refers to a mind that follows sloth and torpor (thina-middha). "Bahiddhā vikkhittaṃ" refers to a mind scattered among the five cords of sensual pleasure...
163:
...scattered among the five cords of sensual pleasure. The terms beginning with "vedanā" (feeling) are taken by way of being the roots of the mental proliferations (papañca) [of craving, conceit, and wrong view]. Indeed, feeling is the root of the arising of craving (taṇhā) by way of pleasant feeling. Perception (saññā) is the root of the arising of wrong view (diṭṭhi) when an object is not clearly perceived. Thought (vitakka) is the root of the arising of conceit (māna) through the thought "I am." "Sappāyāsappāyesu" means in things that are beneficial and non-beneficial. "Nimittaṃ" means cause. The remaining words are clear in meaning in all places.

## Devatāvaggo Catuttho.
The Fourth Chapter, the Chapter on Deities, is finished.

## 5. Mahāyaññavaggo
## 1-2. Sattaviññāṇaṭṭhitisuttādivaṇṇanā
44-45. In the commentary on the first sutta of the fifth chapter, "viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo" refers to the stations for rebirth-linking consciousness. The word "seyyathāpi" is a particle used for illustration, meaning "just as humans." In infinite world systems, among infinite humans, no two people are identical in terms of complexion, shape, and so on. Even if twins in some places are similar in complexion or shape, there is still a difference in their way of looking straight, looking askance, speaking, laughing, walking, standing, and so on. Therefore, it is said they have "diverse bodies (nānattakāyā)."

Their perception associated with rebirth-linking is triple-rooted (tihetuka), double-rooted (duhetuka), or rootless (ahetuka). Therefore, it is said they have "diverse perceptions (nānattasaññino)." "Ekacce ca devā" refers to the deities of the six sensual-sphere heavens. Among those deities, some have a dark blue body, while others have a golden complexion, and so on. Their perception is either double-rooted or triple-rooted; it is never rootless. "Ekacce ca vinipātikā" refers to those who are released from the four states of misery, such as the female yakkhas Uttaramātā, Piyaṅkaramātā, Phussamittā, Dhammaguttā, and other Vēmānika Petas (ghosts with mansions). Their bodies are diverse by way of complexion—such as golden, white, black, or the color of a bedbug's back—and by way of being thin, fat, short, or tall. Like humans, their perceptions are also diverse by way of being double-rooted, triple-rooted, or rootless.

They are not as powerful as the deities; they have little power like destitute humans. They live oppressed by suffering, finding food and clothing with difficulty. Some are miserable during the dark fortnight and happy during the bright fortnight. Therefore, because they have fallen away from a mass of happiness, they are called "vinipātika" (fallen ones). Among these fallen ones, those who are triple-rooted can achieve the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya), like Piyaṅkaramātā and others.
164:
The term 'Brahmakāyika' refers to the Brahmapārisajja, Brahmapurohita, and Mahābrahmā deities. 'Paṭhamābhinibbatta' means that all these Brahmās are produced through the first jhāna. The Brahmapārisajja Brahmās are produced by a limited first jhāna, and their lifespan is one-third of an aeon. The Brahmapurohita Brahmās are produced by a medium first jhāna; their lifespan is half an aeon, and their bodies are larger. The Mahābrahmā deities are produced by a superior first jhāna; their lifespan is one aeon, and their bodies are indeed very large. Thus, these Brahmās should be understood as being 'diverse in body but unified in perception' because of their differing physical forms and their identical rebirth-linking perception through the power of the first jhāna.

Just like those Brahmās, the beings in the four woeful realms are also diverse in body but unified in perception. Specifically, in the hell realms, some beings have a body of one gāvuta, some half a yojana, and some one yojana, while Devadatta's body is one hundred yojanas. Among animals, some are small and some are large. In the realm of pretas, some are sixty cubits tall and some eighty cubits; some are beautiful and some are ugly. Likewise are the Kālakañjika asuras. Furthermore, among these pretas, those known as Dīghapiṭṭhika pretas can even be sixty yojanas in size. However, the perception of all these beings in the woeful realms is only the unwholesome resultant rootless rebirth-linking perception. Therefore, beings in the woeful realms are also reckoned as being diverse in body but unified in perception.

'Ābhassara' (Streaming Radiance) are so called because, like the flame of a torch, the radiance from their bodies streams out in intermittent flashes. Among them, according to the fivefold method, those who are reborn after developing the second and third jhānas to a limited degree are called Parittābhā; their lifespan is two aeons. Those who develop them to a medium degree are called Appamāṇābhā; their lifespan is four aeons. Those who develop the superior jhāna are called Ābhassara; their lifespan is eight aeons. Here, however, all of them are included under the highest classification. Although the bodies of all these Brahmās have the same expansiveness, their perception is diverse, being either a rebirth-linking perception with only sustained application (vicāra) without initial application (vitakka), or one without both initial and sustained application.

'Subhakiṇhā' (Refulgent Glory) means those who are pervaded or scattered with beauty, meaning they have a solid mass of beautiful bodily radiance. The radiance of these Brahmās does not flash intermittently like that of the Ābhassara Brahmās. According to the fivefold method, through the power of the fourth jhāna—whether limited, medium, or superior—they are reborn as Parittasubha, Appamāṇasubha, and Subhakiṇhā, with lifespans of 16, 32, and 64 aeons respectively. Thus, it should be understood that all these Brahmās are unified in body and also unified in perception through the fourth jhāna perception.
165:
It should be understood that they also possess a unified rebirth-linking perception through the perception associated with the fourth jhāna. The Vehapphala Brahmās also belong only to the fourth station of consciousness (viññāṇatthiti). The non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), due to the absence of consciousness, are not included in these stations of consciousness, but they are included in the nine abodes of beings (sattāvāsa).

The Suddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) Brahmās are established on the side of liberation (vivaṭṭapakkhā); they do not exist at all times. They do not appear in a world empty of Buddhas, even for a hundred thousand aeons or an incalculable period. They appear only when Buddhas arise within a span of sixteen thousand aeons. They are like the place where the audience stands when the Blessed One turns the Wheel of Dhamma. Therefore, they are usually not included in either the stations of consciousness or the abodes of beings. However, the Elder Mahāsīva says that the Suddhāvāsa Brahmās are indeed included in the fourth station of consciousness and the fourth abode of beings, based on this sutta: "Sāriputta, that abode is not easily found which has not been lived in by me during this long journey, except for the Suddhāvāsa deities" (M. Ni. 1.160). This statement is accepted because it does not contradict the sutta.

Just as the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception is so called because perception is subtle, so too, because consciousness is subtle, it is neither consciousness nor non-consciousness. Therefore, it is not mentioned among the stations of consciousness. In the second sutta, 'requisites of concentration' (samādhiparikkhārā) refers to the components (sambhāra) of path-concentration.

## 3. Commentary on the First Aggisutta

In the third sutta, all things such as lust (rāga) are called 'fires' (aggi) in the sense of burning. In this sutta beginning with 'āhuneyyaggi', 'āhuna' refers to respect or offerings (sakkāra). Because they are worthy of offerings, they are called 'āhuneyya'. Parents are worthy of offerings because they are of great help to their children. Children who act wrongly toward their parents are reborn in hell and other woeful states. Therefore, although parents do not burn them personally, they are the cause of the burning. Thus, they are called the 'fire of those worthy of offerings' (āhuneyyaggi) in the sense of causing burning. 'Gahapati' refers to the master of the house, the husband. He is of great help to the woman by providing a bed, clothing, ornaments, and so on. A woman who transgresses against him is reborn in hell and other woeful states. Therefore, he too is called the 'householder fire' (gahapataggi) in the sense of causing burning, according to the previous method. In the term 'dakkhiṇeyyaggi', 'dakkhiṇa' refers to the four requisites. The community of monks (bhikkhusaṅgha) is called 'dakkhiṇeyya'. They are of great help to laypeople by urging them toward good qualities such as the three refuges, the five precepts, the ten precepts, supporting parents, and supporting righteous recluses and brahmins. Those who act wrongly toward that Saṅgha...
166:
Laypeople, by abusing and harassing the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, are reborn in hell and so forth. Therefore, that Bhikkhu Saṅgha is also called 'Dakkiṇeyyaggi' (the fire of those worthy of offerings) because, according to the previous method, they cause one to burn (in hell). The natural fire produced from wood is called 'Kaṭṭhaggi' (wood fire).

## 4. Dutiya-aggisutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fourth discourse, 'Uggatasarīra' means that the Brahmin Mahāsāla was exalted and had reached the essence both in terms of his physical person and his wealth; thus, he was known as 'Uggatasarīra' (one with an exalted body). 'Upakkhaṭo' means being prepared or ready. 'Thūṇūpanītāni' refers to (beings) brought to the sacrificial post. 'Yaññatthāya' means for the purpose of killing for sacrifice. 'Upasaṅkami' means that the Brahmin, having prepared all the sacrificial requisites, thought: "The ascetic Gotama is said to be of great wisdom; will he speak of the merits of my sacrifice or its faults? I will ask and find out." For this reason, he approached the Blessed One. 'Aggissa ādānaṃ' means taking up the new auspicious fire for the sacrifice. 'Sabbena sabbaṃ' indicates that all that was heard matches, corresponds, and is identical with all that was heard. 'Satthāni' are called 'weapons' because they are like weapons in the sense of harming. 'Sayaṃ paṭhamaṃ samārambhati' means he himself initiates the effort first. 'Hantuṃ' means for the purpose of killing.

'Pahātabbā' means things to be abandoned. 'Atohayaṃ' means this person is born from parents. 'Āhuto' means having come. 'Sambhūto' means having arisen. 'Ayaṃ vuccati, brāhmaṇa, gahapataggi' refers to the group consisting of wife, children, and so forth; because they act like the master of the house (gahapati) and behave as such, they are called 'Gahapataggi' (the householder's fire). 'Attānaṃ' refers to the mind. 'Damenti' means they tame by taming the senses. 'Samenti' means they calm by calming lust and so forth. They calm them by completely extinguishing those defilements. 'Nikkhipitabbō' means it should be kept or placed so that it does not perish. 'Upavāyatu' means 'let it be cleansed'. Having said this, the Brahmin gave life to all those beings, destroyed the sacrificial shed, and became like a well (a source of refuge) in the Teacher's Dispensation.
167:
## 5-6. Saññāsutta-dvaya-vaṇṇanā

48-49. In the fifth discourse, 'Amato-gadhā' means having Nibbāna as its footing. 'Amatapariyosānā' means having Nibbāna as its end.

In the sixth discourse, 'Methunadhamma-samāpattiyā' means due to being endowed with sexual intercourse. 'Nhārudaddulaṃ' means a mass of nerves or the scraping of nerves. 'Anusandati' means it proceeds. 'Natthi me pubbenāparaṃ viseso' means there is no difference for me between the past time when the meditation on foulness was not yet developed and the subsequent time when it has been developed. 'Lokacitresu' means in the diverse worlds which are the dwelling places of beings in the three realms. 'Ālasye' means in the state of laziness. 'Vissaṭṭhiye' means in the state of being relinquished. 'Ananuyoge' means in the lack of application of effort. 'Ahaṅkāra-mamaṅkāra-mānāpagataṃ' means being free from the view of 'I', the craving of 'mine', and the nine types of conceit.
