'Vidhā-samatikkantaṃ' means transcending the three modes of conceit (vidhā). 'Santaṃ' means calmed from the defilements that are its opposite. 'Suvimuttaṃ' means well-liberated through the five kinds of liberation.

## 7. Methunasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh discourse, 'Upasaṅkami' means he approached after having eaten his breakfast, surrounded by slaves and laborers. 'Bhavampino' means the question, "Does the Venerable also...?" 'Brahmacārī paṭijānāti' means the question, "Do you claim to live the holy life, saying 'I am a practitioner of the holy life'?" That Brahmin previously had this thought: "In the Brahmin tradition, those who learn the Vedas practice the holy life for forty-eight years. But the ascetic Gotama, while living in the household, enjoyed himself with three kinds of dancers in three palaces; what will he say now?" He asked with this meaning in mind. Then the Blessed One, like one catching a cobra with a mantra, or like one stepping on an enemy's neck with his foot, uttered a lion's roar starting with "Yañhi taṃ brāhmaṇa," referring to the fact that during the six years of his great striving, when there was potential for defilement, he never had even a single thought regarding royal happiness or the dancers' excellence in the palaces.

In that passage, 'Dwayaṃ-dwayasamāpattiṃ' refers to the state of union between two persons. 'Dukkhasmā' means from the entire suffering of the round of rebirth. 'Sañjagghati' means speaking joking words. 'Saṅkီḷati' means playing. 'Saṅkeḷāyati' means laughing loudly. 'Cakkhunā cakkhuṃ' means staring into the woman's eyes with one's own eyes. 'Tirokuṭṭaṃ vā tiropākāraṃ vā' means on the other side of a wall or on the other side of a rampart, that is, on the other side of another wall...
170:
The name Veḷukaṇṭaka arose. Parāyana refers to the Dhamma known as Parāyana because it is the way (ayana) to the far shore (pāra), which is Nibbāna.

"Chanting with a voice" means: The noble female disciple, who had attained the three fruits, was sitting in a well-guarded place on the upper floor of a seven-storied mansion. Having spent part of the night through the power of meditative attainment (samāpatti), she emerged and thought, "With what delight shall I spend the remainder of this night?" Deciding on "the delight of Dhamma," she chanted the Parāyana Sutta, consisting of two hundred and fifty verses, in a sweet intonation (sarabhañña). "He heard" means: King Vessavaṇa heard it while traveling in a human-borne vehicle along a path above that mansion, having set aside the celestial mansions in the sky. "Waiting for the end of the discourse, he stood" means: He asked, "Friends, what is this sound?" Being told, "It is the sound of the laywoman Nandamātā chanting in intonation," he descended from the vehicle and stood in the sky nearby, waiting for the end of the teaching.

"Sadhu sister, Sadhu sister" means: "Sister, your Dhamma teaching is well-grasped and well-spoken. I see no difference between what you chanted today and what the Blessed One taught to the sixteen Parāyanika Brahmins while sitting at the Pāsāṇaka Shrine. It is spoken exactly like the Teacher's words, like gold cut in the middle." Saying this, he gave his approval (sādhukāra) and spoke thus. "Noble-faced one, who is this?" means: In this well-guarded place, who is this speaking with such a loud voice? Noble-faced one, is it a Naga, a Garuda, a Deva, a Mara, or a Brahma? Opening the golden-colored window, the noble female disciple, who had attained the three fruits and was free from fear, spoke with Vessavaṇa. "Sister, I am your brother" means: Because he was a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna), he regarded the noble female disciple (who was a Non-returner, anāgāmī) as an elder sister and called her "Sister." Then, because Nandamātā was in her youth, he regarded her as his younger sister, while regarding himself as older since he had a lifespan of nine million years; thus he said "Brother." "Noble-faced one, it is well" means: "Noble-faced deity, it is well, your coming is good; you have come to a place where it is proper to come." "Let this be hospitality for you" means: "Let this chanting of Dhamma be the gift for you as a guest." She said this because she saw no gift superior to this to be given.
171:
The meaning is: "Thus it shall be hospitality for me." Having requested the sharing of merit for himself, he said, "This is the honor for you as a Dhamma preacher." He filled seven hundred and fifty granaries with red rice and made a resolution: "As long as this laywoman lives, let these grains not be exhausted." Then he departed. As long as the laywoman lived, they could not even see the bottom floor of the granaries. From then on, the expression "like the granary of Nandamātā" arose.

"Akata-pātarāso" means one who has not eaten breakfast. "Puññaṃ" refers to the preceding volition (pubba-cetanā) and the volition at the time of giving (muñcana-cetanā). "Puññamahī" refers to the subsequent volition (apara-cetanā). "Sukhāya hotu" means "may it be for happiness and welfare." Thus she shared the merit of her gift with King Vessavaṇa.

"Pakaraṇe" means "due to a cause." "Okkassa pasayha" means "having pulled and overcome." "Yakkha-yoniṃ" refers to the state of an earth-bound deity (bhumma-devatā). "Shows himself with that previous form" means: Creating a body similar to his previous one, he showed himself, adorned and prepared, on the bed in the auspicious chamber. "Upāsikā paṭidesitā" means she made her status as a laywoman known, saying "I am a laywoman." "Yāvade" means "yāvadeva" (only as much as). The remaining words are clear in meaning in all sentences.

## The Fifth Chapter, the Mahāyañña-vagga, is finished.

## The Paṇṇāsaka is finished.
172:
## 6. Abyākata Vagga
## 1. Abyākata Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the sixth chapter, 'abyākatavatthūsu' means in the matters that are not declared by way of categorical answers and so forth. 'Tathāgato' refers to a being. 'Diṭṭhigatametaṃ' means this is merely a wrong view; there is no such thing as a being grasped by that view. 'Paṭipadā' refers to the Noble Path. 'Na chambhati' means one does not tremble by the power of view. The same method applies to the remaining terms. 'Taṇhāgataṃ' refers to craving associated with view. The same method applies to terms like 'saññāgata'. Here, perception associated with view alone is 'saññāgata'; conceit based on view or that which is imagined by view is 'maññita'; the proliferation of view is 'papañcita'; the grasping of view is 'upādāna'; and the distorted state of refuge of view is known as 'vippaṭisāra'. Here, by taking 'diṭṭhi', the sixty-two views are included; by taking 'diṭṭhinirodhagāminīpaṭipadā', the Path of Stream-entry is included.

## 2. Purisagati Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, 'purisagatiyo' refers to the courses of a man's knowledge (ñāṇagati). 'Anupādāparinibbāna' refers to Nibbāna without conditions (apaccayanibbāna). 'No cassa' means if the kamma that produces existence in the past had not existed. 'No ca me siyā' means this existence would not be for me now. 'Na bhavissati' means the kamma that produces future existence will not exist for me now. 'Na ca me bhavissati' means existence will not be for me in the future. 'Yadatthi yaṃ bhūtaṃ' refers to the five aggregates of the present that are evident and have arisen. 'Attaining equanimity with the thought of abandoning those five aggregates' means attaining insight-equanimity (vipassanūpekkhā) with the thought of 'abandoning' through the removal of desire and lust in those present five aggregates. 'Not lusting after existence' means not lusting after the past five aggregates through craving and view. 'Not lusting after arising (sambhava)' means not lusting in the same way after the future. 'There is a state of supreme peace' means there is a state called Nibbāna which is supremely peaceful. 'Sees with right wisdom' means seeing that Nibbāna clearly with path-wisdom (maggapaññā) together with insight. 'Not everything in every way' means not knowing everything in every way because some defilements have not yet been abandoned and the darkness that covers the truths has not been entirely destroyed. 'When struck' means when being struck with a hammer while held with tongs. 'Antarāparinibbāyī' refers to one who attains Nibbāna by the extinguishing of defilements within the interval starting from immediately after rebirth and before reaching the middle of the lifespan. 'Before reaching the ground' means without passing beyond the sky and without reaching the ground, while still in the sky...
173:
...would extinguish. By these three similes, three types of persons who attain Nibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyī) are shown.

'Upahaccaparinibbāyī' refers to one who attains the extinguishing of defilements after passing the middle of the lifespan but before reaching the end. 'Upahacca talaṃ' is like a spark that, while flaming, goes and passes the sky-surface, then strikes the earth-surface and extinguishes just as it falls on the ground. One who attains Nibbāna by exhausting defilements without prompting and with little effort is called an 'asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī'. One who attains Nibbāna by exhausting defilements with prompting and effort is called a 'sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī'. 'Gacchanti' refers to an unprotected forest. 'Dāyanti' refers to a forest that is protected and given for the sake of safety. The remaining words have clear meanings. In this sutta, only noble persons (ariya puggala) are discussed.

## 3. Tissabrahmā Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, 'bhikkhuniyo' refers to the five hundred nuns who were the followers of the Great Pajāpatī. 'Vimuttā' refers to those liberated by the five kinds of liberation. 'Anupādisesā' refers to those liberated completely by the five kinds of liberation without leaving any residue of grasping. 'Saupādisese' or 'saupādiseso' means, in a person with a residue of grasping, "this person has a residue of grasping." The same method applies to the remaining terms. 'Tisso' refers to a Brahmā who was a co-resident of the Elder. 'Anulomikāni' refers to states that are conformable to the practice, secluded, and ultimate. 'Indriyāni' refers to the faculties of insight such as faith (saddhā) and so forth. 'Samannānayamāno' means establishing in attention. Why is the phrase "Na hi pana te" started? It is to show the seventh person. Since the seventh person, the follower by faith (saddhānusārī), had not yet been shown, the Blessed One, wishing to show that person by way of one with strong insight, spoke thus. In that passage, 'sabbanimittānaṃ' refers to all signs such as the sign of permanence and so forth. 'Animitta' refers to strong insight-concentration (vipassanāsamādhi).

## 4. Sīhasenāpati Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, 'maccharī' refers to one possessed of the five kinds of stinginess. 'Kadariyo' refers to one with harsh stinginess who even prevents others from giving. 'Anuppadānaratō' refers to one who delights only in giving repeatedly. 'Anukampantā' refers to compassionating with such a mind as: "Whom shall we favor today? From whom shall we accept gifts? Or to whom shall we preach the Dhamma?"
174:
## 5. Arakkheyya Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, 'nimitta' (sign/cause) refers to both the cause regarding the Dhamma and the cause regarding the person. The Blessed One does not see any 'Dhamma-nimitta' because he does not see even a single word in the Dhamma taught by himself that is badly proclaimed or that does not lead out of Saṃsāra. He is said not to see any 'puggala-nimitta' because he does not see even a single person who would rise up and oppose him, saying, 'The Dhamma was badly proclaimed by you, it is not well-proclaimed.' In the remaining two sentences, the method is the same. The sixth and seventh suttas are clear in their meaning.

## 8. Pacalāyamāna Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, 'pacalāyamāno' (nodding) means that while he was practicing the recluse's Dhamma in a forest grove depending on that village, his body was exhausted from being oppressed by the effort of walking meditation for seven days, and thus he sat nodding at the end of the walking path. 'Pacalāyasi no' means 'Are you sleeping?' 'Anumajjitvā' means 'having rubbed' or 'having cleansed.' 'Ālokasaññā' is the perception of light that dispels drowsiness. 'Divāsaññā' is the perception of daytime. 'Yathā divā tathā rattiṃ' means that just as the perception of the sun's light is established during the day, so too should one establish that perception of light at night. 'Yathā rattiṃ tathā divā' means that just as the perception of the moon's light is established by you at night, so too should one establish that perception of light during the day.

'Sappabhāsaṃ' refers to being with radiance for the sake of divine eye knowledge (dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa). 'Pacchāpuresaññီ' means having the perception that carries forward and backward. 'Antogatehi indriyehi' means with the five sense faculties that are only turned inward without being scattered outward. 'Middhasukhaṃ' is the pleasure of sleep. With these words, the Blessed One taught the Elder Mahāmoggallāna the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) for dispelling drowsiness. 'Soṇḍaṃ' refers to the trunk of pride (māna). In the phrase 'kiccakaraniyāni,' the duties that must definitely be done are called 'kicca,' and other tasks to be performed are called 'karaniya.' 'Maṅkubhāvo' is the state of being without spirit or dejected. With these words, the Teacher taught the Elder the duties of the alms-round (bhikkhācāra-vatta).

Now, in order to encourage him to be one who sets limits in speech, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with 'tasmātiha.' Therein, 'viggāhikakathā' refers to contentious speech that leads to disputes, such as 'You do not understand this Dhamma-Vinaya.' The words beginning with 'nāhaṃ moggallāna' were spoken to avoid association with bad friends. 'Kittāvatā nu kho' is a question meaning 'By how much of a practice?' 'Taṇhāsaṅkhayavimutto hoti' means one is liberated in Nibbāna, the destruction of craving, by inclining the mind toward it as an object.
175:
Because of the state of having a liberated mind, to what extent is one briefly called 'liberated through the destruction of craving' (in Nibbāna)? By what practice does one become liberated through the destruction of craving? He asks, 'Please teach in brief the preliminary practice (pubbabhāga-paṭipadā) of such an Arahant monk.' 'Accantaniṭṭho' means 'accanta' because he has transcended the end known as destruction and decay; he is 'accantaniṭṭho' because he has a finality that transcends the end. The meaning is one who has absolute finality, eternal finality. 'Accantayogakkhemī' means one who is absolutely secure from the four yokes, eternally secure. 'Accantabrahmacārီ' means one who absolutely lives the holy life, eternally lives the holy life. Because that monk has a finality that transcends the end, he is called 'accantapariyosāno' according to the previous method. 'Seṭṭho devamanussānaṃ' means he is excellent, especially noble, among gods and humans. He requests, 'By what means does a monk of such nature come to be? Please teach the practice of that monk in brief.'

In the phrase 'sabbe dhammā nālaṃ abhinivesāya,' 'all things' (sabbe dhammā) refers to the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements. All those things are not fit, not capable, not sufficient, and not suitable for adhering to through the power of craving and views. Why? Because they do not remain according to the manner in which they are grasped. Indeed, even though they are grasped as permanent, pleasant, and self, they turn out to be only impermanent, suffering, and non-self. Therefore, they are not fit for adhering to. 'Abhizānāti' means he specially knows through full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā) as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. 'Parijānāti' means he likewise knows by investigation through full understanding by investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā). 'Yaṃ kiñci vedanaṃ' means he experiences any feeling, even a slight one associated with the five-fold consciousness. With these words, the Blessed One showed the Elder the comprehension of the immaterial (arūpa-pariggaha) by way of feeling.

'Aniccānupassī' means one who repeatedly contemplates as impermanent. In the phrase 'virāgānupassī,' there are two types of dispassion (virāga): destruction-dispassion (khaya-virāga) and absolute-dispassion (accanta-virāga). Among those two, 'virāgānupassanā' refers to both insight (vipassanā) which sees the destruction of formations as destruction, and the path knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) which sees Nibbāna, the absolute dispassion, as dispassion. A person endowed with both is called 'virāgānupassī.' Referring to that person, it is said 'virāgānupassī,' meaning one who repeatedly contemplates with dispassion. The same method applies to 'nirodhānupassī.' For cessation (nirodha) is also of two kinds: destruction-cessation and absolute-cessation. In the phrase 'paṭinissaggānupassī,' relinquishment (paṭinissagga) is called giving up (vossagga). That giving up is of two kinds: giving up as abandonment (pariccāga-vossagga) and giving up as entering into (pakkhandana-vossagga). Therein, giving up as abandonment is insight (vipassanā). For that insight gives up defilements and aggregates by way of substitution of opposites (tadaṅga). Giving up as entering into is the path (magga). For that path enters into Nibbāna by way of making it the object. Or, for two reasons, that path is indeed giving up: because it gives up aggregates and defilements by way of eradication (samuccheda), and because it enters into Nibbāna.
176:
Therefore, because it abandons both defilements (kilesa) and aggregates (khandha), it is called pariccāgavossagga (relinquishment as giving up). Because the mind enters into the element of Nibbāna, which is the state of cessation, it is called pakkhandanavossagga (relinquishment as entering into). Both of these meet in the Path (magga). A person endowed with these two is called a paṭinissaggānupassī (one who contemplates relinquishment) because they are endowed with this paṭinissaggānupassanā. With reference to that person, it is said: "He does not cling to anything in the world." He does not cling to, take hold of, or misapprehend even a single conditioned thing (saṅkhāra) through the power of craving (taṇhā). In the phrase "not clinging, he is not anxious," one who does not take hold of an object is not anxious due to the anxiety of craving. He himself attains Nibbāna through the extinguishing of defilements. By the words "Birth is exhausted," etc., his knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa) is shown. Thus, the Blessed One, being asked about the preliminary practice (paṭipadā) of an Arahant in brief, explained it in brief. This Sutta was both an instruction and a subject of insight (vipassanā) for the Elder. That Elder, having developed insight in this very Sutta, attained Arahantship.

## 9. Mettasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth Sutta, "Monks, do not fear merits" means you who perform merits, do not fear those merits. "Mettacittaṃ bhāvesiṃ" (I developed a mind of loving-kindness) shows that he developed a noble mind associated with loving-kindness belonging to the third and fourth jhānas. "Saṃvaṭṭamāne sudāhaṃ" should be resolved as "saṃvaṭṭamāne sudaṃ ahaṃ." "Saṃvaṭṭamāne" means during the time of burning and destruction [of the world]. "Dhammiko" means one endowed with the ten courses of wholesome action (kusalakamma-patha). "Dhammarājā" is a synonym for that term "dhammika." Or, he is a Dhammarājā because he obtained kingship through righteousness (dhamma). "Cāturanto" means the lord of the earth bounded by the four oceans, such as the eastern ocean. "Vijitāvī" means one who has conquered in battle. Because the country (janapada) attained stability and firmness in that king, he is called janapadatthāvariyappatta. "Parosahassaṃ" means more than a thousand sons. "Sūrā" means those who are brave and fearless. "Vīraṅgarူpā" means those who have the nature of energy (vīriya), which is a limb of the brave. It means they are of the nature of energy, as if made of energy, and are untiring; even if they fight all day, they do not get tired. "Sāgarapariyantaṃ" means the earth ending at the ocean, with Mount Cakkavāḷa as its boundary. "Adaṇḍena" means without the punishment of wealth (fines) or the punishment of weapons such as execution or mutilation. "Asatthena" means without weapons that harm others, such as single-edged swords. "Dhammena abhivijiya" means having conquered the earth in the manner described, solely through righteousness (dhamma), such as "Do not kill living beings," etc., having an arrival welcomed by rival kings saying, "Come, Great King."
177:
"Sukhesino" refers to beings who seek happiness. "Suññabrahmūpago" means reaching the Brahma-abode which is empty of beings. "Pathaviṃ imaṃ" refers to this great earth bounded by the ocean. "Asāhasena" means not by violence or high-handedness. "Samena manusāsitaṃ" means instructed righteously. "Tehi etaṃ sudesitaṃ" means this matter was well-taught by those Buddhas of great compassion. "Pathabyo" means the lord of the earth.

## 10. Bhariyasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth Sutta, "Kevaṭṭā maṇye macchavilope" refers to the very loud noise made by fishermen either at the place where they set down their fish baskets or just as they lift their nets from the water; it is said with reference to that sound. "Sujātā" is the younger sister of Visākhā. That Sujātā not only failed to perform the major and minor duties toward her mother-in-law but did not even regard her as a mother-in-law. "Does not listen to the father-in-law" means she does not listen due to lack of respect and disobedience. The same method applies to the remaining terms. Thus, Anāthapiṇḍika, having observed his daughter-in-law's behavior, sat before the Teacher. Sujātā also stood nearby listening to the sound, thinking, "Will this wealthy merchant speak of my virtues or my faults to the Ten-Powered One?" Then the Teacher called her, saying, "Come, Sujātā."

"Ahitānukampinī" means a woman who does not look after the husband's welfare. "Anyesu" means toward other men. "Atimanyate" means to look down on or despise out of pride. "Dhanena kītassa" means a husband bought with wealth. "Vadhāya ussukā" means they strive to kill. "Yaṃ itthiyā vindati sāmiko dhanaṃ" refers to the wealth the husband obtains because of the woman. "Appampi tassa apahātumicchati" means she desires to take away even a little of that husband's wealth; she even tries to steal a small amount of the rice that should be put into the pot on the stove. "Alasā" means one who stays sitting where she sat, or standing where she stood. "Pharusā" means one who is harsh. "Duruttavādini" means one who speaks bad words, speaking only harsh and cruel speech. In the phrase "Uṭṭhāyakānaṃ abhibhuyya vattati," the plural term "uṭṭhāyakānaṃ" refers to a husband endowed with energetic initiative; she lives by overwhelming and belittling that husband's initiative. "Pamodati" means to be greatly delighted.
178:
It is. *Koleyya* means those of noble birth. *Patibbatā* means one who reveres her husband like a deity (one who has her husband as her deity). *Vadhadandatajjitā* means one who is threatened with a stick and with death, as in saying, "I will kill this person."

*Dāsīsamā* means she has established herself in the refuges, saying, "May the Blessed One regard me as a wife who is like a slave, fulfilling her duties to her husband."

## 11. Kodhana Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the eleventh discourse, the Kodhana Sutta, *sapattakantā* means one who is beloved and dear to enemies, desired and longed for by them. *Sapattakaraṇā* means one who acts for the benefit of enemies. *Kodhapareto* means one who is overwhelmed by anger. *Pacuratthatāya* means because of having much benefit, because of having much welfare. *Anatthampi* refers to the lack of prosperity (misfortune/harm).

"I have taken hold of the benefit" means "I have taken hold of prosperity." Furthermore, *atthaṃ gahetvāna* means having taken hold of prosperity. *Anatthaṃ adhipajjati* means one perceives, "I have taken hold of misfortune." *Vadhaṃ katvāna* means having committed the act of taking life. *Kodhasammadasammatto* means intoxicated with the intoxication of anger, meaning one who is obsessed and gripped by it. *Āyasakyaṃ* means the state of ill-repute, meaning one becomes devoid of fame and is disgraced. *Antarato jātaṃ* means arisen within the body. "He does not know the benefit" means he does not know the benefit of prosperity. "He does not see the Dhamma" means he does not see the Dhamma of tranquility and insight (*samatha-vipassanā*). *Andhatamaṃ* means a thick darkness that causes blindness. *Sahate* means it oppresses and overcomes.

*Dummaṅkuyaṃ* means the state of having an unpleasant face, the state of being without radiance, the state of having an ugly countenance. *Yato patāyati* means when it arises. *Na vāco hoti gāravo* means there is no respectability even in one's speech. *Na dīpaṃ hoti kiñcanaṃ* means there is no refuge or support whatsoever. *Tapanīyāni* means states that cause remorse and burning. *Dhammehi* means by the practices of tranquility and insight. *Ārakā* means in a distant place. *Brāhmaṇaṃ* means an Arahant whose taints are exhausted. *Yāya mātu bhato* means one who was nurtured by a mother. *Pāṇadadiṃ santiṃ* means even though she is the giver of life. *Hanti kuddho puthuttānaṃ* means an angry person kills himself through various means. *Nānārūpesu mucchito* means being infatuated with various objects. *Rajjuyā bajjha mīyanti* means they die by hanging themselves with ropes. *Pabbatamapi kandare* means they die by falling into mountain chasms.
179:
*Bhūnahaccāni* means those that destroy prosperity. *Itāyaṃ* should be resolved as *iti ayaṃ*. *Taṃ damena samucchinde* means one should cut off that anger through restraint. By what kind of restraint (*dama*)? By insight wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*), by bodily and mental energy associated with insight, and by the Right View of the Path (*magga-sammādiṭṭhi*). *Tatheva dhamme sikkhetha* means just as one should cut off unwholesome states, one should likewise train in the practices of tranquility and insight. *Mā no dummaṅkuyaṃ ahū* means desiring this benefit: "May the state of having an unpleasant countenance not happen to us." *Anāyāsā* means being without exhaustion. *Anussukā* means being without anxiety or concern in any matter. The remaining words are clear in meaning in all respects.

## The Sixth Chapter: Abyākata Vagga

## 7. Mahā Vagga

## 1. Hiri-ottappa Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the first discourse of the seventh chapter, the Mahā Vagga, *hatūpaniso* means having a destroyed cause or having the proximate cause cut off. *Yathābhūtañāṇadassanaṃ* refers to tender insight knowledge (*taruṇa-vipassanā*). *Nibbidāvirāgo* refers to both powerful insight knowledge and the Noble Path. *Vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ* refers to the liberation of Arahatship and reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇā*).

## 2. Sattasūriya Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the second discourse, since this *Sattasūriya* teaching was delivered by way of showing the destruction of the world by fire (*tejo-saṃvaṭṭa*), these introductory remarks should be understood first: the three types of destruction (*saṃvaṭṭa*), the three boundaries of destruction (*saṃvaṭṭasīmā*), the three roots of destruction (*saṃvaṭṭamūla*), and the three uproars (*kolāhala*). This matter has been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*, in the section on the recollection of past lives (*Pubbenivāsānussati-niddesa*). *Etadavoca* means He spoke this *Sattasūriyopama Sutta*, beginning with "Bhikkhus, formations are impermanent," for the purpose of showing the ruin of formations, both internal (*upādinnaka*) and external (*anupādinnaka*), according to the inclination of five hundred monks who were meditating on the meditation subject of impermanence. Therein, *aniccā* means impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having come to be. *Saṅkhārā* means the conditioned phenomena, both internal and external. *Adhuvā* means not lasting, in the sense of not enduring for long.
180:
"Anassāsikā" means they are devoid of the nature of being desirable because they lack permanence. "Alameva" means it is indeed suitable.

"Ajjhogāḷho" refers to one who has entered into the water. "Accuggato" refers to one who has risen above the surface of the water. "No rain falls" means that first, the world-destroying rain appears as a single cloud across a hundred thousand crores of world systems and falls. At that time, seeds that have been sown do not return to the house again. From then on, it is as if the water is blocked in a water-strainer (dhammakaraṇa), and not even a single drop of rain falls again; this should be understood as the measure of the discourse on the comparison. When the world is being destroyed, first, starting from the Avīci hell, it becomes empty and void of beings. Rising from there, beings are reborn in the human world and in the animal realms. Even those reborn in the animal realms, having regained loving-kindness (mettā) towards their kinsmen and brothers, are reborn in the deva and human worlds upon death. Devas traveling through the sky announce: "This place is not permanent, it is not eternal; develop loving-kindness, develop compassion, appreciative joy, and equanimity." Having developed loving-kindness and so on, when they pass away from there, they are reborn in the Brahma world.

In the term "Bījagāma," bījagāma refers to the five kinds of seeds. "Bhūtagāma" refers to any green plant that has sprouted roots and leaves. In the term "Oṣadhitiṇavanappatayo," "oṣadhī" refers to medicinal plants. "Tiṇā" refers to trees with external heartwood, such as palmyra and coconut. "Vanappatayo" refers to the great trees that are the chiefs of the forest. "Kunnadiyo" refers to the small rivers, excluding the five great rivers. "Kusobbhā" refers to the small lakes, excluding the seven great lakes. When two suns appear, when one rises, the other sets. When three suns appear, when one rises, another sets, and one is in the middle. When four suns appear, it is like four alms-collectors standing in order at the doors in a village of four families. When five or more suns appear, the same method applies. "Palujjanti" means they break and fall repeatedly. "Neither ash nor soot is perceived" means that when such places as the great earth of the world system, Sineru the king of mountains, the Himavā, the Cakkavāḷa mountains, the six sensual heavens, and the first jhana Brahma worlds are burnt, not even an amount of ash or charcoal that could be picked up with a snap of the fingers is perceived. "Who is able to make one believe? Who will believe?" means who is capable of making that person believe, or who will believe it? Except for the noble disciples who are stream-enterers and have seen the state (of Nibbāna)...
181:
Except for the noble disciples (ariya-sāvaka) who are stream-enterers (sotāpanna) and have seen the state (diṭṭhapada), who else will believe? This is the meaning. "Vītarāgo" means one who is free from lust through the power of suppression (vikkhamphana). "Sāsanaṃ ājāniṃsu" means they understood the instruction; they practiced the path (magga) for the sake of companionship in the Brahma world. "Samasamagatiyo" means having a destination that is equal in every way in the second existence, having a single destination. "Uttari mettaṃ bhāveyyaṃ" means if one were to develop loving-kindness (mettā) more excellently, making it sublime up to the third and fourth jhanas. "Cakkhumā" means one who is endowed with the five eyes. "Parinibbuto" means one who has attained Nibbāna through the extinction of defilements (kilesa-parinibbāna) right at the seat of enlightenment (bodhi-pallaṅka). Thus, having shown the characteristic of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa), when the Teacher concluded the discourse, those five hundred monks who were practicing the meditation on impermanence (anicca-kammaṭṭhāna), sending forth their knowledge according to the discourse, attained Arahatship while still on their seats.

## 3. Nagaropamasutta Vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, "yato" means when. "Paccantimaṃ" refers to a city situated at the border of a country, at the end of a country. However, there is no task of protection for a city in the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa); therefore, it is not taken here. "Nagaraparikkhārehi supari-kkhittaṃ" means well-adorned with the ornaments of a city. "Akaraṇīyaṃ" means that which should not be done, or unconquerable by enemies. "Gambhīranemi" means having deep moats. "Sunikhāta" means well and firmly planted. That gate-pillar (esikā-pillar) is made of bricks, stones, or heartwood such as khadira and so on. Those who make it for the security of the city plant it outside the city; those who make it for decoration plant it inside the city. Those who make it of bricks dig a large hole, build up the brickwork, make the upper part octagonal, and plaster it with mortar. When it does not shake even when struck by an elephant with its tusks, only then is it called well-plastered (firm). Stone pillars and others are also octagonal. If those pillars are eight cubits long, about four cubits enter the hole, and about four cubits remain above. The same method applies to pillars of sixteen or twenty cubits. Indeed, half of all pillars are below ground, and half are above. They are curved like the flow of cow's urine (gomutta-vaṅka); therefore, it is possible to perform the work of fighting by placing planks between them. Those pillars are made with intricate artistic work and have banners and flags raised upon them.
182:
A moat (parikhā) is a ditch (mātikā) that exists surrounding [the city]. A circumvallation path (anupariyāyapatha) is a great road inside the wall that runs along with the wall; warriors stationed on that road fight with those who are outside the wall. Sallaka (salāka) refers to projectile weapons such as arrows, javelins, and so on. Yavanika (jevanika) refers to other weapons used for concealing the body.

Elephant-riders (hatthāroha) include all elephant masters, elephant doctors, elephant keepers, and so on. Horse-riders (assāroha) include all horse masters, horse doctors, horse keepers, and so on. Charioteers (rathika) include all chariot masters, chariot warriors, chariot guards, and so on. Archers (dhanuggaha) refer to archery masters and bowmen.

Celaka are those who go in front holding the victory banner during battle. Calaka are the military strategists who arrange the army's formation, saying, "Let the King's place be here; let such-and-such a great minister's place be here." Piṇḍadāyika are fierce great warriors. It is said that they enter the enemy army, cutting and hacking them like lumps of food, and then leap out. Alternatively, this name also refers to those who enter the midst of the battlefield carrying food and drink for the soldiers.

Uggarājaputta are noble princes who are highly eminent and experienced in the battlefield. Pakkhandino (Chargers) are those who ask, "Whose head or weapon shall I bring?" and when told, "The head or weapon of such-and-such a person," they rush into the battlefield and bring back only that item. Because they rush in, they are called Pakkhandī. They are called Mahānāga because they are as brave as great elephants; this is a designation for warriors who do not retreat even when faced with elephants and other such forces.

Sūra are the truly brave ones. They are capable of swimming across the ocean even while wearing chainmail or armor. Cammayodhino are those who fight either by wearing leather tunics or by holding leather shields that protect against arrows. Dāsakaputta are household slave-warriors who have strong affection and attachment for their masters. Dovārika is a gatekeeper.

Vāsanālepanasampanna means being endowed with covering that leaves no gaps and with the plastering of lime. Alternatively, it means being endowed with an outer fortification known as a wall of stakes, and with thick, smooth lime plastering, displaying rows of full pots (puṇṇaghaṭa) and raising banners decorated with exquisite artistry.

Grass, wood, and water (tiṇakaṭṭhodaka) refer to: grass brought and kept in many places for the fodder of elephants, horses, etc., as well as for roofing houses; wood brought and kept for building houses and for cooking; and water brought in by machines and stored in ponds. These materials are well-collected and stored in advance in various places. This is for the delight and enjoyment of the city dwellers.
183:
“Aparitassāya” means for the purpose of preventing those dangers from arising. “Sāliyavaka” means various kinds of rice and barley. “Tilamuggamāsāparanna” means sesame, mung beans, black grams, and other remaining grains.

Now, although the Tathāgata has no business in a city, this simile is brought forth with the intention of showing the noble disciple who is like a city, the seven qualities which are like the city’s requisites, and the four jhānas which are like the four kinds of food, and then concluding the discourse by establishing Arahantship in eleven places. Therefore, to reveal that teaching, the passage beginning with “Even so...” (evam-eva kho) is commenced. Therein, “saddhammehi” means with good qualities. “Saddho” (faithful) means being endowed with conviction-faith (okappaṇasaddhā) and direct-realization-faith (paccakkhasaddhā). Among them, the faith that arises in performing meritorious deeds such as giving and virtue, believing in their fruits, is called okappaṇasaddhā. The faith attained through the Path is called paccakkhasaddhā. It is also called pasādasaddhā (faith of devotion). Its analysis should be understood through its characteristics and so on.

According to the words, “O Great King, faith has the characteristic of aspiring (sampakkhandana) and the characteristic of clarifying (sampasādana),” this is indeed the characteristic of faith. The point taught in the manner beginning with, “Bhikkhus, a person of faith and devotion is to be known by three grounds. What three? He desires to see those who are virtuous,” is called the sign (nimitta) of faith. The words, “What is the nutriment of faith? It should be said: hearing the True Dhamma (saddhammassavana),” refer to its nutriment (āhāra). The point, “Bhikkhus, for a monk who has gone forth through faith, this is the practice in accordance with the Dhamma (anudhamma): that he dwells with much disenchantment (nibbidā) regarding form,” is called the anudhamma of faith. In various suttas such as: “Faith binds the provisions,” “Splendor is the dwelling place of wealth,” “Faith is a man’s partner,” “By faith one crosses the flood,” “Faith is the seed, austerity the rain,” and “The Great Elephant, the Buddha, has faith as his hand (trunk) and equanimity as his white tusks,” the Blessed One has revealed the various natures of faith due to its similarity to a bundle of provisions and so forth. However, in this Nagarūpama Sutta, faith is shown as being like a gate-pillar (esikāthambha) because of its unshakeable and well-established nature.

“Saddhesikော” means that the noble disciple abandons the unwholesome by making faith his gate-pillar; this method should be applied to all terms. Indeed, in this context, through conscience (hiri) and moral dread (ottappa), restraint in the three doors is accomplished, and that restraint [constitutes] the fourfold purity of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla)...
184:
Thus, in this sutta, it should be understood that the pinnacle of the teaching is reached by incorporating the fruit of Arahantship into the eleven instances.

## 4. Dhammaññūsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, 'knows the time' (kālaṃ jānāti) means knowing the appropriate and suitable time. 'This is the time for recitation' (uddesa) means this is the time for learning the word of the Buddha. 'The time for inquiry' (paripucchā) means the time for discerning what is meaningful and what is not, and what is a cause and what is not. 'The time for application' (yoga) means the time for applying oneself to the practice of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna). 'The time for seclusion' (paṭisallāna) means the time for dwelling in solitude, for being alone. 'Practicing in accordance with the Dhamma' (dhammānudhammapappaṭipanna) means practicing the preliminary path of insight (vipassanā) which is suitable for the nine supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma). 'Monks, in this way a monk is one who knows the differences between individuals' (puggalaparoparaññū) means that in this way, a monk is capable of knowing the sharpness or dullness of individuals relative to one another.

## 5. Pāricchattakasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, 'fallen leaves' (pannapalāsa) means having leaves that have fallen. 'Budding' (jālakajāta) means having a well-formed network of leaves and flowers. Indeed, the network of leaves and the network of flowers of that Pāricchattaka tree emerge simultaneously. 'Distinctly budding' (khārakajāta) means being endowed with a network of leaves and flowers that are individually well-formed and well-distributed. 'In bud' (kuṭumulakajāta) means having well-formed buds. 'In full bud' (korakajāta) means being endowed with flowers that have not yet opened, which have large interiors and open edges. 'In full bloom' (sabbapāliphulla) means being well-bloomed in every way. 'For four divine months' means four months by the lifespan of the devas. By human calculation, however, those four months are twelve thousand years. 'They enjoy themselves' (paricārenti) means they exercise their sense faculties here and there; it means they play and delight.

'Pervaded by radiance' means that much of the area is pervaded by the radiance of the Pāricchattaka flowers. The radiance of those flowers is like that of the rising sun; the leaves are the size of parasols, and inside there is pollen the size of a large container. When the Pāricchattaka tree is in bloom, there is no need for climbing, nor for taking a hook to bend the branches, nor for a flower basket to carry the flowers. The wind that cuts the stalks arises and cuts the flowers from their stalks; the wind that receives them catches them; the wind that brings them in carries them into the Sudhamma assembly hall of the devas; the wind that sweeps removes the old flowers; and the wind that spreads them out arranges the petals and filaments beautifully. In the center...
186:
## 7. Bhāvanāsutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, 'ananuyuttassa' refers to one who dwells without applying effort or exertion. With the words, "Monks, just as a hen's eggs...", he speaks of two types of similes by way of the dark side (unwholesome) and the light side (wholesome). Among these two, the dark side simile does not complete the meaning, while the other (the light side simile) does; therefore, only the meaning of the light side simile should be understood. 'Seyyathā' is a particle in the sense of a simile. 'Api' is in the sense of making something clear. By both of these, the meaning "Monks, just as..." is shown. Regarding "a hen's eggs, whether eight, ten, or twelve," although a hen's eggs may be fewer or more than the stated number, this is said for the sake of smooth speech. Only when said thus is speech considered smooth in the world. 'Tānassu' means "if those eggs should be."

"Well-sat upon by the hen" means well-sat upon by that mother hen spreading her wings and lying over those eggs. "Well-steamed" means well-steamed all around, or warmed, by letting them receive heat from time to time. "Well-prepared" means well-prepared all around from time to time, meaning having been made to receive the scent of the hen.

"If to that hen..." means even if that hen, while being diligent by performing these three actions, does not have such a wish arise. Nevertheless, those chicks are capable of breaking out of the eggshell safely in the manner described. This is because those eggs, being protected by the hen through these three modes, do not become rotten. The moist sap within those eggs also dries up, the shell becomes thin, the tips of the claws and the beak become hard, and they reach maturity on their own. Because the shell is thin, the light from outside becomes apparent inside; therefore, with the desire to come out, thinking, "Indeed, we have slept for a long time in a cramped place with our hands and feet curled; now we see light outside, and here we shall live happily," they kick the shell with their feet and stretch their necks, and then that shell breaks into two. Then those chicks, shaking their wings and chirping in accordance with that moment, indeed come out. Having come out, they wander about, beautifying the village fields.
187:
"Evameva kho" is the application of the simile. That meaning should be understood by comparison thus: Just as that hen performs the three actions such as sitting on the eggs, the time when this monk is devoted to meditation (bhāvanā) should be understood. Just as the eggs do not rot because the hen completes the three actions, the non-decline of insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) for the monk devoted to meditation by completing the three types of contemplation (anupassanā) should be understood. Just as the hen performs the three actions and the moist sap of the eggs dries up, the drying up of the moisture of craving (taṇhā) that follows the three realms of existence for that monk by completing the three types of contemplation should be understood. Just as the eggshells become thin, the thinning of the monk's eggshell of ignorance (avijjāṇḍakosa) should be understood. Just as the tips of the claws and beaks of the chicks become firm, the sharpness, toughness, extreme clarity, and courage of the monk's insight knowledge should be understood. Just as the time of maturity for the chicks, the time of maturity, growth, and the taking of the "womb" of the monk's insight knowledge should be understood. Just as the time when the chicks break the eggshell with the tips of their claws or with their beaks, shake their wings, and are born safely, the time when that monk, who wanders having taken the "womb" of insight knowledge, obtains suitable weather (utu-sappāya), suitable food (bhojana-sappāya), a suitable person (puggala-sappāya), or suitable hearing of the Dhamma (dhammassavana-sappāya), and while sitting in a single seat, develops insight and reaches Arahantship safely by breaking the eggshell of ignorance with the gradually attained Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga) and shaking the wings of higher knowledge (abhiññā), should be understood.

Furthermore, just as the mother hen, knowing the maturity of the chicks, breaks the eggshell, the Teacher (the Buddha), knowing the maturity of the knowledge of such a monk, also—

"Cut off your own affection, like an autumn lotus with the hand;
Cherish the path of peace, the Nibbāna taught by the Sugata."

By such means, he radiates light and strikes the eggshell of ignorance with a verse. At the end of the verse, that monk breaks the eggshell of ignorance and reaches Arahantship. From then on, just as those chicks wander about beautifying the village fields, this great Arahant also wanders about beautifying the monastery (saṅghārāma), entering the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) with Nibbāna as the object.
188:
Phalagaṇḍa means a carpenter. That carpenter is called a phalagaṇḍa because he lets down the phala, known as a plumb line, and removes the knots (gaṇḍa) of the wood. Vāsijaṭe refers to the place where the handle of the adze is held. For a person who has gone forth, the taints (āsavas) are constantly being exhausted through brief instruction, inquiry, wise attention, and the fulfillment of duties and practices. Even as they are being exhausted, such knowledge does not arise in that monk: "So much was exhausted today, so much was exhausted yesterday." By this simile, the benefits of insight (vipassanā) are illustrated.

Hemantikena means in the winter season. Paṭippassambhanti means they deteriorate from their firm state. Here, the Dispensation (Sāsana) should be understood as the great ocean. The practitioner (yogāvacara) should be understood as the ship. Just as the ship wanders in the great ocean, this monk's wandering and living in the presence of teachers and preceptors during the period before completing five years [of monkhood] should be understood. Just as the bindings of the ship rot due to the water of the great ocean, the thinning of the fetters (saṃyojanas) due to the monk's brief instruction, inquiry, etc., should be understood. Just as when the ship is hauled up onto dry land, the time when the monk, freed from dependence (nissaya), takes up a meditation subject and lives in the forest should be understood. Just as there is drying by wind and sun during the day, the drying up of the moisture of craving (taṇhā) by insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) should be understood. Just as there is wetting by dew at night, the wetting of the mind by the joy and gladness (pīti-pāmojja) arisen based on the meditation subject should be understood. Just as the bindings, which are dried and wetted day and night by wind, sun, and dew, become weak, the extreme weakening of the fetters due to insight knowledge and joy and gladness should be understood. The knowledge of the path of arahantship (arahatta-magga-ñāṇa) should be understood as a heavy rain cloud. Just as the interior of the ship rots due to rainwater, the attainment of the fruit of arahantship (arahatta-phala) by the monk developing insight, when the meditation subject becomes clear, having obtained suitable weather etc. on a certain day while sitting in a single cross-legged posture, should be understood. Just as the ship with rotted bindings remains for some time, the Arahant whose fetters are exhausted remaining for the duration of his life while benefiting the multitude should be understood. Just as the rotted ship gradually breaks up and reaches a state where it can no longer be designated, the state of the Arahant whose taints are exhausted, who attains final Nibbāna through the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu) upon the breakup of the aggregates and reaches a state where he can no longer be designated, should be understood. By this simile, the weakening of the fetters is illustrated.
189:
## 8. Aggikkhandhopama Sutta Vaṇṇanā
The eighth sutta is taught along with its origin story. Its origin story has already been explained in detail below in the commentary on the Cūḷacchara Saṅghāta Sutta. "Passatha no" means "passatha nu" (behold!). "Āliṅgitvā" means having embraced. "Upanisīdeyya" means sitting down close by. "Upanipajjeyya" means lying down after approaching. "Ārocayāmi" means I announce. "Paṭivedayāmi" means I inform and speak. "Vālarajjuyā" means with a rope twisted from horsehair or cow-hair. "Paccorasmim" means in the middle of the chest. "Pheṇuddehakāṃ" means causing foam to rise (to surge up). "Attatthaṃ" means one's own welfare, consisting of welfare in the present life, welfare in the future life, and mundane and supramundane welfare. The same method applies to parattha (welfare of others) and ubhayattha (welfare of both). Everything else that should be said in this sutta has already been mentioned in the origin story of the Cūḷacchara Saṅghāta Sutta. After teaching this sutta, the Blessed One continued to teach the Cūḷacchara Saṅghāta Sutta. The ninth sutta has a clear meaning.

## 10. Araka Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, "parittaṃ" means small or little. The life of those beings is indeed small by its own nature, by its duration (moment), and by its stability. It is called "lahukaṃ" because it arises and ceases quickly. "Mantāyaṃ boddhabbaṃ" means it should be understood with wisdom. "Pabbateyyā" means those originating in the mountains. "Hārahārinī" means capable of carrying away things that can be carried away, such as trees, reeds, and bamboos. Everything else has a clear meaning.

## Mahāvagga the Seventh.
## 8. Vinaya Vagga
## 1. Paṭhamavinayadhara Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the eighth vagga, "āpattiṃ jānāti" means knowing an offense as an offense. The same method applies to the remaining terms.
190:
## 2. Commentary on the Second Vinayadhara Sutta
In the second sutta, *svāgatāni* means well-come, that is, well-mastered (memorized by heart). *Suvibhattāni* means well-analyzed by way of sections (categories). *Suppavattīni* means well-functioning in every instance of reflection, firmly mastered. *Suvinicchitāni* means well-determined. *Suttaso* means by way of the Vibhaṅga. *Anubyañjanaso* means by way of the Khandhaka and Parivāra.

## 3. Commentary on the Third Vinayadhara Sutta
In the third sutta, *vinaye kho pana ṭhito hoti* means one who is established in the characteristics of the Vinaya. *Asaṃhīro* means one who cannot be made to give up the view he has taken.

## 9. Commentary on the Satthusāsana Sutta
In the ninth sutta, *eko* means without a companion. *Vūpakaṭṭho* means one who is secluded and distant, both physically from the group and mentally from the defilements. *Appamatto* means one who dwells in non-separation from mindfulness. *Pahitatto* means one whose mind is sent (towards Nibbāna). *Nibbidāya* means for the purpose of disenchantment with the round of suffering. *Virāgāya* means for the purpose of the fading away of lust and so forth. *Nirodhāya* means for the purpose of making (defilements) non-arising. *Vūpasamāya* means for the purpose of the calming and non-arising of defilements. *Abhiññāya* means for the purpose of knowing with higher knowledge by applying the three characteristics. *Sambodhāya* means for the purpose of enlightenment, which is called the Path (Magga). *Nibbānāya* means for the purpose of realizing Nibbāna.

## 10. Commentary on the Adhikaraṇasamatha Sutta
In the tenth sutta, they are called *adhikaraṇasamathas* because they settle legal issues. *Uppannuppannānaṃ* means those that have arisen and arisen. *Adhikaraṇānaṃ* means of these four legal issues: *vivādādhikaraṇa* (disputes), *anuvādādhikaraṇa* (accusations), *āpattādhikaraṇa* (offences), and *kiccādhikaraṇa* (duties). *Samathāya vūpasamāya* means for the purpose of settling and for the purpose of complete settling. These seven *samathas*, from *sammukhāvinaya* to *tiṇavatthāraka*, should be given (applied). The decision regarding these *samathas* should be taken from the Vinaya commentary (Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā). Furthermore, in the Dīgha Nikāya,
191:
In the commentary on the Saṅgīti Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā, Volume 3, Adhikaraṇasamathasattaka-vaṇṇanā), and likewise in the commentary on the Sāmagāma Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya, it has already been explained in detail.

## The Eighth Chapter: Vinaya Vagga

## Manorathapūraṇī, the Commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya
